```yaml
    Properties:
      EnableIAMDatabaseAuthentication: true  # Critical: turns on IAM DB auth for the cluster
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable IAM authentication on an existing RDS/Aurora cluster
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  cluster_identifier                   = "<example_resource_id>"
  iam_database_authentication_enabled = true  # Critical: enables IAM DB auth so the check passes
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases
2. Select the DB Cluster (not the instances)
3. Click Modify
4. In Database authentication, enable IAM database authentication
5. Choose Apply immediately and click Modify cluster
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **IAM database authentication** on supported clusters and enforce **least privilege**. Grant only necessary `rds-db:connect` permissions to specific principals, prefer role-based access for workloads to obtain short-lived tokens, require **TLS**, and deprecate static DB passwords. Pair with auditing and segmentation for **defense in depth**.

aws.rds_cluster_integration_cloudwatch_l.title: RDS cluster has CloudWatch Logs export enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Runtime Behavior Analysis
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.rds_cluster_integration_cloudwatch_l.description: **RDS clusters** running Aurora MySQL, Aurora PostgreSQL, MySQL, or PostgreSQL are assessed for **CloudWatch Logs publishing**, confirming that database logs are exported to a CloudWatch Logs group.
aws.rds_cluster_integration_cloudwatch_l.risk:
Without publishing to CloudWatch, database events lack centralized visibility and retention.
Brute-force, SQL injection, or privilege misuse may go undetected, hindering forensics and response, risking data confidentiality and integrity and delaying recovery.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Enable CloudWatch Logs export for an RDS/Aurora DB cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      Engine: <engine>
      MasterUsername: <example_username>
      MasterUserPassword: <example_password>
      EnableCloudwatchLogsExports:
        - <engine_supported_log_type>  # CRITICAL: Enables at least one supported log type (e.g., 'error' for MySQL or 'postgresql' for PostgreSQL) to pass the check
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform: Enable CloudWatch Logs export for an RDS/Aurora DB cluster
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  engine            = "<engine>"
  master_username   = "<example_username>"
  master_password   = "<example_password>"

  enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports = [
    "<engine_supported_log_type>" # CRITICAL: Enables at least one supported log type (e.g., "error" for MySQL or "postgresql" for PostgreSQL) to pass the check
  ]
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases
2. Select your DB cluster and choose Modify
3. Under Log exports, check at least one supported log type for your engine (e.g., error/general/slowquery/audit for MySQL, postgresql for PostgreSQL)
4. Choose Continue, then Apply immediately, and click Modify cluster
remediation.recommendationText:
Publish RDS/Aurora logs to **CloudWatch Logs** and centralize analysis.
Select appropriate types (e.g., `error`, `general`, `slowquery`, `audit`), define retention, and create alarms. Limit log access with **least privilege** and integrate with SIEM for defense-in-depth monitoring.

aws.rds_cluster_minor_version_upgrade_en.title: RDS cluster has automatic minor version upgrades enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/Patch Management
Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.rds_cluster_minor_version_upgrade_en.description:
**RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters** are configured for **automatic minor engine upgrades** via `auto_minor_version_upgrade`.

The evaluation checks these clusters to see if this setting is enabled so preferred minor releases are applied during the maintenance window.
aws.rds_cluster_minor_version_upgrade_en.risk: Without automatic minor upgrades, clusters can miss **security patches**, enabling exploitation of known flaws (confidentiality). Unfixed defects may corrupt data (**integrity**) or trigger crashes and failovers (**availability**). Emergency patching raises downtime and operational risk.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation snippet to enable automatic minor version upgrades on an RDS DB cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      AutoMinorVersionUpgrade: true  # Critical: enables automatic minor engine version upgrades to pass the check
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform snippet to enable automatic minor version upgrades on an RDS DB cluster
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  cluster_identifier         = "<example_resource_id>"
  auto_minor_version_upgrade = true  # Critical: enables automatic minor engine version upgrades to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases
2. Select your Multi-AZ DB cluster
3. Click Modify
4. Set Auto minor version upgrade to Enabled
5. Click Continue, then Modify cluster
remediation.recommendationText: Enable `auto_minor_version_upgrade` on **RDS Multi-AZ clusters** and align updates with approved maintenance windows. Validate changes in non-production, and document any exceptions with a strict manual patch cadence. This strengthens **defense in depth** and improves **availability**.

aws.rds_cluster_multi_az.title: RDS cluster has Multi-AZ enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.rds_cluster_multi_az.description: **RDS DB clusters** are assessed for deployment across **multiple Availability Zones** (*Multi-AZ*), verifying that redundant instances exist to support **automatic failover** instead of a single-AZ configuration.
aws.rds_cluster_multi_az.risk: A **single-AZ cluster** is a single point of failure. AZ outages, instance/storage faults, or maintenance can cause extended **downtime**, failed transactions, and worse **RTO/RPO**. Without cross-AZ replicas, recovery may require restores, increasing outage duration and risking service disruption and data consistency impacts.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: create an RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster (non-Aurora)
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      Engine: mysql  # CRITICAL: using mysql/postgres with the properties below creates a Multi-AZ DB cluster
      DBClusterInstanceClass: db.r6g.large  # CRITICAL: required to make it a Multi-AZ DB cluster (creates 1 writer + 2 readers across AZs)
      AllocatedStorage: 100  # CRITICAL: required for Multi-AZ DB clusters
      Iops: 1000             # CRITICAL: required for Multi-AZ DB clusters
      StorageType: io1       # CRITICAL: required for Multi-AZ DB clusters
      MasterUsername: <USERNAME>
      MasterUserPassword: <PASSWORD>
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform: create an RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster (non-Aurora)
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  cluster_identifier         = "<example_resource_id>"
  engine                     = "mysql"           # CRITICAL: mysql/postgres with the lines below creates a Multi-AZ DB cluster
  db_cluster_instance_class  = "db.r6g.large"    # CRITICAL: makes this a Multi-AZ DB cluster (1 writer + 2 readers across AZs)
  storage_type               = "io1"             # CRITICAL: required for Multi-AZ DB clusters
  allocated_storage          = 100                # CRITICAL: required for Multi-AZ DB clusters
  iops                       = 1000               # CRITICAL: required for Multi-AZ DB clusters
  master_username            = "<USERNAME>"
  master_password            = "<PASSWORD>"
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS console, go to RDS > Databases > Create database
2. Engine: select MySQL or PostgreSQL
3. Under Availability and durability, select Multi-AZ DB cluster
4. Enter DB cluster identifier and master credentials
5. Choose a DB instance class and create the database
6. Migrate data to this new Multi-AZ DB cluster and switch your applications to its endpoint
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **Multi-AZ** for production DB clusters to ensure cross-AZ redundancy and **automatic failover**. Choose a model that meets your SLA (one standby or two readable standbys; Aurora spans 3 AZs). Place subnets in distinct AZs, implement connection retries, and regularly test failover to validate **RTO/RPO** and readiness.

aws.rds_cluster_non_default_port.title: RDS cluster uses a non-default port for its database engine
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Network Reachability
TTPs/Discovery
aws.rds_cluster_non_default_port.description:
**RDS DB clusters** are assessed for use of a **non-default database port**.

Evaluation focuses on whether the cluster listens on the engine's well-known default port (e.g., `3306`, `5432`, `1433`, `1521`, `50000`) or on a custom port.
aws.rds_cluster_non_default_port.risk:
Using a **default DB port** eases discovery via mass scans and banner-grabbing, enabling:
- Engine-specific exploit attempts
- Brute-force/credential-stuffing of logins
- Targeted DDoS on the service

Impacts: **confidentiality** (unauthorized reads), **integrity** (data changes), **availability** (service disruption).

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Set a non-default port on an RDS/Aurora DB cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      Engine: <engine>
      MasterUsername: <username>
      MasterUserPassword: <password>
      Port: <non-default-port>  # Critical: change to a non-default engine port to pass the check
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform: Set a non-default port on an RDS/Aurora DB cluster
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  engine          = "<engine>"
  master_username = "<username>"
  master_password = "<password>"
  port            = <non-default-port> # Critical: use a non-default engine port to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases
2. Select your DB cluster (not an individual instance)
3. Click Modify
4. Set Database port to a non-default value for the engine
5. Check Apply immediately
6. Click Continue, then Modify cluster
remediation.recommendationText:
Use a **non-default port** and enforce **least-privilege** network access:
- Allow only approved sources
- Keep databases in private subnets
- Require TLS and strong, centralized auth
- Monitor failed connections

Update application connection strings to the new `port` as part of defense-in-depth.

aws.rds_cluster_protected_by_backup_plan.title: RDS cluster is protected by an AWS Backup plan
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.rds_cluster_protected_by_backup_plan.description: **RDS DB clusters** are covered by an **AWS Backup backup plan** when resource assignments include the cluster, either explicitly, by tags, or via an appropriate resource scope.
aws.rds_cluster_protected_by_backup_plan.risk: Lack of centralized backups enables irreversible **data loss** and **corruption**, reducing **availability** and **integrity**. Accidental deletion, ransomware, or bad changes may become unrecoverable. Weak retention or no immutability undermines rollback and can breach recovery objectives.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: assign RDS clusters to an AWS Backup plan
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupSelection
    Properties:
      BackupPlanId: "<example_backup_plan_id>"
      BackupSelection:
        SelectionName: "rds-clusters"
        IamRoleArn: "arn:aws:iam::<example_account_id>:role/service-role/AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole"
        Resources:
          - "arn:aws:rds:*:*:cluster:*"  # Critical: includes all RDS clusters in the plan to mark them protected
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Assign RDS clusters to an existing AWS Backup plan
resource "aws_backup_selection" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name         = "rds-clusters"
  plan_id      = "<example_backup_plan_id>"
  iam_role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::<example_account_id>:role/service-role/AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole"

  resources = [
    "arn:aws:rds:*:*:cluster:*" # Critical: includes all RDS clusters in the plan to pass the check
  ]
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Backup console, go to Settings > Service opt-in and enable RDS if it is not enabled.
2. Go to Backup plans and select an existing plan (create a minimal plan if none exists).
3. Click Assign resources.
4. Set a name and choose IAM role: AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole.
5. Under Resources, choose By resource ID and select the target RDS DB cluster (or use the ARN), then click Assign resources.
6. The cluster now appears as protected by the backup plan.
remediation.recommendationText: Include RDS clusters in an **AWS Backup backup plan**. Apply **defense in depth**: define schedules and retention, enable immutable vault controls and cross-Region copies, use tags for consistent coverage, enforce **least privilege** for backup roles, and regularly test restores to validate RPO/RTO.

aws.rds_cluster_storage_encrypted.title: RDS cluster storage is encrypted
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.rds_cluster_storage_encrypted.description: **RDS DB clusters** are assessed for **encryption at rest** via AWS KMS. It determines whether cluster storage-and related artifacts like automated backups and snapshots-are encrypted with a KMS key.
aws.rds_cluster_storage_encrypted.risk: Unencrypted clusters expose data on disk, logs, and snapshots to unauthorized reading if storage or backups are obtained. This compromises **confidentiality**, enables offline exfiltration from leaked snapshots, and can widen blast radius during incidents and migrations.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Create an encrypted RDS/Aurora DB cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      Engine: <ENGINE>
      MasterUsername: <MASTER_USERNAME>
      MasterUserPassword: <MASTER_PASSWORD>
      StorageEncrypted: true  # Critical: enables encryption at rest for the cluster
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform: Create an encrypted RDS/Aurora DB cluster
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  engine          = "<ENGINE>"
  master_username = "<MASTER_USERNAME>"
  master_password = "<MASTER_PASSWORD>"
  storage_encrypted = true  # Critical: enables encryption at rest for the cluster
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases > Create database
2. Select your engine (Aurora or Multi-AZ DB cluster)
3. In the configuration, enable Storage encryption (Enable encryption)
4. Leave the KMS key as default (aws/rds or aws/aurora) unless you require a custom key
5. Create the cluster, migrate traffic, then delete the unencrypted cluster
remediation.recommendationText: Create clusters with `StorageEncrypted=true` using **AWS KMS**, preferably **customer-managed keys**. Apply **least privilege** to key usage, enable rotation and monitoring, and separate key administration from DB operations. Ensure snapshots and cross-account copies remain encrypted for **defense in depth**.

aws.rds_instance_backup_enabled.title: RDS instance has backup retention period greater than 0 days
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
Effects/Data Destruction
aws.rds_instance_backup_enabled.description: **RDS DB instances** are evaluated for **automated backups** by confirming the backup retention period is greater than `0` days, indicating point-in-time recovery is configured.
aws.rds_instance_backup_enabled.risk:
Without automated backups, you lose **point-in-time recovery**, impacting **availability** and **integrity**.

Accidental deletes, destructive queries, or compromised accounts can cause unrecoverable data loss and prolonged outages, preventing reliable rollback during incidents.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: enable automated backups on an RDS instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceClass: db.t3.micro
      Engine: mysql
      AllocatedStorage: 20
      MasterUsername: admin
      MasterUserPassword: <example_password>
      BackupRetentionPeriod: 1  # CRITICAL: Enables automated backups (>0 days)
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform: enable automated backups on an RDS instance
resource "aws_db_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  allocated_storage      = 20
  engine                 = "mysql"
  instance_class         = "db.t3.micro"
  username               = "admin"
  password               = "<example_password>"
  backup_retention_period = 1  # CRITICAL: Enables automated backups (>0 days)
}
```
remediation.other:
1. Open the AWS Management Console and go to RDS > Databases
2. Select the target DB instance and click Modify
3. In Backup section, set Backup retention period to 1 day (or more)
4. Check Apply immediately
5. Click Continue (if shown) and then Modify DB instance
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable **automated backups** with retention > `0` aligned to RPO/RTO. Regularly test restores to validate **PITR**.

Apply **least privilege** to backup access, encrypt snapshots, and replicate critical backups to separate locations for **defense in depth** and resilient recovery.

aws.rds_instance_certificate_expiration.title: RDS instance SSL/TLS certificate has more than 3 months of validity remaining
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Patch Management
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.rds_instance_certificate_expiration.description: **RDS DB instances** are evaluated for **server certificate validity** windows, including default and **customer-managed certificates**. Certificates **expired** or **approaching expiration** (e.g., `<1 month`, `<3 months`, `3-6 months`, `>6 months`) are identified using the certificate `valid_till` date.
aws.rds_instance_certificate_expiration.risk:
Without timely rotation:
- TLS failures block DB connections, impacting **availability**
- Bypassed or weak validation enables **MITM**, risking **confidentiality** and **integrity**
- Emergency changes increase **operational risk** and error rates

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: update RDS instance CA to a current certificate
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      CACertificateIdentifier: rds-ca-rsa2048-g1  # CRITICAL: rotates to a valid CA to restore >3 months certificate validity
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Set a current CA on the RDS instance
resource "aws_db_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  identifier          = "<example_resource_id>"
  ca_cert_identifier  = "rds-ca-rsa2048-g1"  # CRITICAL: rotates to a valid CA to ensure certificate validity >3 months
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases and select the DB instance
2. Click Modify
3. In Connectivity (or Certificate authority), select rds-ca-rsa2048-g1
4. Check Apply immediately
5. Click Continue (if shown) and then Modify DB instance
remediation.recommendationText:
Establish a **certificate lifecycle** for RDS:
- Rotate server/CA certs well before expiry; avoid pinned or outdated CAs
- Keep client trust stores current and enforce TLS with validation
- Monitor expiry and automate alerts/rotation
- For custom certs, apply **least privilege**, **separation of duties**, and periodic key rotation; test changes

aws.rds_instance_copy_tags_to_snapshots.title: RDS DB instance has copy tags to snapshots enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
aws.rds_instance_copy_tags_to_snapshots.description:
**RDS DB instances** are assessed for propagating instance tags to their **DB snapshots** using `CopyTagsToSnapshot`.

*Aurora engines manage this at the cluster level and aren't evaluated per instance.*
aws.rds_instance_copy_tags_to_snapshots.risk: Snapshots without inherited tags lose ownership, environment, and sensitivity context, degrading visibility and governance. Missing metadata weakens **ABAC**, cost allocation, and lifecycle policies, enabling unintended backup access, orphaned snapshots, and retention drift that impact confidentiality and availability.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: enable copying tags to snapshots on an RDS DB instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      CopyTagsToSnapshot: true  # Critical: ensures DB instance tags are copied to snapshots
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases and select the non-Aurora DB instance
2. Click Modify
3. Under Additional configuration, enable Copy tags to snapshots
4. Check Apply immediately and click Modify DB instance
remediation.recommendationText: Enable `CopyTagsToSnapshot` on non-Aurora RDS instances so snapshots inherit required metadata. Establish a consistent **tag taxonomy** and automate enforcement to support **least privilege** via ABAC, cost tracking, and retention controls. For Aurora, configure tag copy at the cluster level.

aws.rds_instance_critical_event_subscrip.title: RDS instance event subscription is enabled for maintenance, configuration change, and failure categories
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
aws.rds_instance_critical_event_subscrip.description:
**RDS event subscriptions** for DB instances are assessed for coverage of the critical categories `maintenance`, `configuration change`, and `failure`.

The evaluation looks for enabled `db-instance` subscriptions and confirms these categories are included or that all events are selected.
aws.rds_instance_critical_event_subscrip.risk: Without these notifications, critical DB events go unseen, undermining **availability** and **integrity**. Missed outages, unexpected restarts, or silent parameter changes can delay response, prolong downtime, corrupt data flows, and leave misconfigurations unaddressed.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: RDS DB instance event subscription
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::EventSubscription
    Properties:
      SnsTopicArn: <sns-topic-arn>           # critical: SNS topic to receive notifications
      SourceType: db-instance                # critical: subscribe to DB instance events
      EventCategories:                       # critical: required categories for PASS
        - maintenance
        - configuration change
        - failure
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform: RDS DB instance event subscription
resource "aws_db_event_subscription" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name            = "<example_resource_name>"
  sns_topic       = "<sns-topic-arn>"
  source_type     = "db-instance"                           # critical: DB instance events
  event_categories = ["maintenance", "configuration change", "failure"]  # critical: required categories
}
```
remediation.other:
1. Open the AWS Console and go to RDS
2. In the left menu, select Event subscriptions > Create event subscription
3. Send notifications to: select an existing SNS topic (<sns-topic-arn>)
4. Source type: choose Instances
5. Event categories: select Maintenance, Configuration change, and Failure
6. Create the subscription
remediation.recommendationText:
Establish and sustain **RDS event subscriptions** for `db-instance` that include `maintenance`, `configuration change`, and `failure`.
- Deliver to monitored channels (ticketing/chat/paging)
- Enforce **least privilege** on topics
- Test alert delivery and runbooks
- Periodically review coverage across Regions

aws.rds_instance_default_admin.title: RDS instance does not use the default master username (admin or postgres)
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
TTPs/Credential Access
aws.rds_instance_default_admin.description: **RDS DB instances** are evaluated for use of a **custom administrator username**. The finding identifies instances or clusters where the admin user matches common defaults like `admin` or `postgres` (checked at the instance or cluster level).
aws.rds_instance_default_admin.risk: Using a predictable admin name enables **password spraying**, **credential stuffing**, and username **enumeration**. A successful login can expose data (**confidentiality**), allow tampering (**integrity**), and disrupt service (**availability**). Defaults also attract automated scans targeting known usernames.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Create an RDS instance with a non-default master username
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      Engine: mysql
      DBInstanceClass: db.t3.micro
      AllocatedStorage: 20
      MasterUsername: <non_default_username>  # Critical: use a custom admin username (not "admin" or "postgres")
      MasterUserPassword: <example_password>
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform: Create an RDS instance with a non-default master username
resource "aws_db_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  engine            = "mysql"
  instance_class    = "db.t3.micro"
  allocated_storage = 20
  username          = "<non_default_username>" # Critical: custom admin username (not "admin" or "postgres")
  password          = "<example_password>"
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases and click Create database
2. Choose your engine and select Standard create
3. In Settings, set Master username to a value that is not "admin" or "postgres"
4. Complete creation and note the new endpoint
5. Migrate data from the old instance to the new one (e.g., dump/restore or replication)
6. Update applications to use the new endpoint, then delete the old instance
7. If the instance is part of an Aurora cluster, create a new cluster with a non-default master username and migrate to it
remediation.recommendationText:
Adopt a **unique, non-default admin username** for each database and avoid enabling default accounts.
- Enforce **least privilege** with separate admin and app users
- Use strong, rotated secrets in a manager and prefer **IAM DB authentication**
- Restrict network exposure and audit authentication activity

aws.rds_instance_deletion_protection.title: RDS instance has deletion protection enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
Effects/Data Destruction
aws.rds_instance_deletion_protection.description: **RDS DB instances** are assessed for **deletion protection**. If an instance belongs to an Aurora cluster, the setting is evaluated at the cluster level; otherwise, it is evaluated on the instance itself.
aws.rds_instance_deletion_protection.risk: Without **deletion protection**, a user or pipeline can delete a database in one action, causing immediate loss of availability and possible data loss if backups are stale or missing. This heightens exposure to insider misuse, compromised credentials, or faulty automation, increasing recovery time and cost.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: enable deletion protection
Resources:
  <example_db_instance_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DeletionProtection: true  # Critical: enables deletion protection for standalone instances

  <example_db_cluster_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      DeletionProtection: true  # Critical: enables deletion protection at cluster level (required for Aurora members)
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS console, go to RDS > Databases
2. For a standalone DB instance: select the instance > Modify > enable Deletion protection > Continue > Apply immediately > Modify DB instance
3. For an Aurora/clustered instance: switch to the cluster (Writer) > Modify > enable Deletion protection > Continue > Apply immediately > Modify cluster
remediation.recommendationText: Enable `deletion protection` on production RDS instances and Aurora clusters. Enforce **least privilege** for delete/modify actions and require change control to disable protection. Use **defense in depth** with reliable backups and tested restores to limit impact if a deletion occurs.

aws.rds_instance_deprecated_engine_versi.title: RDS instance uses a supported engine version
type: Software and Configuration Checks/Patch Management
Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
aws.rds_instance_deprecated_engine_versi.description: **RDS DB instances** use a **supported, non-deprecated engine version** for MariaDB, MySQL, or PostgreSQL. The instance's `engine` and `engine_version` are evaluated against versions currently supported in the region.
aws.rds_instance_deprecated_engine_versi.risk:
Deprecated engine versions lack security fixes and support, enabling exploitation of known flaws impacting **confidentiality** and **integrity**. **Availability** can suffer from forced maintenance or failed upgrades.
- Unpatched CVEs
- TLS/client incompatibilities
- Replication or backup/restore issues

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: upgrade RDS engine version for an existing instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceIdentifier: <example_resource_id>
      Engine: <engine>
      DBInstanceClass: db.t3.micro
      EngineVersion: <SUPPORTED_ENGINE_VERSION>  # CRITICAL: move to a supported engine version
      AllowMajorVersionUpgrade: true             # CRITICAL: required if upgrading major version
      ApplyImmediately: true                     # CRITICAL: apply change now to pass the check
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Upgrade RDS engine version
resource "aws_db_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  identifier         = "<example_resource_id>"
  engine             = "<engine>"
  instance_class     = "db.t3.micro"
  allocated_storage  = 20

  engine_version               = "<SUPPORTED_ENGINE_VERSION>"  # CRITICAL: use a supported version
  allow_major_version_upgrade  = true                           # CRITICAL: needed for major upgrades
  apply_immediately            = true                           # CRITICAL: apply now to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases
2. Select the DB instance
3. Click Modify
4. Under DB engine version, select a supported version
5. If moving to a new major version, check Allow major version upgrade
6. Check Apply immediately
7. Click Continue, then Modify DB instance
remediation.recommendationText:
Standardize on **supported engine versions** and keep them current.
- Plan and test upgrades; back up and define rollback
- Enable `AutoMinorVersionUpgrade` where acceptable
- Monitor deprecation notices and upgrade before EoS
- Enforce **least privilege** to limit blast radius during incidents

aws.rds_instance_enhanced_monitoring_ena.title: RDS instance has enhanced monitoring enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Runtime Behavior Analysis
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.rds_instance_enhanced_monitoring_ena.description: **RDS DB instances** are evaluated for **Enhanced Monitoring** being enabled, which publishes real-time **OS-level metrics** (CPU, memory, disk, network) to CloudWatch Logs for each instance.
aws.rds_instance_enhanced_monitoring_ena.risk:
Without **Enhanced Monitoring**, you lack **real-time OS telemetry**, delaying detection of resource saturation and abnormal activity.

This raises MTTR and risks **availability** impacts (timeouts, failovers), reduces **integrity** assurance during incidents, and weakens forensic visibility.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: enable Enhanced Monitoring on an existing RDS instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceIdentifier: <example_resource_id>
      MonitoringRoleArn: <monitoring_role_arn>   # CRITICAL: IAM role RDS uses to publish OS metrics to CloudWatch Logs
      MonitoringInterval: 60                     # CRITICAL: >0 enables Enhanced Monitoring (seconds)
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable Enhanced Monitoring on an existing RDS instance
resource "aws_db_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  # ...existing required configuration...
  monitoring_role_arn = "<monitoring_role_arn>"  # CRITICAL: Role for publishing OS metrics
  monitoring_interval = 60                        # CRITICAL: >0 enables Enhanced Monitoring (seconds)
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases and select the DB instance
2. Click Modify
3. In Monitoring, check Enable Enhanced Monitoring and set Granularity to any non-zero value (e.g., 60 seconds)
4. Set Monitoring role to Default (creates rds-monitoring-role) or select an existing role
5. Click Continue, then Modify DB instance to apply
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **Enhanced Monitoring** on RDS, using a `>0s` collection interval aligned to workload and cost. Assign a **least-privilege** role for log delivery, and apply **defense in depth** by centralizing logs, setting **alerts** on key OS metrics, and defining **retention** to support incident response and trend analysis.

aws.rds_instance_event_subscription_para.title: RDS DB parameter group event subscription is enabled and subscribes to configuration change events or all categories
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.rds_instance_event_subscription_para.description: **RDS event subscriptions** for **DB parameter groups** notify on `configuration change` events (or all categories) when the subscription is enabled
aws.rds_instance_event_subscription_para.risk: Missing alerts on parameter changes erodes visibility. Attackers or mistakes can lower TLS requirements, disable auditing, or relax auth, enabling data exposure (**confidentiality**), unauthorized writes (**integrity**), or outages from unsafe settings (**availability**).

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::EventSubscription
    Properties:
      SnsTopicArn: <sns-topic-arn>
      SourceType: db-parameter-group  # Critical: targets DB parameter group events
      EventCategories:
        - configuration change        # Critical: subscribes to configuration change events
      Enabled: true                   # Critical: subscription must be enabled
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "aws_db_event_subscription" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name             = "<example_resource_name>"
  sns_topic        = "<sns-topic-arn>"
  source_type      = "db-parameter-group"          # Critical: target DB parameter groups
  event_categories = ["configuration change"]       # Critical: include configuration change events
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to Amazon RDS > Event subscriptions
2. Click Create event subscription
3. Send notifications to: select an existing SNS topic
4. Source type: Parameter groups
5. Event categories: select Configuration change (or choose All event categories)
6. Ensure Enabled is On
7. Click Create
remediation.recommendationText:
Create and maintain an **SNS-backed event subscription** for **DB parameter groups** that includes `configuration change` (or all) and keep it enabled.

- Apply **least privilege** to SNS topics
- Route to on-call/SIEM and test alerts
- Enforce change control and monitoring across all Regions

aws.rds_instance_event_subscription_secu.title: RDS event subscription for DB security groups is enabled for configuration change and failure events
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.rds_instance_event_subscription_secu.description: **RDS event subscriptions** are evaluated for **database security group** events. The check expects an enabled subscription with source type `db-security-group` that includes the `configuration change` and `failure` event categories.
aws.rds_instance_event_subscription_secu.risk: Missing alerts on **security group changes** or **failures** reduces visibility and slows response. Undetected rule changes can expose databases, while unnoticed failures prolong outages, impacting **confidentiality** and **availability** through unauthorized access or service disruption.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::EventSubscription
    Properties:
      SnsTopicArn: <SNS_TOPIC_ARN>
      SourceType: db-security-group  # Critical: subscribe to DB security group events
      EventCategories:               # Critical: required categories
        - configuration change
        - failure
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "aws_db_event_subscription" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name            = "<example_resource_name>"
  sns_topic       = "<SNS_TOPIC_ARN>"
  source_type     = "db-security-group"        # Critical: DB security group events
  event_categories = ["configuration change", "failure"]  # Critical: required categories
}
```
remediation.other:
1. Open the AWS Console > RDS > Event subscriptions
2. Click Create event subscription
3. Set Name to <SUBSCRIPTION_NAME> and select an existing SNS topic
4. Set Source type to Security group
5. Under Event categories, select Configuration change and Failure
6. Leave Targets as All security groups (no specific IDs)
7. Ensure Enabled is On and click Create
remediation.recommendationText: Create or update an **RDS event subscription** for source type `db-security-group` including `configuration change` and `failure`. Route alerts to monitored channels, restrict topic access (**least privilege**), integrate with **incident response**, and enforce change control and **separation of duties** for security group updates.

aws.rds_instance_extended_support.title: RDS instance is not enrolled in RDS Extended Support
type: Software and Configuration Checks/Patch Management
Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
aws.rds_instance_extended_support.description: **RDS DB instances** are evaluated for enrollment in Amazon RDS Extended Support. The check fails if `EngineLifecycleSupportis` set to `open-source-rds-extended-support`, indicating the instance will incur additional charges after standard support ends.
aws.rds_instance_extended_support.risk: DB instances enrolled in RDS Extended Support can incur additional charges after the end of standard support for the running database major version. Remaining on older major versions can also delay necessary upgrades, increasing operational and security risk.

remediation.cli:
aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier <DB_INSTANCE_IDENTIFIER> --engine-version <TARGET_ENGINE_VERSION> --allow-major-version-upgrade --apply-immediately
# For new DB instances created via automation, prevent enrollment by setting the lifecycle option:
aws rds create-db-instance ... --engine-lifecycle-support open-source-rds-extended-support-disabled
remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: upgrade RDS engine version for an existing instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceIdentifier: <example_resource_id>
      Engine: <engine>
      DBInstanceClass: db.t3.micro
      EngineVersion: <SUPPORTED_ENGINE_VERSION>  # CRITICAL: move to a supported engine version
      AllowMajorVersionUpgrade: true             # CRITICAL: required if upgrading major version
      ApplyImmediately: true                     # CRITICAL: apply change now to pass the check
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Upgrade RDS engine version
resource "aws_db_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  identifier         = "<example_resource_id>"
  engine             = "<engine>"
  instance_class     = "db.t3.micro"
  allocated_storage  = 20

  engine_version               = "<SUPPORTED_ENGINE_VERSION>"  # CRITICAL: use a supported version
  allow_major_version_upgrade  = true                           # CRITICAL: needed for major upgrades
  apply_immediately            = true                           # CRITICAL: apply now to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other: If your automation (CloudFormation/Terraform/SDK) creates or restores DB instances, set EngineLifecycleSupport/LifeCycleSupport to open-source-rds-extended-support-disabled where supported, and ensure your upgrade process keeps engines within standard support.
remediation.recommendationText: Upgrade enrolled DB instances to an engine version covered under standard support to stop Extended Support charges. For new DB instances and restores created via automation, explicitly set the engine lifecycle support option to avoid unintended enrollment in RDS Extended Support when that is your policy.

aws.rds_instance_iam_authentication_enab.title: RDS instance has IAM database authentication enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
TTPs/Credential Access
aws.rds_instance_iam_authentication_enab.description: **RDS DB instances** using MySQL, MariaDB, or PostgreSQL engines (including Aurora variants) have **IAM database authentication** enabled at the instance level or, when part of a cluster, evaluated for cluster-level enablement.
aws.rds_instance_iam_authentication_enab.risk:
Absent **IAM-based, short-lived tokens**, databases rely on **static passwords** in code and configs, increasing theft and reuse.

Compromised DB creds enable unauthorized queries, leading to **data exfiltration** and tampering, and weaken **centralized access control** and rotation.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: enable IAM DB authentication on an RDS instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceIdentifier: <example_resource_id>
      EnableIAMDatabaseAuthentication: true  # Critical: enables IAM DB auth to pass the check
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS console, go to RDS > Databases
2. Select the DB instance and choose Modify
3. Under Database authentication, select "Password and IAM database authentication"
4. Choose Apply immediately and click Modify DB instance
5. If the instance is part of an Aurora DB cluster: select the DB cluster instead, choose Modify, enable IAM database authentication, Apply immediately, then Modify
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable **IAM database authentication** for supported engines and apply **least privilege** with scoped IAM policies. Prefer **short-lived tokens** over static DB passwords, enforce TLS, and phase out embedded credentials.

Monitor authentication activity with audit logs for **defense in depth**.

aws.rds_instance_inside_vpc.title: RDS instance is deployed in a VPC
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Network Reachability
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.rds_instance_inside_vpc.description:
**RDS DB instances** are assessed for **VPC placement** by the presence of a `vpc_id` indicating deployment within a VPC.

Instances without this association are treated as outside VPC networking.
aws.rds_instance_inside_vpc.risk: Without VPC isolation, databases may expose internet-reachable endpoints and lack granular network controls. This degrades **confidentiality** and **availability** via scanning/brute force and data exfiltration, and threatens **integrity** through unauthorized connections and lateral movement.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: move RDS instance into a VPC by assigning a DB subnet group
Resources:
  <example_db_subnet_group>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBSubnetGroup
    Properties:
      DBSubnetGroupDescription: "subnets for rds"
      SubnetIds:
        - <example_resource_id>  # CRITICAL: Subnets in the target VPC
        - <example_resource_id>  # CRITICAL: At least two AZs recommended

  <example_db_instance>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBSubnetGroupName: !Ref <example_db_subnet_group>  # CRITICAL: Ensures the DB instance is deployed in a VPC
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Subnet groups and create/select a DB subnet group in the target VPC (with subnets in at least two AZs)
2. Go to RDS > Databases, select the DB instance, click Modify
3. Under Connectivity, set DB subnet group to the VPC subnet group from step 1 (select a VPC security group if prompted)
4. Check Apply immediately and choose Continue > Modify DB instance
remediation.recommendationText: Deploy all RDS instances in a **VPC**, preferably in **private subnets**. Enforce **least privilege** with security groups, network ACLs, and restrictive routing. Use private connectivity (peering, VPN, Direct Connect), avoid public exposure, and apply **defense in depth** through segmentation and monitoring.

aws.rds_instance_integration_cloudwatch_.title: RDS instance exports logs to CloudWatch Logs
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.rds_instance_integration_cloudwatch_.description:
**RDS DB instances** are configured to **publish database logs** to **CloudWatch Logs** (e.g., `error`, `general`, `slowquery`, `audit`).

The evaluation identifies instances that have log exports enabled to a CloudWatch log group.
aws.rds_instance_integration_cloudwatch_.risk: Without centralized RDS logs, database activity lacks visibility, hindering detection and response. Credential misuse, SQL injection, data exfiltration, and privilege abuse may go unnoticed, risking **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Unseen errors and slow queries can lead to outages, impacting **availability**.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceIdentifier: <example_resource_id>
      # Critical: enabling at least one log type exports it to CloudWatch Logs and makes the check PASS
      EnableCloudwatchLogsExports:
        - <log_type>
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "aws_db_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  identifier = "<example_resource_id>"
  # Critical: export at least one supported log type to CloudWatch Logs to pass the check
  enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports = ["<log_type>"]
}
```
remediation.other:
1. Open AWS Console > RDS > Databases
2. Select your DB instance and choose Modify
3. In Log exports, select at least one supported log type (e.g., error/general/slowquery/audit/postgresql/alert)
4. Choose Continue, then Modify DB instance
remediation.recommendationText: Enable export of relevant RDS logs to **CloudWatch Logs** (`error`, `general`, `slowquery`, `audit`) and standardize across engines. Enforce **least privilege** on log access, set retention, and define metrics/alarms for critical patterns. Integrate with a SIEM. Apply **separation of duties** and **defense in depth** to protect log integrity and monitoring.

aws.rds_instance_minor_version_upgrade_e.title: RDS instance has minor version upgrade enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/Patch Management
aws.rds_instance_minor_version_upgrade_e.description: **RDS DB instances** are evaluated for the `auto_minor_version_upgrade` setting that enables **automatic minor engine updates** during maintenance windows.
aws.rds_instance_minor_version_upgrade_e.risk: Without automatic minor upgrades, databases miss **security patches**, leaving known vulnerabilities exploitable and risking **unauthorized data access**. Unapplied fixes can cause **data corruption** and outages, harming **integrity** and **availability**.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Enable auto minor version upgrades on an RDS instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceIdentifier: <example_resource_id>
      DBInstanceClass: db.t3.micro
      Engine: mysql
      MasterUsername: <username>
      MasterUserPassword: <password>
      AllocatedStorage: '20'
      AutoMinorVersionUpgrade: true  # Critical: ensures RDS applies minor engine updates automatically
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable auto minor version upgrades on an RDS instance
resource "aws_db_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  allocated_storage          = 20
  engine                     = "mysql"
  instance_class             = "db.t3.micro"
  username                   = "<username>"
  password                   = "<password>"
  auto_minor_version_upgrade = true  # Critical: turns on automatic minor engine upgrades
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases
2. Select the DB instance and click Modify
3. Find "Auto minor version upgrade" and set it to Enable
4. Click Continue, check Apply immediately, then click Modify DB instance
remediation.recommendationText: Enable `auto_minor_version_upgrade` on RDS instances so minor releases are applied promptly. Use maintenance windows and stage testing to limit impact. Follow **defense in depth** and **least privilege**; keep reliable backups and Multi-AZ to preserve continuity if upgrades require rollback.

aws.rds_instance_multi_az.title: RDS instance has Multi-AZ enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
aws.rds_instance_multi_az.description: **RDS DB instances** are evaluated for **Multi-AZ** configuration, either enabled on the instance or inherited from the associated DB cluster.
aws.rds_instance_multi_az.risk: Without **Multi-AZ**, an Availability Zone or instance failure can cause extended downtime and rely on restores, risking loss of recent writes. This degrades **availability** and may affect **integrity**, interrupting applications and breaching SLAs.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: enable Multi-AZ on an existing RDS DB instance
Resources:
  RDSInstance:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      MultiAZ: true  # Critical: enables Multi-AZ to pass the check
```
remediation.other:
1. Open the AWS Management Console and go to RDS > Databases
2. Select the affected DB instance and click Modify
3. Under Availability & durability, set Multi-AZ deployment to Enabled (create a standby)
4. Check Apply immediately
5. Click Continue, then Modify DB instance
6. Wait until status is Available and Multi-AZ shows Yes
remediation.recommendationText: Apply fault-tolerance and redundancy principles: enable **Multi-AZ** for production RDS workloads. Choose one standby or two readable standbys based on RTO/RPO and performance needs. Regularly test failover, monitor configuration drift, and allow exceptions only with documented, risk-based approval.

aws.rds_instance_no_public_access.title: RDS instance is not publicly exposed to the Internet
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Network Reachability
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark
TTPs/Initial Access
aws.rds_instance_no_public_access.description: **RDS DB instances** are assessed for **internet exposure** using the `PubliclyAccessible` setting, security group ingress to the DB port from any address, and whether subnets are **public**. Instances that combine an internet-facing endpoint, open ingress, and public subnets are identified.
aws.rds_instance_no_public_access.risk:
An internet-reachable database invites:
- Brute-force and vulnerability probing, risking **availability** and **integrity**
- Unauthorized queries and dumps leading to **confidentiality** loss

Compromise can enable **lateral movement** and persistence within the VPC.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: make the RDS instance private
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceIdentifier: <example_resource_id>
      PubliclyAccessible: false  # CRITICAL: disables public access so the instance is not Internet-facing
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS console, go to RDS > Databases and select your DB instance
2. Click Modify
3. In Connectivity (Connectivity & security), set Public access to No (Not publicly accessible)
4. Choose Continue, select Apply immediately (or during the next window), then click Modify DB instance
remediation.recommendationText:
Keep databases private by applying **least privilege** at the network layer:
- Set `PubliclyAccessible` to `false`
- Place instances in private subnets
- Deny `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0` on the DB port
- Expose access via private endpoints, VPN, or an application tier/DB proxy

Adopt **defense in depth** with monitoring and strong auth.

aws.rds_instance_non_default_port.title: RDS instance uses a non-default port for its engine
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Network Reachability
TTPs/Discovery
aws.rds_instance_non_default_port.description: **RDS DB instances** are evaluated for use of a port that differs from the engine's default. Matching an engine with its default port-`3306` (MySQL/MariaDB/Aurora MySQL), `5432` (PostgreSQL/Aurora), `1521` (Oracle), `1433` (SQL Server), `50000` (Db2)-indicates the instance uses the default listener.
aws.rds_instance_non_default_port.risk: Using a **default DB port** increases exposure to broad scans and eases **service fingerprinting**. With weak network controls, attackers can run **credential brute force**, target known **engine exploits**, or trigger **DoS** on the predictable port, threatening confidentiality and availability.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: set a non-default port on an RDS instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      Port: <non-default_port>  # Critical: use a non-default DB engine port to pass the check
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to Amazon RDS > Databases
2. Select the DB instance and click Modify
3. Set "Database port" to a non-default value for the engine (e.g., not 3306, 5432, 1521, 1433, or 50000)
4. Click Continue, then Modify DB instance
remediation.recommendationText:
Use a **non-default DB port** and enforce **defense in depth**:
- Apply **least-privilege** network rules
- Keep databases in **private subnets**; avoid public exposure
- Require strong authentication and audit logging

*Update client connection strings and security rules when the port changes.*

aws.rds_instance_protected_by_backup_pla.title: RDS instance is protected by an AWS Backup plan
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
Effects/Data Destruction
aws.rds_instance_protected_by_backup_pla.description:
**RDS DB instances** (non-Aurora) are included in an **AWS Backup plan**, indicating scheduled backups and retention are applied to the resource.

*Aurora engines are evaluated separately.*
aws.rds_instance_protected_by_backup_pla.risk: Without an **AWS Backup plan**, databases lack assured recovery, degrading **availability** and **integrity**. Likely outcomes: accidental deletion, corruption, or malicious wipes with no recent restore point. Expect missed `RPO/RTO`, extended outages, and data inconsistency after incidents.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: assign an RDS instance to an AWS Backup plan
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupSelection
    Properties:
      BackupPlanId: <example_backup_plan_id>  # CRITICAL: targets the backup plan to protect the instance
      BackupSelection:
        SelectionName: <selection_name>
        IamRoleArn: <example_role_arn>        # CRITICAL: role AWS Backup uses to back up the resource
        Resources:
          - <rds-instance-arn>                # CRITICAL: assigns the RDS instance to the plan
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Assign an RDS instance to an AWS Backup plan
resource "aws_backup_selection" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name         = "<selection_name>"
  plan_id      = "<example_backup_plan_id>"   # CRITICAL: attaches to the backup plan
  iam_role_arn = "<example_role_arn>"         # CRITICAL: role AWS Backup uses
  resources    = ["<rds-instance-arn>"]       # CRITICAL: RDS instance protected by the plan
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, open AWS Backup
2. Go to Settings > Service opt-in and enable Amazon RDS (if not already)
3. Go to Backup plans and select an existing plan (or Create backup plan with defaults)
4. Click Assign resources
5. Enter a name, select an IAM role, and add the RDS instance (by ARN or resource picker)
6. Click Assign resources to save
remediation.recommendationText: Assign all non-Aurora RDS to an **AWS Backup plan** aligned to business `RPO/RTO`. Use **tags** for automatic coverage, define retention and lifecycle, and store backups in **immutable** vaults where possible. Regularly perform restore tests. Enforce **least privilege** and **separation of duties** for backup administration.

aws.rds_instance_storage_encrypted.title: RDS DB instance storage is encrypted at rest
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/NIST 800-53 Controls (USA)
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/NIST CSF Controls (USA)
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/PCI-DSS
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/ISO 27001 Controls
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/HIPAA Controls (USA)
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/GDPR Controls (Europe)
Effects/Data Exposure
aws.rds_instance_storage_encrypted.description: **RDS DB instances** are assessed for **KMS-based encryption at rest** (`StorageEncrypted=true`), covering instance storage and derived artifacts such as snapshots, automated backups, and read replicas.
aws.rds_instance_storage_encrypted.risk: Without **encryption at rest**, database files, snapshots, and automated backups remain in plaintext. An attacker with access to copied snapshots, compromised backups, or underlying storage can read sensitive data, causing loss of **confidentiality** and enabling large-scale exfiltration.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: create an encrypted RDS DB instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceClass: "<instance_class>"
      Engine: "<engine>"
      AllocatedStorage: 20
      MasterUsername: "<username>"
      MasterUserPassword: "<password>"
      StorageEncrypted: true  # CRITICAL: enables encryption at rest so the instance passes the check
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform: create an encrypted RDS DB instance
resource "aws_db_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  engine            = "<engine>"
  instance_class    = "<instance_class>"
  username          = "<username>"
  password          = "<password>"
  allocated_storage = 20

  storage_encrypted = true  # CRITICAL: enables encryption at rest to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases, select the unencrypted DB instance, then choose Actions > Take snapshot.
2. After the snapshot is available, go to Snapshots, select it, choose Actions > Copy snapshot, enable encryption, and select a KMS key (or aws/rds).
3. When the encrypted copy is ready, select it and choose Actions > Restore snapshot to create a new (encrypted) DB instance.
4. Update your application/endpoint to use the new encrypted DB instance.
5. Decommission the old unencrypted instance after cutover.
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **encryption at rest** for all RDS instances. Prefer **customer-managed KMS keys** to control rotation and fine-grained access, applying **least privilege** and **defense in depth**. Restrict key usage, monitor key activity, and manage key lifecycle. Migrate unencrypted instances via encrypted snapshot copy and restore.

aws.rds_instance_transport_encrypted.title: RDS instance or cluster enforces SSL/TLS encryption for client connections
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Network Security
aws.rds_instance_transport_encrypted.description: **RDS DB instances** and **DB clusters** enforce **SSL/TLS** for client connections via parameter groups. The check looks for `rds.force_ssl=1` (PostgreSQL, SQL Server) or `require_secure_transport` enabled (MySQL-family) and identifies databases where encryption enforcement isn't active.
aws.rds_instance_transport_encrypted.risk: Without enforced **TLS**, clients can connect or downgrade to plaintext, exposing credentials and queries to interception. Adversaries can perform **MITM**, steal secrets, and tamper traffic, undermining **confidentiality** and **integrity** and enabling reuse of captured database credentials.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: set required parameter to enforce SSL/TLS
Resources:
  ExampleDBParameterGroupPostgres:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Family: <DB_PARAMETER_FAMILY>
      Description: Enforce SSL/TLS
      Parameters:
        rds.force_ssl: "1"  # Critical: requires SSL/TLS for PostgreSQL/SQL Server instances

  ExampleDBParameterGroupMySQL:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Family: <DB_PARAMETER_FAMILY>
      Description: Enforce SSL/TLS
      Parameters:
        require_secure_transport: "1"  # Critical: requires SSL/TLS for MySQL/MariaDB instances

  ExampleDBClusterParameterGroupAuroraPostgres:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBClusterParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Family: <DB_CLUSTER_PARAMETER_FAMILY>
      Description: Enforce SSL/TLS
      Parameters:
        rds.force_ssl: "1"  # Critical: requires SSL/TLS for Aurora PostgreSQL clusters

  ExampleDBClusterParameterGroupAuroraMySQL:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBClusterParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Family: <DB_CLUSTER_PARAMETER_FAMILY>
      Description: Enforce SSL/TLS
      Parameters:
        require_secure_transport: ON  # Critical: requires SSL/TLS for Aurora MySQL clusters
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Parameter groups
2. For DB instances:
   - Edit the DB parameter group attached to the instance (or create one and attach it)
   - Set rds.force_ssl = 1 for PostgreSQL/SQL Server, or require_secure_transport = 1 for MySQL/MariaDB
   - Save. If the parameter is static, reboot the instance
3. For Aurora clusters:
   - Edit the DB cluster parameter group attached to the cluster (or create one and attach it)
   - Set rds.force_ssl = 1 for Aurora PostgreSQL, or require_secure_transport = ON for Aurora MySQL
   - Save. Reboot instances if changes are pending-reboot
4. Verify the parameter group is associated to the target instance/cluster and status shows the new value applied
remediation.recommendationText:
Enforce transport encryption at the database layer:
- Enable `rds.force_ssl=1` or `require_secure_transport` in parameter groups
- Configure clients to require certificate validation and prevent fallback
- Use current TLS versions and trusted CAs
- Prefer private network access as **defense in depth**

aws.rds_snapshots_encrypted.title: RDS DB instance snapshot or DB cluster snapshot is encrypted
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark
Effects/Data Exposure
aws.rds_snapshots_encrypted.description: **RDS DB snapshots** and **DB cluster snapshots** are evaluated for **encryption at rest**, identifying snapshots created with a KMS key versus unencrypted ones.
aws.rds_snapshots_encrypted.risk: Unencrypted snapshots enable direct access to full database data if backups are leaked, cross-account shared, or stolen. Adversaries can harvest data offline, bypassing network controls, leading to **loss of confidentiality**. Restores from such snapshots propagate the exposure to new instances.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "aws_db_snapshot_copy" "<example_resource_name>" {
  source_db_snapshot_identifier = "<example_resource_id>"
  target_db_snapshot_identifier = "<example_resource_id>-encrypted"
  kms_key_id                    = "<KMS_KEY_ID>" # Critical: encrypts the copied snapshot using the specified KMS key
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Snapshots
2. Select the unencrypted snapshot (for clusters, use the DB cluster snapshots tab)
3. Click Actions > Copy snapshot
4. Check Enable encryption and choose a KMS key
5. Click Copy snapshot and wait for completion
6. After verifying the new encrypted snapshot, delete the original unencrypted snapshot (Actions > Delete snapshot)
remediation.recommendationText: Encrypt all RDS snapshots at rest using **KMS**, preferably **customer-managed keys**. Apply **least privilege** to key usage, enforce encryption via templates and automation, and prevent sharing of unencrypted backups. Use **key rotation**, separation of duties, and ensure copies and cross-account shares remain encrypted.

aws.rds_snapshots_public_access.title: RDS snapshot is not publicly shared
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
Effects/Data Exposure
TTPs/Collection
aws.rds_snapshots_public_access.description:
**RDS DB snapshots** and **DB cluster snapshots** with **public visibility** (shared with `all` AWS accounts) are detected.

Snapshots limited to specific accounts or kept private are identified as restricted.
aws.rds_snapshots_public_access.risk:
Public RDS snapshots expose full database copies to all AWS accounts, risking:
- Loss of confidentiality via data exfiltration (PII, secrets)
- Offline cracking of hashes and schema reconnaissance
- Credential harvesting from dumps enabling lateral movement
This directly compromises confidentiality and fuels targeted attacks.

remediation.other:
1. Open the Amazon RDS console and go to Snapshots
2. Select the public snapshot (DB snapshot or DB cluster snapshot)
3. Click Actions > Share snapshot
4. Set visibility to Private (remove "All" from permissions) and click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Keep **RDS snapshots** and **cluster snapshots** private. Share only with explicit AWS account IDs using **least privilege** and time-bound access.

Enforce guardrails to block `public` visibility, require approvals for sharing, and audit snapshot permissions. Use encryption with strict key policies to control who can restore data.

aws.redshift_cluster_audit_logging.title: Redshift cluster has audit logging enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.redshift_cluster_audit_logging.description: Amazon Redshift clusters are evaluated for **database audit logging** that exports connection, user, and user-activity events to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch.
aws.redshift_cluster_audit_logging.risk: Without audit logs, malicious logins and queries can evade detection, impacting **confidentiality** (data exfiltration), **integrity** (unauthorized user/role changes), and **availability** of investigations due to missing evidence for forensics and incident response.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::Redshift::Cluster
    Properties:
      ClusterType: single-node
      NodeType: dc2.large
      DBName: mydb
      MasterUsername: masteruser
      MasterUserPassword: <PASSWORD>
      # Critical: Enables Redshift audit logging to S3
      LoggingProperties:
        BucketName: <S3_BUCKET_NAME>  # Critical: Required to turn on logging
```
remediation.other:
1. Open the Amazon Redshift console and go to Clusters
2. Select the target cluster and open the Properties tab
3. In Database audit logging, click Edit
4. Enable logging and select an S3 bucket
5. Click Save changes
remediation.recommendationText: Enable comprehensive **Redshift audit logging** and include user-activity events. Centralize logs in a protected destination, enforce **least privilege** access, retention, and immutability. Implement **alerts** for anomalous connections and queries as part of **defense in depth**.

aws.redshift_cluster_automated_snapshot.title: Redshift cluster has automated snapshots enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.redshift_cluster_automated_snapshot.description: **Amazon Redshift clusters** are evaluated for **automated snapshots** being enabled with a retention period `> 0`, confirming that periodic backups are created and retained.
aws.redshift_cluster_automated_snapshot.risk:
Without **automated snapshots**, clusters lack recent recovery points, degrading **availability** and **integrity**.

Accidental deletion, malicious changes, or failed ETL can cause data loss and prolonged recovery, increasing RPO/RTO and limiting effective forensic analysis.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Enable automated snapshots for a Redshift cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::Redshift::Cluster
    Properties:
      ClusterType: single-node
      NodeType: <NODE_TYPE>
      DBName: <DB_NAME>
      MasterUsername: <MASTER_USERNAME>
      MasterUserPassword: <MASTER_PASSWORD>
      AutomatedSnapshotRetentionPeriod: 1  # Critical: enables automated snapshots by retaining them for 1 day
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform: Enable automated snapshots for a Redshift cluster
resource "aws_redshift_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  cluster_identifier = "<example_resource_id>"
  cluster_type       = "single-node"
  node_type          = "<NODE_TYPE>"
  database_name      = "<DB_NAME>"
  master_username    = "<MASTER_USERNAME>"
  master_password    = "<MASTER_PASSWORD>"

  automated_snapshot_retention_period = 1  # Critical: enables automated snapshots by retaining them for 1 day
}
```
remediation.other:
1. Open the AWS Console and go to Amazon Redshift
2. Select your cluster and click Modify
3. Under Backup, set Automated snapshot retention period to 1 (or greater)
4. Click Save changes and apply the modification
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable **automated snapshots** with retention aligned to RPO/RTO. Enforce **least privilege** on snapshot access and use **encryption**. Regularly test restores and monitor backup health.

*For resilience*, replicate snapshots to another Region/account and separate backup administration from data owners.

aws.redshift_cluster_automatic_upgrades.title: Redshift cluster has automatic version upgrade enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/Patch Management
Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
aws.redshift_cluster_automatic_upgrades.description: **Amazon Redshift clusters** have automatic major engine upgrades allowed via `AllowVersionUpgrade` so updates are applied during the maintenance window.
aws.redshift_cluster_automatic_upgrades.risk:
Without automatic upgrades, clusters can run **vulnerable engine versions**, enabling exploits against known flaws.

Attackers may read or tamper data (**confidentiality/integrity**), and unresolved bugs can cause downtime (**availability**). Delayed patching increases exposure window and operational risk.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation to ensure Redshift allows major version upgrades
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::Redshift::Cluster
    Properties:
      ClusterType: single-node
      DBName: <db_name>
      MasterUsername: <master_username>
      MasterUserPassword: <master_user_password>
      NodeType: <node_type>
      AllowVersionUpgrade: true  # Critical: enables automatic major version upgrades during the maintenance window
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Redshift cluster allowing automatic major version upgrades
resource "aws_redshift_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  cluster_identifier = "<example_resource_id>"
  node_type          = "<node_type>"
  master_username    = "<master_username>"
  master_password    = "<master_user_password>"

  allow_version_upgrade = true  # Critical: enables automatic major version upgrades
}
```
remediation.other:
1. Open the Amazon Redshift console
2. Go to Clusters and select your cluster
3. Click Edit (or Edit maintenance settings)
4. Enable "Major version upgrades" (Allow version upgrade)
5. Click Save changes
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable `AllowVersionUpgrade` to keep clusters patched. Use a controlled maintenance window and an appropriate maintenance track; validate upgrades in staging before production.

Align with **secure-by-default** and **defense in depth**; keep tested backups and rollback plans. *Document justified exceptions and review regularly*.

aws.redshift_cluster_encrypted_at_rest.title: Redshift cluster is encrypted at rest
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark
Effects/Data Exposure
aws.redshift_cluster_encrypted_at_rest.description: **Amazon Redshift clusters** use **encryption at rest**. The evaluation inspects the cluster's encryption setting to determine if on-disk data and snapshots are protected with a managed key.
aws.redshift_cluster_encrypted_at_rest.risk: Without **encryption at rest**, data blocks and snapshots can be read if storage media or backups are accessed by unauthorized parties. This compromises **confidentiality**, enabling bulk **data exfiltration** and exposure of sensitive analytics, which can facilitate further compromise.

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Enable at-rest encryption for a Redshift cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::Redshift::Cluster
    Properties:
      ClusterIdentifier: "<example_resource_id>"
      DBName: "<DB_NAME>"
      MasterUsername: "<MASTER_USERNAME>"
      MasterUserPassword: "<MASTER_PASSWORD>"
      NodeType: "<NODE_TYPE>"
      ClusterType: "<CLUSTER_TYPE>"
      Encrypted: true  # Critical: enables encryption at rest to pass the check
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform: Enable at-rest encryption for a Redshift cluster
resource "aws_redshift_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  cluster_identifier = "<example_resource_id>"
  node_type          = "<NODE_TYPE>"
  cluster_type       = "<CLUSTER_TYPE>"
  master_username    = "<MASTER_USERNAME>"
  master_password    = "<MASTER_PASSWORD>"

  encrypted = true  # Critical: enables encryption at rest to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. Open the AWS Management Console and go to Amazon Redshift
2. Choose Clusters, then select your cluster
3. Open the Properties tab > Database configurations > Edit > Edit encryption
4. Select Enable encryption (use AWS-managed or a specific KMS key)
5. Click Save changes
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **encryption at rest** for all clusters and prefer **customer-managed keys** (`CMEK`) for control and auditing. Apply **least privilege** to key usage, rotate keys, and restrict snapshot access and cross-Region copies. Monitor key health and access events as part of **defense-in-depth**.

aws.redshift_cluster_enhanced_vpc_routin.title: Redshift cluster has Enhanced VPC Routing enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Network Reachability
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
aws.redshift_cluster_enhanced_vpc_routin.description: **Amazon Redshift clusters** are assessed for the `EnhancedVpcRouting` setting, which routes all `COPY` and `UNLOAD` traffic between the cluster and data repositories through the VPC, enabling use of VPC security controls and logging.
aws.redshift_cluster_enhanced_vpc_routin.risk:
**Without enhanced VPC routing**, `COPY`/`UNLOAD` transfers can leave VPC oversight, reducing control and visibility.
- VPC egress filtering and endpoint policies can be bypassed (confidentiality)
- Limited flow-log telemetry (visibility)
- Higher risk of unauthorized exfiltration or tampering (confidentiality, integrity)

remediation.nativeIaC:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Enable Enhanced VPC Routing on a Redshift cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::Redshift::Cluster
    Properties:
      ClusterIdentifier: <example_resource_name>
      ClusterType: single-node
      NodeType: ra3.xlplus
      DBName: dev
      MasterUsername: <USERNAME>
      MasterUserPassword: <PASSWORD>
      EnhancedVpcRouting: true  # Critical: forces COPY/UNLOAD traffic through the VPC
```
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform: Enable Enhanced VPC Routing on a Redshift cluster
resource "aws_redshift_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  cluster_identifier  = "<example_resource_name>"
  cluster_type        = "single-node"
  node_type           = "ra3.xlplus"
  master_username     = "<USERNAME>"
  master_password     = "<PASSWORD>"
  enhanced_vpc_routing = true  # Critical: routes COPY/UNLOAD via VPC
}
```
remediation.other:
1. Open the AWS Console and go to Amazon Redshift
2. Choose Provisioned clusters, select your cluster
3. Click Actions > Modify
4. In Network and security, turn on Enhanced VPC routing
5. Click Save changes (apply immediately if prompted)
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable `EnhancedVpcRouting` and enforce **least privilege** egress:
- Prefer private access with VPC endpoints and restrictive policies
- Constrain outbound paths via security groups, NACLs, and routing
- Monitor transfers with VPC Flow Logs

This strengthens **defense in depth** and **zero trust** for data movement.

aws.redshift_cluster_in_transit_encrypti.title: Redshift cluster is encrypted in transit
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
