Use versionless key URIs in dependent services, apply **least privilege** to rotation roles, enable near-expiry notifications, and monitor events for **defense in depth**.

azure.keyvault_key_rotation_enabled.notes: There are an additional costs per operation in running the needed applications.

azure.keyvault_logging_enabled.title: Key Vault has at least one diagnostic setting with audit logging enabled
azure.keyvault_logging_enabled.description: **Azure Key Vault** diagnostic settings capture **audit logs** (`AuditEvent`) when category groups `audit` and `allLogs` are enabled and routed to a supported destination. Logged events include management and data-plane operations on vaults, keys, secrets, and certificates.
azure.keyvault_logging_enabled.risk:
Without **Key Vault audit logging**, access and changes to keys, secrets, and certificates are untracked.

Attackers can misuse keys to decrypt data, alter or delete crypto material, and evade detection-eroding **confidentiality** and **integrity** and delaying **incident response**.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable diagnostic settings on Key Vault with audit + allLogs
resource "azurerm_monitor_diagnostic_setting" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                       = "<example_resource_name>"
  target_resource_id         = "<example_resource_id>"           # Key Vault resource ID
  log_analytics_workspace_id = "<example_resource_id>"           # Destination workspace ID

  enabled_log {                                                  # critical: audit category group
    category_group = "audit"                                    # enables audit logs
  }
  enabled_log {                                                  # critical: allLogs category group
    category_group = "allLogs"                                  # enables all logs
  }
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to your Key Vault > Monitoring > Diagnostic settings
2. Click Add diagnostic setting
3. Under Category groups, select audit and allLogs
4. Choose a destination (e.g., Send to Log Analytics workspace) and select the workspace
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **diagnostic settings** to collect `AuditEvent` logs-covering category groups `audit` and `allLogs`-and send them to a central sink. Apply **least privilege** to log access, enforce secure **retention/immutability**, monitor with alerts for anomalous operations, and use **separation of duties** to prevent logging bypass.

azure.keyvault_logging_enabled.notes: By default, Diagnostic AuditEvent logging is not enabled for Key Vault instances.

azure.keyvault_non_rbac_secret_expiratio.title: Secret in non-RBAC Key Vault has expiration date set
azure.keyvault_non_rbac_secret_expiratio.description: Each **enabled secret** in an **Azure Key Vault (non-RBAC)** is assessed to confirm it has an **explicit expiration date** (`expires` attribute) defined.
azure.keyvault_non_rbac_secret_expiratio.risk:
Secrets without expiration persist indefinitely, widening the window for misuse.

If leaked or forgotten, they allow long-term, covert access to services and data, undermining **confidentiality** and **integrity**, and complicating incident response and revocation.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_key_vault_secret" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name         = "<example_resource_name>"
  value        = "<example_value>"
  key_vault_id = "<example_resource_id>"

  expiration_date = "2025-12-31T23:59:59Z" # CRITICAL: sets the secret expiration so the check passes
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Key vaults and open your vault
2. Select Secrets, then click the secret that failed
3. Click + New version
4. Set Expiration date and click Create
5. Repeat for any other secret without an expiration
remediation.recommendationText:
Set an **expiration** on every secret and enforce a **rotation policy** aligned with risk and compliance.

Automate rotation and alerts, disable or purge stale versions, and apply **least privilege**. *Where possible*, use **managed identities** to reduce secret sprawl.

azure.keyvault_non_rbac_secret_expiratio.notes: Secrets cannot be used beyond their assigned expiry date respectively. Secrets need to be rotated periodically wherever they are used.

azure.keyvault_private_endpoints.title: Key Vault uses private endpoints
azure.keyvault_private_endpoints.description: **Azure Key Vault** has **private endpoint connections** to serve secret and key operations over a private IP within your virtual network via Azure Private Link.
azure.keyvault_private_endpoints.risk: Without **private endpoints**, the vault relies on a public endpoint, expanding exposure to scanning and misconfigured allowlists. Egress controls are harder to enforce, enabling unauthorized secret retrieval for **data exfiltration** and potential key misuse, impacting confidentiality and integrity.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Create a Private Endpoint for an existing Key Vault
resource "azurerm_private_endpoint" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<LOCATION>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  subnet_id           = "<example_resource_id>" # Critical: subnet resource ID for the private endpoint NIC

  private_service_connection {
    name                           = "<example_resource_name>"
    private_connection_resource_id = "<example_resource_id>" # Critical: Key Vault resource ID to connect
    subresource_names              = ["vault"]               # Critical: targets Key Vault subresource to create the connection
  }
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure portal, open your Key Vault
2. Go to Networking > Private endpoint connections > + Create
3. Basics: select Subscription and Resource group, then Next
4. Resource: Service = Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults (your vault is preselected), Subresource = vault, Next
5. Configuration: choose Virtual network and Subnet, then Next and Create
6. Wait for the connection state to show Approved (auto-approves if you have permission)
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **Private Endpoints** for each Key Vault and disable public network access. Use private DNS so the vault FQDN resolves to the private IP. Apply **least privilege** with RBAC and managed identities, restrict traffic with NSGs and routing, and monitor access logs as part of **defense in depth**.

azure.keyvault_private_endpoints.notes: Incorrect or poorly-timed changing of network configuration could result in service interruption. There are also additional costs tiers for running a private endpoint perpetabyte or more of networking traffic.

azure.keyvault_rbac_enabled.title: Key Vault uses Azure RBAC for access control
azure.keyvault_rbac_enabled.description:
**Azure Key Vault** uses the **Azure RBAC permission model** for data-plane access to keys, secrets, and certificates, rather than legacy access policies.

Evaluates whether data access is managed through role assignments at the vault.
azure.keyvault_rbac_enabled.risk:
Without **Azure RBAC**, data access relies on coarse access policies. **Control-plane Contributors** can grant themselves data-plane rights, enabling secret or key exfiltration and unauthorized crypto operations.

Lack of JIT and least-privilege weakens **confidentiality** and **integrity** and hinders auditing.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_key_vault" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                       = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                   = "<location>"
  resource_group_name        = "<example_resource_name>"
  tenant_id                  = "<tenant_id>"
  sku_name                   = "standard"
  enable_rbac_authorization  = true // Critical: enables Azure RBAC to satisfy the control
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Key Vaults and open <KEY_VAULT_NAME>
2. Under Settings, select Properties
3. Set Permission model to Azure role-based access control
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Adopt **Azure RBAC** for Key Vault data access and design roles with **least privilege** at appropriate scopes (prefer vault-level per app/env). Use **Privileged Identity Management** for JIT, restrict control-plane Contributor rights, and monitor role assignments. *Role assignments aren't preserved after soft-delete recovery*.

azure.keyvault_rbac_enabled.notes: Implementation needs to be properly designed from the ground up, as this is a fundamental change to the way key vaults are accessed/managed. Changing permissions to key vaults will result in loss of service as permissions are re-applied. For the least amount of downtime, map your current groups and users to their corresponding permission needs.

azure.keyvault_rbac_key_expiration_set.title: Key in RBAC-enabled Key Vault has expiration date set
azure.keyvault_rbac_key_expiration_set.description: Each **enabled key** in an **Azure Key Vault** with **RBAC-enabled access control** is assessed to confirm it has an **expiration** (`exp`) attribute defined.
azure.keyvault_rbac_key_expiration_set.risk:
**Keys without expiration** can remain active indefinitely.
If exposed, attackers can decrypt data, forge signatures (code/tokens), and maintain persistence, undermining **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Absent end-of-life also weakens rotation discipline and crypto agility.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Set an expiration date on a Key Vault key
resource "azurerm_key_vault_key" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name         = "<example_resource_name>"
  key_vault_id = "<example_resource_id>"
  key_type     = "RSA"

  expiration_date = "2025-12-31T23:59:59Z" # Critical: ensures the key has an expiration date to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Key vaults and open <vaultName>
2. Select Keys and choose the key missing an expiration
3. Open the current version and click Update/Edit
4. Set Expiration date (UTC) and click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
- Set `exp` on all enabled keys and enforce a **rotation policy** with short lifetimes and automated renewal.
- Use **governance policies** to require expiration and alert before expiry.
- Apply **least privilege** and **separation of duties** for key admins vs consumers.

azure.keyvault_rbac_key_expiration_set.notes: Keys cannot be used beyond their assigned expiration dates respectively. Keys need to be rotated periodically wherever they are used.

azure.keyvault_rbac_secret_expiration_se.title: Secret in RBAC-enabled Key Vault has expiration date set
azure.keyvault_rbac_secret_expiration_se.description: Each **enabled secret** in an **Azure Key Vault (RBAC)** is assessed to confirm it has an `exp` (expiration) date configured.
azure.keyvault_rbac_secret_expiration_se.risk: Without an **expiration**, secrets become perpetual credentials. Leaked or abandoned values can grant persistent access, undermining **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Attackers can reuse old secrets to maintain footholds, perform unauthorized API calls, and exfiltrate data.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_key_vault_secret" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name         = "<example_resource_name>"
  value        = "<secret_value>"
  key_vault_id = "<example_resource_id>"

  # CRITICAL: sets the secret expiration timestamp
  expiration_date = "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Key vaults and open your vault
2. Select Secrets, choose the secret, then open its Current version
3. Set Expiration date (UTC) and click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Set an **expiration** on all enabled secrets and enforce a **regular rotation policy**.

Prefer **short-lived, identity-based access** to reduce secret usage. Apply **least privilege** for secret access, alert on upcoming expirations, and automate rotation and version cleanup to minimize exposure.

azure.keyvault_rbac_secret_expiration_se.notes: Secrets cannot be used beyond their assigned expiry date respectively. Secrets need to be rotated periodically wherever they are used.

azure.keyvault_recoverable.title: Key Vault has soft delete and purge protection enabled
azure.keyvault_recoverable.description: **Azure Key Vault** recoverability requires both `enable_soft_delete` and `enable_purge_protection`. With these enabled, vault objects remain recoverable after deletion and cannot be permanently purged during the retention period.
azure.keyvault_recoverable.risk: Absent these protections, deleted vaults or objects can be permanently removed, cutting access to keys, secrets, and certificates. This can render data unreadable, break app authentication, and halt signing/verification, degrading **availability** and **integrity**. Malicious insiders can purge to block recovery.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_key_vault" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<location>"
  resource_group_name = "<resource_group_name>"
  tenant_id           = "<tenant_id>"
  sku_name            = "standard"

  soft_delete_enabled      = true  # Critical: enables soft delete
  purge_protection_enabled = true  # Critical: enables purge protection
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Key vaults and open <keyVaultName>
2. Select Properties > Recovery
3. Turn on Soft delete and Purge protection
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable both `enable_soft_delete` and `enable_purge_protection` on all vaults. Enforce with policy, restrict purge/recover to **least privilege** and apply **separation of duties**. Keep backups and test recovery. Monitor delete/purge with alerts. *Adjust retention to business needs* to strengthen defense in depth.

azure.keyvault_recoverable.notes: Once purge-protection and soft-delete are enabled for a Key Vault, the action is irreversible.

azure.monitor_alert_create_policy_assign.title: Subscription has an Azure Monitor activity log alert for policy assignment creation
azure.monitor_alert_create_policy_assign.description: **Azure Monitor Activity Log alert** configurations are assessed for an **activity log alert** on `Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/write`, indicating monitoring of newly created **Azure Policy assignments**
azure.monitor_alert_create_policy_assign.risk: Absent alerts on new policy assignments, unauthorized or accidental changes can silently weaken governance. Adversaries could assign permissive policies or replace deny rules, enabling misconfigurations, privilege expansion, and data exposure-degrading **integrity** and threatening **confidentiality** and **availability**.

remediation.cli: az monitor activity-log alert create --name '<activity log rule name>' --resource-group '<resource group name>' --location global --scopes '/subscriptions/<subscription ID>' --condition "category=Administrative and operationName=Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/write" --enabled true
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure Portal, go to Monitor > Alerts > Alert rules
2. Click + Create > Alert rule
3. Scope: Select the target Subscription and click Apply
4. Condition: Choose Activity log, then set Category = Administrative and Operation name = Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/write; click Apply
5. Actions: Skip or select an existing Action group (optional)
6. Details: Enter a Name and ensure Enable alert rule upon creation is checked
7. Click Review + create, then Create
remediation.recommendationText:
Implement an **activity log alert** for `Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/write` and route to an action group for timely response.

Apply across all subscriptions, restrict assignment rights (**least privilege**), require change approval, and integrate notifications with your SIEM for **defense in depth**.

azure.monitor_alert_create_policy_assign.notes: By default, no monitoring alerts are created.

azure.monitor_alert_create_update_nsg.title: Subscription has an Activity Log alert for Network Security Group create or update operations
azure.monitor_alert_create_update_nsg.description: **Azure Monitor Activity Log alert** monitors **Network Security Group** changes via the `Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/write` operation to capture create/update events across the subscription
azure.monitor_alert_create_update_nsg.risk: Lack of alerting on NSG changes allows **unauthorized network policy modifications** to go unnoticed. Adversaries or mistakes could open ports, reduce segmentation, and enable **lateral movement**, impacting data **confidentiality** and service **availability** through exposure or disruption of critical traffic

remediation.cli: az monitor activity-log alert create --resource-group '<example_resource_name>' --name '<example_resource_name>' --scopes '/subscriptions/<subscription ID>' --condition "category=Administrative and operationName=Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/write" --location global
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Monitor > Alerts > Alert rules > Create
2. Scope: Select your subscription and click Apply
3. Condition: Choose Activity log, set Category to Administrative, set Operation name to Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/write, then Done
4. Actions: Skip (optional)
5. Details: Name the rule and set Region to Global, ensure Enable upon creation is checked
6. Review + create > Create
remediation.recommendationText:
Implement a subscription-wide **Activity Log alert** for NSG change operations and route notifications to an **action group** for rapid triage.

Apply **least privilege** for change tooling, enforce **change management**, and add complementary alerts for `Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/securityRules/write` and `.../delete`. *Integrate with SIEM for correlation*

azure.monitor_alert_create_update_nsg.notes: By default, no monitoring alerts are created.

azure.monitor_alert_create_update_public.title: Subscription has an Activity Log Alert for Public IP address create or update operations
azure.monitor_alert_create_update_public.description: **Azure Monitor activity log alert** for **Public IP addresses** tracks `Microsoft.Network/publicIPAddresses/write` events at the subscription level, covering any creation or update of public IP resources.
azure.monitor_alert_create_update_public.risk:
Without this alert, unauthorized or mistaken public IP changes can go unnoticed, exposing workloads to the Internet.
- Confidentiality: unexpected ingress paths
- Integrity: shadow endpoints for control
- Availability: larger DDoS surface and outages

remediation.cli: az monitor activity-log alert create --resource-group <example_resource_name> --name <example_resource_name> --scopes /subscriptions/<example_resource_id> --condition "category=Administrative and operationName=Microsoft.Network/publicIPAddresses/write" --location global
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Monitor > Alerts > Alert rules > Create
2. Scope: Select your subscription and click Done
3. Condition: Choose Activity log, then select the signal "Create or Update Public Ip Address (publicIPAddresses)"
4. Details: Enter an alert rule name; Region: Global; Ensure Enable alert rule upon creation is checked
5. Click Review + create, then Create
remediation.recommendationText:
Create a subscription-wide **activity log alert** on `Microsoft.Network/publicIPAddresses/write` and route it to an **action group**.

Enforce **least privilege** for IP management, apply **change control**, and use **defense in depth** (private endpoints, bastions, VPN) to minimize public exposure and speed response.

azure.monitor_alert_create_update_public.notes: By default, no monitoring alerts are created.

azure.monitor_alert_create_update_securi.title: Subscription has Activity Log alert for Security Solution create or update
azure.monitor_alert_create_update_securi.description: **Azure Monitor activity log alert** is configured to capture **Security Solutions** create/update operations (`Microsoft.Security/securitySolutions/write`) at subscription scope.
azure.monitor_alert_create_update_securi.risk: Without this alert, **unauthorized or mistaken changes** to security tooling can go undetected. Attackers could disable defenses, alter integrations, or weaken policies, eroding the **integrity** of controls, creating blind spots that threaten **confidentiality**, and delaying incident response.

remediation.cli: az monitor activity-log alert create --name "<activity log rule name>" --resource-group "<example_resource_name>" --scopes "/subscriptions/<example_resource_id>" --condition "category=Administrative and operationName=Microsoft.Security/securitySolutions/write" --location Global
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Monitor > Alerts > + Create > Alert rule
2. Scope: Select your Subscription and click Apply
3. Condition: Choose Activity log, set Signal name to Administrative, then add a filter Operation name = Microsoft.Security/securitySolutions/write
4. Actions: Skip (no action group required)
5. Details: Enter a Name, set Region to Global, ensure Enable alert rule upon creation is checked
6. Review + create > Create
remediation.recommendationText:
Configure an **activity log alert** for `Microsoft.Security/securitySolutions/write` and route it to action groups for prompt notification/automation.

Apply **least privilege**, require **change control**, and forward alerts to a central SIEM to strengthen **defense in depth**.

azure.monitor_alert_create_update_securi.notes: By default, no monitoring alerts are created.

azure.monitor_alert_create_update_sqlser.title: Subscription has an Activity Log alert for SQL Server firewall rule create or update events
azure.monitor_alert_create_update_sqlser.description:
**Azure Monitor activity log alerts** are configured for **Azure SQL Server firewall rule changes**, targeting the `Microsoft.Sql/servers/firewallRules/write` operation.

This evaluates whether notifications or automated actions are set when firewall rules are created or updated.
azure.monitor_alert_create_update_sqlser.risk:
Without alerting on firewall rule changes, unauthorized or accidental openings can remain unnoticed, exposing databases to untrusted networks.

This harms **confidentiality** (data exfiltration via widened IP ranges) and **integrity** (unauthorized queries), while increasing attacker dwell time.

remediation.cli: az monitor activity-log alert create --name <activity_log_rule_name> --resource-group <resource_group_name> --scopes /subscriptions/<subscription_id> --condition "category=Administrative and operationName=Microsoft.Sql/servers/firewallRules/write" --location global
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Monitor > Alerts > + Create > Alert rule
2. Scope: Select the subscription and click Done
3. Condition: Choose Signal type "Activity log", then set
   - Category: Administrative
   - Operation name: Microsoft.Sql/servers/firewallRules/write
   Click Done
4. Actions: Skip (no action group required)
5. Details: Enter an Alert rule name and ensure Enable alert rule upon creation is checked
6. Review + create > Create
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable an activity log alert for `Microsoft.Sql/servers/firewallRules/write` and route it to responsive action groups.

Apply **least privilege** for firewall management, enforce change approvals, and use **defense in depth**: prefer **private endpoints** and avoid broad public network access.

azure.monitor_alert_create_update_sqlser.notes: By default, no monitoring alerts are created.

azure.monitor_alert_delete_nsg.title: Subscription has an Activity Log alert for Network Security Group delete operations
azure.monitor_alert_delete_nsg.description: **Azure Monitor activity log alerts** include the NSG deletion signal (`Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/delete` or `Microsoft.ClassicNetwork/networkSecurityGroups/delete`). The finding indicates whether a subscription has an alert rule configured to trigger when a Network Security Group is deleted.
azure.monitor_alert_delete_nsg.risk: Without alerting on **NSG deletions**, network segmentation can be removed unnoticed, exposing services to broad ingress/egress. Malicious actors or automation may delete NSGs to enable **lateral movement** and **data exfiltration**. Missing alerts delay response, impacting confidentiality and availability.

remediation.cli: az monitor activity-log alert create --name "<activity log rule name>" --resource-group "<resource group name>" --scopes "/subscriptions/<subscription ID>" --condition "category=Administrative and operationName=Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/delete" --location global
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Monitor > Alerts > Alert rules
2. Click + Create > Alert rule
3. Scope: Select the target subscription and click Apply
4. Condition: Choose Activity log, select the signal "Delete Network Security Group" (operation Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/delete); ensure Category is Administrative
5. Details: Enter a name; leave other settings as default
6. Click Review + create, then Create
remediation.recommendationText: Configure a subscription-wide **activity log alert** for the NSG delete operation (`Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/delete`; include Classic if applicable) and route notifications via **action groups**. Enforce **least privilege** for NSG changes, require **change control**, and integrate with your **SIEM** for correlation.

azure.monitor_alert_delete_nsg.notes: By default, no monitoring alerts are created.

azure.monitor_alert_delete_policy_assign.title: Subscription has an Activity Log alert for policy assignment deletion
azure.monitor_alert_delete_policy_assign.description: **Azure Monitor Activity log alerts** for policy assignment deletions using the `Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/delete` operation at subscription scope
azure.monitor_alert_delete_policy_assign.risk: Without this alert, **policy assignment deletions** can go unnoticed, eroding configuration **integrity** and enabling governance drift. Malicious or accidental changes may remove guardrails, increasing exposure and threatening **confidentiality** of protected resources.

remediation.cli: az monitor activity-log alert create --resource-group <example_resource_name> --name <example_resource_name> --scopes "/subscriptions/<example_resource_id>" --condition "operationName=Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/delete" --location global
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Monitor > Alerts > Alert rules
2. Click + Create > Alert rule
3. Scope: Select your subscription and click Apply
4. Condition: Choose Activity log, then set Operation name equals "Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/delete"
5. Actions: Skip (optional)
6. Details: Enter a name and set Enable alert rule upon creation
7. Click Create
remediation.recommendationText:
- Configure an activity log alert for `Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/delete` and route to an action group.
- Enforce **least privilege** and **separation of duties** for policy changes and require approvals.
- Integrate alerts with your SIEM and define playbooks for rapid response.

azure.monitor_alert_delete_policy_assign.notes: By default, no monitoring alerts are created.

azure.monitor_alert_delete_public_ip_add.title: Azure subscription has an Activity Log alert for public IP address deletion
azure.monitor_alert_delete_public_ip_add.description: **Azure Monitor activity log alert** exists for the **Delete Public IP Address** operation (`Microsoft.Network/publicIPAddresses/delete`), capturing subscription-wide events when Public IP resources are removed.
azure.monitor_alert_delete_public_ip_add.risk: Unmonitored deletion of Public IPs can abruptly sever ingress/egress, break DNS and allowlists, and take services offline (**availability**). Attackers or misconfigurations can delete IPs to cause **DoS** or evade controls, and delayed visibility hinders **incident response** and **forensics**.

remediation.cli: az monitor activity-log alert create --name <activity_log_rule_name> --resource-group <resource_group_name> --location global --scopes /subscriptions/<subscription_id> --condition category=Administrative and operationName=Microsoft.Network/publicIPAddresses/delete
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Monitor > Alerts > + Create > Alert rule
2. Scope: Select your subscription and click Apply
3. Condition: Choose Activity log, then set Category = Administrative and Operation name = Microsoft.Network/publicIPAddresses/delete; click Apply
4. Actions: Skip (no action group required to pass)
5. Details: Enter an alert name, set Region to Global, ensure Enable alert rule upon creation is checked
6. Review + create > Create
remediation.recommendationText:
Implement an activity log alert for `Microsoft.Network/publicIPAddresses/delete` and route it to an action group for rapid response.
- Apply **least privilege** and change approval for IP deletions
- Use **resource locks** on critical IPs
- Centralize alerts in your SIEM and define runbooks for containment

azure.monitor_alert_delete_public_ip_add.notes: By default, no monitoring alerts are created.

azure.monitor_alert_delete_security_solu.title: Subscription has an Azure Monitor Activity Log alert for Microsoft.Security/securitySolutions delete operations
azure.monitor_alert_delete_security_solu.description:
**Azure activity log alerts** monitor deletions of **Security Solutions** by targeting the operation `Microsoft.Security/securitySolutions/delete` at subscription scope.

Identifies whether notifications are configured for security solution removal events.
azure.monitor_alert_delete_security_solu.risk: Without this alert, **unauthorized or accidental deletions** of security tooling may go **unnoticed**, reducing the **availability** of protections and the **integrity** of monitoring. Adversaries can evade defenses, prolong dwell time, and enable **data exfiltration** under reduced visibility.

remediation.other:
1. In Azure portal, go to Monitor > Alerts > + Create > Alert rule
2. Scope: Select your subscription and click Apply
3. Condition: Click Add condition, search and select "Delete Security Solutions (Microsoft.Security/securitySolutions)", then Add
4. Ensure no filters for Level or Status are set
5. Details: Enter an Alert rule name and choose a resource group
6. Create: Review + create, then Create
remediation.recommendationText: Configure a **dedicated activity log alert** for `Microsoft.Security/securitySolutions/delete` and route it to resilient **action groups** (email, chat, ticketing, SIEM). Apply **least privilege** and **resource locks** to deter tampering. Test alerting routinely and integrate it into **defense-in-depth** monitoring.

azure.monitor_alert_delete_security_solu.notes: By default, no monitoring alerts are created.

azure.monitor_alert_delete_sqlserver_fr.title: Subscription has an Activity Log Alert for SQL Server firewall rule deletions
azure.monitor_alert_delete_sqlserver_fr.description: **Azure Monitor Activity log alerts** watch the admin operation `Microsoft.Sql/servers/firewallRules/delete`, indicating when an **Azure SQL firewall rule** is removed across a subscription.
azure.monitor_alert_delete_sqlserver_fr.risk: Without alerting on firewall rule deletions, unexpected changes to SQL network allowlists can go unnoticed, causing **availability** loss for apps and masking **unauthorized tampering**. A compromised admin could remove rules to disrupt service, erode control **integrity**, and delay response.

remediation.cli: az monitor activity-log alert create --resource-group <resource_group_name> --name <alert_name> --scopes /subscriptions/<subscription_id> --condition "category=Administrative and operationName=Microsoft.Sql/servers/firewallRules/delete" --location global
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure Portal, go to Monitor > Alerts > + Create > Alert rule
2. Scope: Select the target Subscription and click Done
3. Condition: Click Add condition, choose Signal type = Activity log, search for and select the operation with type "Microsoft.Sql/servers/firewallRules/delete" (display name like "Delete Server Firewall Rule"), then Click Apply
4. Actions: Skip (optional)
5. Details: Enter an Alert rule name and ensure Enable upon creation is selected
6. Click Create
remediation.recommendationText:
Create an **activity log alert** for `Microsoft.Sql/servers/firewallRules/delete` and route it via an **action group** for rapid triage.

Enforce **least privilege** and **separation of duties** on SQL admins, add alerts for related create/update operations, integrate with **SIEM**, and require *change approval* to strengthen defense in depth.

azure.monitor_alert_delete_sqlserver_fr.notes: By default, no monitoring alerts are created.

azure.monitor_alert_service_health_exist.title: Azure subscription has an enabled Activity Log alert for Service Health incidents
azure.monitor_alert_service_health_exist.description: **Azure Monitor Activity Log alert** is configured for **Service Health** notifications where `category` is `ServiceHealth` and `properties.incidentType` is `Incident`, with the rule enabled.
azure.monitor_alert_service_health_exist.risk: Without alerts for **Service Health incidents**, teams may miss Azure outages or degradations, harming **availability** and delaying failover. Unseen incidents can cause cascading errors, timeouts, deployment failures, and SLA breaches across dependent workloads.

remediation.cli: az monitor activity-log alert create --resource-group <resource-group> --name <alert-rule> --scopes /subscriptions/<subscription-id> --condition "category=ServiceHealth and properties.incidentType=Incident"
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Service Health > Health alerts > Create service health alert
2. Scope: select your Subscription and choose the Resource group to save the alert
3. Event types: select only Service issues (Incidents)
4. Leave other filters as default, ensure Enable rule is On, then click Create
remediation.recommendationText:
Create and maintain an enabled **Activity Log alert** for **Service Health Incident** events.
- Route via **Action Groups** to on-call channels
- Filter to critical services/regions
- Test routing and refine recipients regularly
- Integrate with **incident response** and **defense-in-depth** monitoring

azure.monitor_alert_service_health_exist.notes: By default, in your Azure subscription there will not be any activity log alerts configured for Service Health events.

azure.monitor_diagnostic_setting_with_ap.title: Subscription has a diagnostic setting capturing Administrative, Security, Alert, and Policy categories
azure.monitor_diagnostic_setting_with_ap.description: **Azure Monitor Diagnostic Settings** capture **control-plane events** at the subscription level. This evaluates whether at least one setting collects the categories: `Administrative`, `Security`, `Policy`, and `Alert`.
azure.monitor_diagnostic_setting_with_ap.risk: Without these categories, critical control-plane actions may go unrecorded. Attackers could change policies, roles, or alerts unnoticed, enabling privilege escalation and resource tampering. This erodes **integrity**, threatens **confidentiality**, and weakens **availability** and **incident response**.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Subscription Activity Log diagnostic setting capturing required categories
resource "azurerm_monitor_diagnostic_setting" "example" {
  name                       = "<example_resource_name>"
  target_resource_id         = "/subscriptions/<example_resource_id>" # Critical: scope set to the subscription
  log_analytics_workspace_id = "<example_resource_id>"                 # Critical: destination workspace

  enabled_log { category = "Administrative" } # Critical: required category
  enabled_log { category = "Security" }      # Critical: required category
  enabled_log { category = "Alert" }         # Critical: required category
  enabled_log { category = "Policy" }        # Critical: required category
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure portal, go to Monitor > Activity log
2. Click Diagnostic settings > Add diagnostic setting
3. Name the setting
4. Under Categories, check: Administrative, Security, Alert, Policy
5. Under Destination, select Send to Log Analytics workspace and choose your workspace
6. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Collect `Administrative`, `Security`, `Policy`, and `Alert` via a subscription diagnostic setting and route them to a centralized, tamper-resistant destination. Enforce **least privilege** on log access, set retention, and create **alerts** for high-risk changes as part of **defense in depth**.

azure.monitor_diagnostic_setting_with_ap.notes: When the diagnostic setting is created using Azure Portal, by default no categories are selected.

azure.monitor_diagnostic_settings_exists.title: Subscription has an Activity Log diagnostic setting
azure.monitor_diagnostic_settings_exists.description: **Azure Monitor Diagnostic Settings** are configured to export the **Activity Log** to an external destination (Log Analytics, Storage, Event Hub, or partner).
azure.monitor_diagnostic_settings_exists.risk:
Without exporting the **Activity Log**, control-plane events lack **centralization and retention**.

Undetected RBAC changes, policy updates, and resource deletions reduce **detectability**, hinder **forensics**, and weaken incident response and audit evidence.

remediation.cli: az monitor diagnostic-settings subscription create --subscription <subscription id> --name <example_resource_name> --workspace <log analytics workspace ID> --logs '[{"category":"Administrative","enabled":true}]'
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Subscriptions and select your subscription
2. Open Monitoring > Activity log, then click Diagnostic settings
3. Click + Add diagnostic setting and enter a name
4. Under Destination details, select Send to Log Analytics workspace and choose your workspace
5. Under Categories, select Administrative
6. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable **subscription Diagnostic Settings** to send the **Activity Log** to a trusted destination.

Use **immutable storage** or a **SIEM**, enforce coverage with **Azure Policy**, apply **least privilege** to log access, include essential categories, and set retention aligned to regulatory needs.

azure.monitor_diagnostic_settings_exists.notes: By default, diagnostic setting is not set.

azure.monitor_storage_account_with_activ.title: Storage account storing Activity Log data is encrypted with a customer-managed key
azure.monitor_storage_account_with_activ.description: **Azure Monitor Activity Logs** sent to a **Storage account** are evaluated to confirm encryption with **Customer-Managed Keys** (`CMK`) instead of **Microsoft-managed keys**.
azure.monitor_storage_account_with_activ.risk: Storing activity logs without **CMK** weakens confidentiality and control of audit data. You lose independent key ownership, limiting rapid rotation/revocation and separation of duties. If storage credentials are compromised, attackers can exfiltrate logs that map resources and changes, aiding targeted attacks and hindering effective incident response.

remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Storage accounts and open the account used by your Activity Log diagnostic setting
2. Select Identity > System assigned > set Status to On > Save
3. Go to Settings > Encryption
4. Select Customer-managed keys, choose your Key vault and Key, then click Save
5. Ensure the storage account's identity has Get, Wrap Key, and Unwrap Key permissions on the key in Key Vault
remediation.recommendationText: Encrypt the storage account that holds exported **Activity Logs** with **Customer-Managed Keys** via Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM. Apply **least privilege** to key usage, enforce regular rotation and revocation, and enable soft delete and purge protection. Complement with network isolation and immutable retention for **defense in depth**.

azure.monitor_storage_account_with_activ.notes: NOTE: You must have your key vault setup to utilize this. All Audit Logs will be encrypted with a key you provide. You will need to set up customer managed keys separately, and you will select which key to use via the instructions here. You will be responsible for the lifecycle of the keys, and will need to manually replace them at your own determined intervals to keep the data secure.

azure.monitor_storage_account_with_activ.title: Storage account storing activity logs does not allow public blob access
azure.monitor_storage_account_with_activ.description: **Azure Monitor Activity Logs** sent to a **Storage account** are evaluated for **Blob public access**. The finding identifies whether the account that stores the logs has `AllowBlobPublicAccess` turned on.
azure.monitor_storage_account_with_activ.risk:
Exposed log data undermines **confidentiality** by revealing operations, resource IDs, IPs, and identities.

Adversaries gain **reconnaissance** to map controls, craft targeted attacks, and time actions to avoid detection, enabling **lateral movement** and broader compromise.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Disable public blob access on the storage account
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                     = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name      = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                 = "<example_resource_name>"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"

  allow_blob_public_access = false # Critical: disables public access at the account level
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to the storage account used by the diagnostic/Activity Log export
2. Under Settings, select Configuration
3. Set "Allow Blob public access" to Disabled
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Set `AllowBlobPublicAccess=false` on the storage account holding logs. Enforce **least privilege** via RBAC or scoped SAS, use **private endpoints** and network restrictions, and enable **immutability** for log containers to add **defense in depth** and prevent unauthorized access.

azure.monitor_storage_account_with_activ.notes: Configuring container Access policy to private will remove access from the container for everyone except owners of the storage account. Access policy needs to be set explicitly in order to allow access to other desired users.

azure.mysql_flexible_server_audit_log_co.title: MySQL flexible server has audit_log_events including CONNECTION
azure.mysql_flexible_server_audit_log_co.description: **Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server** audit configuration includes the `CONNECTION` event in `audit_log_events`.
azure.mysql_flexible_server_audit_log_co.risk: Without **CONNECTION auditing**, login attempts are invisible, weakening detection of **brute-force**, **credential stuffing**, and anomalous access. This enables unnoticed account takeover and lateral movement, impacting **confidentiality** and **integrity**, and hinders **forensics** and timely response.

remediation.cli: az mysql flexible-server parameter set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --server-name <SERVER_NAME> --name audit_log_events --value CONNECTION
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_mysql_flexible_server_configuration" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "audit_log_events"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_group>"
  server_name         = "<example_server_name>"
  value               = "CONNECTION" # Critical: includes CONNECTION in audit logs to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure Portal, go to Azure Database for MySQL flexible server
2. Select your server, then go to Server parameters
3. Search for audit_log_events
4. Set its value to CONNECTION
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Include `CONNECTION` in `audit_log_events` to capture login activity. Centralize and retain **audit logs**, restrict access by **least privilege**, and protect logs from tampering. Monitor for anomalous sign-in patterns and alert. Pair with **defense-in-depth** controls (MFA, network allow-listing) to reduce exposure.

azure.mysql_flexible_server_audit_log_co.notes: There are further costs incurred for storage of logs. For high traffic databases these logs will be significant. Determine your organization's needs before enabling.

azure.mysql_flexible_server_audit_log_en.title: MySQL flexible server has audit_log_enabled set to ON
azure.mysql_flexible_server_audit_log_en.description: **Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server** with `audit_log_enabled` set to `ON` generates **audit logs** for connections, authentication, DDL/DML, and administrative actions.
azure.mysql_flexible_server_audit_log_en.risk: Missing **audit logs** reduces **accountability** and obscures activity affecting **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Unauthorized logins, privilege abuse, or suspicious queries may go undetected, impeding **forensics**, slowing incident response, and enabling covert data exfiltration.

remediation.cli: az mysql flexible-server parameter set --name audit_log_enabled --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --server-name <SERVER_NAME> --value ON
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable audit logs on MySQL Flexible Server
resource "azurerm_mysql_flexible_server_configuration" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "audit_log_enabled"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  server_name         = "<example_resource_name>"
  value               = "ON" # CRITICAL: enables audit logging to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal
2. Go to: Azure Database for MySQL flexible server > Your server
3. Under Settings, select Server parameters
4. Find audit_log_enabled and set it to ON
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **audit logging** (`audit_log_enabled=ON`) and select events that matter. Export `MySqlAuditLogs` to a centralized store, enforce **least privilege** on log access, set retention, and create alerts for anomalies. Regularly review logs as part of **defense in depth**.

azure.mysql_flexible_server_minimum_tls_.title: MySQL flexible server enforces TLS 1.2 or higher
azure.mysql_flexible_server_minimum_tls_.description: **Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server** uses the `tls_version` setting to permit only **modern TLS** for client connections, requiring `TLSv1.2+` and excluding `TLSv1.0` and `TLSv1.1`.
azure.mysql_flexible_server_minimum_tls_.risk: Allowing legacy TLS (`TLSv1.0`/`TLSv1.1`) weakens **confidentiality** and **integrity** of data in transit. Attackers can force downgrades and perform **man-in-the-middle** interception, exposing credentials and queries or altering results, leading to unauthorized access and data exfiltration.

remediation.cli: az mysql flexible-server parameter set --resource-group <resourceGroupName> --server-name <serverName> --name tls_version --value TLSv1.2
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enforce TLS 1.2 on MySQL Flexible Server
resource "azurerm_mysql_flexible_server_configuration" "tls" {
  name                = "tls_version"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_group>"
  server_name         = "<example_server_name>"
  value               = "TLSv1.2" # Critical: sets minimum TLS to 1.2 (no 1.0/1.1)
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure portal, go to Azure Database for MySQL flexible server <example_resource_name>
2. Select Server parameters
3. Search for tls_version
4. Set the value to TLSv1.2
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enforce a **minimum TLS** of `TLSv1.2` (prefer `TLSv1.3`) and disable `TLSv1.0`/`TLSv1.1`. Ensure clients and drivers support modern TLS, deprecate weak cipher suites, and validate in staging. Apply **defense in depth** with private connectivity and restricted network access.

azure.mysql_flexible_server_ssl_connecti.title: MySQL Flexible Server enforces SSL connections
azure.mysql_flexible_server_ssl_connecti.description: **Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server** uses the `require_secure_transport` parameter to enforce **encrypted connections**. This evaluation determines whether the server is configured to require **TLS/SSL** for all client sessions.
azure.mysql_flexible_server_ssl_connecti.risk: Without **TLS enforcement**, credentials and queries may traverse the network in cleartext, enabling **man-in-the-middle**, **credential theft**, tampering, and data exfiltration. This directly impacts **confidentiality** and **integrity** and can lead to compliance violations.

remediation.cli: az mysql flexible-server parameter set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --server-name <SERVER_NAME> --name require_secure_transport --value ON
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enforce SSL/TLS on MySQL Flexible Server
resource "azurerm_mysql_flexible_server_configuration" "secure" {
  name                = "require_secure_transport"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_group>"
  server_name         = "<example_server_name>"
  value               = "ON" # Critical: enables SSL enforcement
}
```
remediation.other:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal
2. Go to: Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server > <your server>
3. Select Server parameters
4. Find require_secure_transport and set it to ON
5. Click Save
6. Verify by refreshing Server parameters and confirming the value is ON
remediation.recommendationText: Set `require_secure_transport=ON` and permit only **TLS 1.2+**. Ensure clients validate certificates and use FQDNs. Combine with **private access** (Private Link or VNet), restrictive firewall rules, and **least privilege** to reduce exposure. *Avoid legacy TLS or plaintext connections.*

azure.network_bastion_host_exists.title: Azure subscription has at least one Bastion Host
azure.network_bastion_host_exists.description: **Azure subscription** contains an **Azure Bastion host** for secure RDP/SSH brokering over TLS on `443/TCP` to virtual machines using private IPs. The assessment identifies whether such a bastion is available.
azure.network_bastion_host_exists.risk:
Absent **Bastion**, admins often assign public IPs or open `22/3389`, expanding attack surface.

This enables Internet brute force, credential stuffing, and RDP/SSH exploits, leading to unauthorized access, data exfiltration, and lateral movement. CIA impact: confidentiality/integrity loss and potential downtime from ransomware.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Minimal Terraform to create one Bastion Host (fixes FAIL by ensuring existence)
resource "azurerm_resource_group" "example" {
  name     = "<example_resource_name>"
  location = "eastus"
}

resource "azurerm_virtual_network" "example" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>-vnet"
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.example.location
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  address_space       = ["10.0.0.0/24"]
}

resource "azurerm_subnet" "bastion" {
  name                 = "AzureBastionSubnet"
  resource_group_name  = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  virtual_network_name = azurerm_virtual_network.example.name
  address_prefixes     = ["10.0.0.0/27"]
}

resource "azurerm_public_ip" "example" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>-pip"
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.example.location
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  allocation_method   = "Static"
  sku                 = "Standard"
}

resource "azurerm_bastion_host" "example" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.example.location
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.example.name

  # Critical: creating the Bastion Host resource is what changes the check to PASS
  sku = "Basic"  # Critical: required for Bastion creation

  ip_configuration {                     
    name                 = "IpConf"
    subnet_id            = azurerm_subnet.bastion.id            # Critical: attaches Bastion to AzureBastionSubnet
    public_ip_address_id = azurerm_public_ip.example.id         # Critical: associates required Public IP
  }
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Networking > Bastions > Create
2. Select your Subscription and a Resource group
3. Enter a Name and Region
4. Under Virtual network, select an existing VNet or click Create new
5. Ensure a subnet named AzureBastionSubnet exists with a /27 address space; create it if prompted
6. For Public IP address, click Create new and accept defaults
7. Click Review + create, then Create
8. After deployment completes, the subscription now has a Bastion Host (check passes)
remediation.recommendationText:
Standardize on **Azure Bastion** for admin access.

Remove VM public IPs and deny inbound `22`/`3389` via perimeter controls and NSGs. Apply **least privilege** and just-in-time access, integrate **Entra ID** with **MFA** and conditional access, monitor sessions/logs, and segment networks so only Bastion can reach management ports.

azure.network_bastion_host_exists.notes: The Azure Bastion service incurs additional costs and requires a specific virtual network configuration. The Standard tier offers additional configuration options compared to the Basic tier and may incur additional costs for those added features.

azure.network_flow_log_captured_sent.title: Network Watcher has flow logs enabled and sent to a Log Analytics workspace
azure.network_flow_log_captured_sent.description: **Azure Network Watcher** has **flow logs** enabled for supported targets, such as **virtual networks** and **network security groups**, and configured with **Traffic Analytics** to forward records to a centralized **Log Analytics workspace**
azure.network_flow_log_captured_sent.risk:
Missing, disabled, or non-centralized flow logging blinds visibility into network behavior, hindering detection of:
- **Lateral movement** and internal scanning
- **C2 beacons** and exfiltration patterns
This degrades incident response and correlation, impacting **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

remediation.cli: az network watcher flow-log create --location <REGION> --name <FLOW_LOG_NAME> --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --target-resource-id <TARGET_RESOURCE_ID> --storage-account <STORAGE_ACCOUNT_ID> --enabled true --workspace <LOG_ANALYTICS_WORKSPACE_ID>
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable flow logs for a supported target and send analytics to Log Analytics
resource "azurerm_network_watcher_flow_log" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                 = "<example_resource_name>"
  network_watcher_name = "<example_network_watcher_name>"
  resource_group_name  = "<example_resource_group_name>"
  target_resource_id   = "<example_target_resource_id>"
  storage_account_id   = "<example_storage_account_id>"

  enabled = true

  traffic_analytics {
    enabled               = true
    workspace_id          = "<example_workspace_id>"
    workspace_region      = "<REGION>"
    workspace_resource_id = "<example_log_analytics_workspace_id>"
  }
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure portal, go to Network Watcher > Flow logs
2. Click + Create
3. Select the subscription and region
4. Choose the appropriate flow log type and target resource, such as a virtual network or network security group
5. Set Status to On
6. Select a Storage account
7. Enable Traffic analytics and select the Log Analytics workspace
8. Click Review + create, then Create
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable and centrally aggregate **flow logs** for supported Network Watcher targets, including **virtual networks** and **network security groups**, to a **Log Analytics workspace**.

- Enforce least privilege on log data
- Define retention and secure storage
- Use layered monitoring (e.g., Traffic Analytics)
- Ensure coverage across regions, subscriptions, and critical network segments

azure.network_flow_log_captured_sent.notes: Configuring flow logs and Traffic Analytics increases storage and analytics costs. For new Azure deployments, prefer virtual network flow logs where they satisfy your monitoring requirements because NSG flow logs are on the retirement path.

azure.network_flow_log_more_than_90_days.title: Network Watcher has all flow logs enabled with retention set to 0 or at least 90 days
azure.network_flow_log_more_than_90_days.description: **Azure Network Watcher** has **flow logs** enabled for supported targets, such as **virtual networks** and **network security groups**, and configured to retain for at least `90` days (or `0` for unlimited). The evaluation checks that flow logging is enabled and that the retention policy meets the required duration for each configured log.
azure.network_flow_log_more_than_90_days.risk:
Absent or short-retained **flow logs** reduce visibility into IP flows, delaying detection of port scans, brute force, data exfiltration, and lateral movement.

Forensics and accountability degrade, threatening **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

remediation.cli: az network watcher flow-log create --location <LOCATION> --name <example_flow_log_name> --target-resource-id <example_target_resource_id> --storage-account <example_storage_account_id> --enabled true --retention 90
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable flow logs with retention >= 90 days
resource "azurerm_network_watcher_flow_log" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                 = "<example_resource_name>"
  network_watcher_name = "<example_network_watcher_name>"
  resource_group_name  = "<example_resource_group_name>"
  target_resource_id   = "<example_target_resource_id>"
  storage_account_id   = "<example_storage_account_id>"

  enabled = true

  retention_policy {
    enabled = true
    days    = 90
  }
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Network Watcher > Flow logs
2. Select the relevant flow log or create one for the target resource, such as a virtual network or network security group
3. Set Status to On
4. Set Retention (days) to 0 (unlimited) or at least 90
5. Select a Storage account
6. Click Save or Review + create
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **flow logs** and keep retention `90` days (`0` for unlimited) for supported targets, including **virtual networks** and **network security groups**. Restrict and monitor access to logs, store immutably, and stream to a SIEM to detect anomalies. Apply **defense in depth** and **least privilege**. Prefer **virtual network flow logs** for new deployments as NSG flow logs are being retired.

azure.network_flow_log_more_than_90_days.notes: Longer retention improves investigation depth but increases storage cost. For new Azure deployments, prefer virtual network flow logs where they satisfy your monitoring requirements because NSG flow logs are on the retirement path.

azure.network_http_internet_access_restr.title: Network security group restricts inbound HTTP (port 80) access from the Internet
azure.network_http_internet_access_restr.description: **Azure NSG** are evaluated for inbound rules that allow public **HTTP** access on `TCP 80`, including cases where `80` is covered by a port range, from `0.0.0.0/0`, `Internet`, or `*`.
azure.network_http_internet_access_restr.risk:
Exposing `TCP 80` to the Internet increases attack surface:
- Web recon and exploits compromise **integrity** and **availability**
- Cleartext HTTP can leak credentials, cookies, and data, harming **confidentiality**
- Public endpoints enable bot abuse and footholds for lateral movement

remediation.cli: az network nsg rule update --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --nsg-name <NSG_NAME> --name <RULE_NAME> --access Deny
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Deny inbound HTTP from Internet on an existing NSG
resource "azurerm_network_security_rule" "deny_http_internet" {
  name                        = "deny-http-internet"
  resource_group_name         = "<example_resource_name>"
  network_security_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  priority                    = 100
  direction                   = "Inbound"
  access                      = "Deny"           # CRITICAL: Deny so HTTP from Internet is not allowed
  protocol                    = "Tcp"
  source_address_prefix       = "Internet"       # CRITICAL: Matches traffic from the Internet
  destination_address_prefix  = "*"
  source_port_range           = "*"
  destination_port_range      = "80"             # CRITICAL: Blocks port 80 (HTTP)
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Network Security Groups and select your NSG
2. Open Inbound security rules
3. Find any rule with Action Allow, Protocol TCP or Any, Destination port 80 (or range including 80), and Source Internet/*/0.0.0.0/0
4. Select the rule and click Edit
5. Change Action to Deny (or delete the rule)
6. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Apply **least privilege** at NSGs:
- Remove broad allows to `TCP 80`, or restrict to trusted sources
- Enforce **HTTPS (443)** and redirect or block HTTP
- Use **private access** patterns and segmentation for **defense in depth**
- If exposure is necessary, place services behind a **WAF**, enable **DDoS** protections, and monitor

azure.network_public_ip_shodan.title: Azure public IP address is not listed in Shodan
azure.network_public_ip_shodan.description: **Azure Public IP addresses** are detected as **indexed by Shodan**, indicating Internet-visible services with open `ports` and service banner metadata.
azure.network_public_ip_shodan.risk: Shodan-visible IPs are easy to discover and target, elevating risks to **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Adversaries can enumerate banners, probe open ports, brute-force access, and exploit known CVEs, enabling unauthorized entry, data exfiltration, and lateral movement.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# NIC without a public IP association
resource "azurerm_network_interface" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<LOCATION>"
  resource_group_name = "<RESOURCE_GROUP>"

  ip_configuration {
    name                          = "ipconfig1"
    subnet_id                     = "<example_resource_id>"
    private_ip_address_allocation = "Dynamic"
    # CRITICAL: Omit public_ip_address_id -> no public IP, preventing Shodan listing
  }
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Public IP addresses and select the affected IP
2. Click Dissociate and confirm to remove it from the attached resource
3. Click Delete to remove the Public IP from your subscription
remediation.recommendationText: Minimize **public exposure**: prefer **private endpoints** or VPN/bastion, restrict ingress per least privilege (avoid `0.0.0.0/0`), close unused ports, patch and harden services, and apply defense-in-depth segmentation. Continuously inventory public IPs and rotate them if sensitive banners were exposed.

azure.network_rdp_internet_access_restri.title: Network security group does not allow inbound RDP (TCP 3389) from the Internet
azure.network_rdp_internet_access_restri.description: **Azure NSG inbound rules** are evaluated for **public RDP exposure**. The finding flags rules that `Allow` `TCP` traffic to `port 3389` from broad sources like `0.0.0.0/0`, `Internet`, or `*`, including ranges that cover `3389`.
azure.network_rdp_internet_access_restri.risk:
Exposed **RDP** enables Internet-wide **brute force** and **credential stuffing**, risking unauthorized console access.

Compromise can cause data theft (**confidentiality**), tampering or malware deployment (**integrity**), VM lockout or disruption (**availability**), and **lateral movement** within the VNet.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# NSG with RDP allowed only from a restricted CIDR (not Internet)
resource "azurerm_network_security_group" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<region>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"

  security_rule {
    name                       = "Allow-RDP-Restricted"
    priority                   = 100
    direction                  = "Inbound"
    access                     = "Allow"
    protocol                   = "Tcp"
    source_port_range          = "*"
    destination_port_range     = "3389"
    destination_address_prefix = "*"
    source_address_prefix      = "<AUTHORIZED_CIDR>" # CRITICAL: restrict source; not "*", "Internet", or "0.0.0.0/0" so the check passes
  }
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Network Security Groups and open the NSG attached to the resource
2. Select Inbound security rules
3. Find any rule that allows TCP 3389 with Source set to Any/Internet/*/0.0.0.0/0
4. Delete the rule, or edit it and set Source to a specific IP/CIDR (e.g., <AUTHORIZED_CIDR>)
5. Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Enforce **least privilege** for remote admin:
- Remove `Allow` to `3389` from `0.0.0.0/0`
- Limit access to fixed IPs or private networks
- Prefer Azure Bastion, JIT, or VPN/ExpressRoute
- Harden auth (strong keys, MFA) and monitor

Adopt **zero trust** and **defense in depth**.

azure.network_ssh_internet_access_restri.title: Network security group does not allow inbound SSH (TCP port 22) from the Internet
azure.network_ssh_internet_access_restri.description:
**Azure NSG** inbound rules that allow **SSH** on `TCP 22` from `0.0.0.0/0`, `Internet`, or `*` are identified, including rules where port ranges include `22` and protocol is `TCP` or `*`.

Indicates NSGs exposing SSH to the Internet.
azure.network_ssh_internet_access_restri.risk: Public **SSH** access weakens **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Open `22` invites brute force and key theft, enabling remote shell control, persistence, and **lateral movement**. Attackers can pivot into VNets, exfiltrate data, deploy crypto-miners, and impact **availability**.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Restrict SSH to a specific source so port 22 is not open to the Internet
resource "azurerm_network_security_rule" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                        = "<example_rule_name>"
  resource_group_name         = "<example_resource_name>"
  network_security_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  priority                    = 100
  direction                   = "Inbound"
  access                      = "Allow"
  protocol                    = "Tcp"
  source_port_range           = "*"
  destination_port_range      = "22"
  source_address_prefix       = "<ALLOWED_CIDR>" # CRITICAL: restrict SSH source; not Internet/*/0.0.0.0/0
  destination_address_prefix  = "*"
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Network security groups and open <NSG_NAME>
2. Select Inbound security rules
3. Find any rule that allows TCP 22 from Internet/Any/0.0.0.0/0
4. Delete the rule, or Edit it and set Source to IP Addresses with only your allowed CIDR(s)
5. Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Apply **least privilege** on SSH:
- Remove public rules to `TCP 22` from `0.0.0.0/0`
- Allowlist specific admin IPs or management subnets
- Prefer **Azure Bastion**, **JIT access**, or **VPN/ExpressRoute** for admin
- Use key-based auth, disable passwords, and remove unnecessary public IPs

Adopt **defense in depth** with logging and periodic reviews.

azure.network_udp_internet_access_restri.title: Network security group does not allow inbound UDP from the Internet
azure.network_udp_internet_access_restri.description: **Azure NSG rules** are assessed for **inbound UDP** exposure to the public Internet (e.g., `0.0.0.0/0`, `*`, `Internet`). The finding identifies allow rules that permit unsolicited **UDP** traffic from any external source to attached resources.
azure.network_udp_internet_access_restri.risk: Publicly reachable **UDP** services enable **DDoS reflection/amplification**, exhausting bandwidth and compute and degrading **availability** for workloads and networks. Open services (DNS, NTP, SSDP, SNMP, CLDAP) can be abused with spoofed traffic, turning endpoints into amplifiers and disrupting adjacent resources.

remediation.cli: az network nsg rule update --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --nsg-name <NSG_NAME> --name <RULE_NAME> --access Deny
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Modify the existing NSG rule to deny UDP from the Internet
resource "azurerm_network_security_rule" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                        = "<example_resource_name>"  # existing rule name
  resource_group_name         = "<example_resource_name>"
  network_security_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  priority                    = 100
  direction                   = "Inbound"
  access                      = "Deny" # CRITICAL: Change access to Deny to remove the Allow condition
  protocol                    = "Udp"
  source_address_prefix       = "*"
  destination_address_prefix  = "*"
  source_port_range           = "*"
  destination_port_range      = "*"
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Network security groups and open the NSG attached to the resource
2. Select Inbound security rules
3. Find any rule with Protocol = UDP, Direction = Inbound, Action = Allow, and Source set to Any/Internet/0.0.0.0/0
4. Click the rule, set Action to Deny (or change Source to a specific trusted range), then Save
5. Repeat for any remaining UDP Allow rules from the Internet
remediation.recommendationText:
Apply **least privilege** on NSG rules:
- Deny Internet `UDP` inbound by default
- Allow only required sources/ports
- Prefer private access (VNets, private endpoints, VPN/ExpressRoute)
- Use **defense in depth** with Azure Firewall and DDoS Protection
- Monitor and disable or rate-limit unnecessary UDP services

azure.network_watcher_enabled.title: Network Watcher is enabled for all locations in the subscription
azure.network_watcher_enabled.description: **Azure Network Watcher** presence across the subscription's regions. The assessment checks that a Network Watcher instance exists in every subscription location where resources may be deployed.
azure.network_watcher_enabled.risk: Absent **Network Watcher** in a region creates blind spots in **network telemetry and diagnostics**, hindering detection of anomalies. Attackers can exploit unnoticed NSG or routing issues for lateral movement or data exfiltration, degrading **confidentiality** and **availability** and slowing incident triage.

remediation.cli: az network watcher configure --resource-group NetworkWatcherRG --enabled true --locations <LOCATION_1> <LOCATION_2>
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, search for "Network Watcher" and open it
2. Select the target subscription
3. In Overview, under Regions, for each region with Status = Disabled, click Enable
4. Confirm all regions show Enabled
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable **Network Watcher** in all regions and keep it enabled as your footprint expands.

Apply **defense in depth** by centralizing network logs and analytics, enforce coverage with policy, and restrict tool access by **least privilege**. Align retention and monitoring to support timely detection and investigation.

azure.network_watcher_enabled.notes: There are additional costs per transaction to run and store network data. For high-volume networks these charges will add up quickly.

azure.policy_ensure_asc_enforcement_enab.title: Security Center built-in policy assignment has enforcement mode set to Default
azure.policy_ensure_asc_enforcement_enab.description: **Defender for Cloud default policy assignment** (`SecurityCenterBuiltIn`) uses enforcement mode `Default` rather than `DoNotEnforce`
azure.policy_ensure_asc_enforcement_enab.risk: With `DoNotEnforce`, policy effects like `deny` and `deployIfNotExists` aren't applied, letting insecure configs persist. This erodes **confidentiality** and **integrity** (exposed endpoints, weak encryption) and can affect **availability** via unpatched or misconfigured services, enabling compromise and lateral movement.

remediation.cli: az policy assignment update --name SecurityCenterBuiltIn --scope /subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID> --enforcement-mode Default
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Set enforcement mode to Default for the Security Center built-in assignment
resource "azurerm_policy_assignment" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                 = "SecurityCenterBuiltIn"
  scope                = "/subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID>"
  policy_definition_id = "<POLICY_OR_INITIATIVE_DEFINITION_ID>"
  enforcement_mode     = "Default" # CRITICAL: Enables enforcement to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure portal, go to Policy > Assignments
2. Find the assignment named "SecurityCenterBuiltIn" and select it
3. Click Edit assignment
4. Set Enforcement mode to Enabled (Default)
5. Click Review + save to apply
remediation.recommendationText: Keep enforcement mode `Default` on the default initiative and avoid disabling critical effects. Apply at scale for consistent governance, align with **least privilege** and **defense in depth**, validate changes in `Audit` in non-prod, and manage justified exceptions via time-bound policy exemptions instead of turning enforcement off.

azure.postgresql_flexible_server_allow_a.title: PostgreSQL flexible server has 'Allow public access from any Azure service' disabled
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_allow_a.description: **Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server** firewall should not include the rule that allows connections from **any Azure service**, represented by `start_ip=0.0.0.0` and `end_ip=0.0.0.0`.
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_allow_a.risk: Allowing **all Azure services** erodes network isolation, permitting unsolicited connections from other subscriptions and tenants. This enables credential brute force and unauthorized access paths, risking data **confidentiality** and **integrity**, and increasing the chance of service disruption (**availability**).

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Update the existing rule to not use 0.0.0.0 (disables "Allow Azure services")
resource "azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server_firewall_rule" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name             = "<example_rule_name>"
  server_id        = "<example_resource_id>"
  start_ip_address = "<START_IP>" # critical: not 0.0.0.0
  end_ip_address   = "<END_IP>"   # critical: not 0.0.0.0
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server and select your server
2. Open Networking > Firewall rules
3. Find the rule where Start IP and End IP are both 0.0.0.0
4. Select it and click Delete
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Remove the `0.0.0.0` rule and apply **least privilege**:
- Use **Private Endpoints** for access
- Allow only required source IP ranges
- Isolate with VNET rules and NSGs
- Enforce TLS and strong authentication
- Monitor connection logs for anomalies

azure.postgresql_flexible_server_connect.title: Flexible PostgreSQL server has connection_throttling enabled
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_connect.description: **Azure PostgreSQL flexible servers** where the `connection_throttling` parameter is set to `ON`
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_connect.risk:
Without `connection_throttling`, bursts of new sessions can exhaust connection slots and CPU, degrading **availability** and causing timeouts.

Reduced telemetry delays detection of **DoS** or runaway clients, extending impact and recovery time.

remediation.cli: az postgres flexible-server parameter set --resource-group <resourceGroupName> --server-name <serverName> --name connection_throttle.enable --value on
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server_configuration" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name      = "connection_throttle.enable"
  server_id = "<example_resource_id>"
  value     = "on" # CRITICAL: Enables connection_throttle.enable to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. Sign in to Azure Portal and go to Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible servers
2. Select the target server
3. In Settings, click Server parameters
4. Search for connection_throttle.enable
5. Set the value to ON and click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable `connection_throttling` and align connection limits with expected load.

Apply **defense in depth**: use connection pooling, exponential backoff, and alerts on connection spikes; prefer private access and restrictive networking to reduce exposure.

azure.postgresql_flexible_server_enforce.title: PostgreSQL Flexible Server enforces SSL connections
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_enforce.description: **Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible servers** are evaluated for **encrypted in-transit connections**, specifically whether `require_secure_transport` is set to `ON` to force TLS for all client sessions.
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_enforce.risk: Without enforced **TLS**, clients may connect in plaintext or with weak settings, exposing credentials and data to **man-in-the-middle**, query tampering, and session hijacking. This undermines **confidentiality** and **integrity**, and can enable lateral movement if stolen creds are reused.

remediation.cli: az postgres flexible-server parameter set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --server-name <SERVER_NAME> --name require_secure_transport --value ON
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable SSL/TLS enforcement on a PostgreSQL Flexible Server
resource "azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server_configuration" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name      = "require_secure_transport"   # CRITICAL: Target the SSL enforcement parameter
  server_id = "<example_resource_id>"      # ID of the target flexible server
  value     = "ON"                          # CRITICAL: Enforce SSL/TLS
}
```
remediation.other:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal
2. Go to: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server > your server
3. Select Server parameters
4. Search for require_secure_transport
5. Set it to ON
6. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enforce encryption in transit: set `require_secure_transport=ON`, prefer **TLS 1.3** (or at least `ssl_min_protocol_version=1.2`), and require clients to verify server identity. Disable mixed modes, rotate certificates, and restrict access via **private endpoints** to apply **defense in depth**.

azure.postgresql_flexible_server_entra_i.title: Microsoft Entra ID authentication is enabled for PostgreSQL Flexible Server
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_entra_i.description: **PostgreSQL Flexible Servers** must set `authConfig.activeDirectoryAuth` to `Enabled` and keep at least one **Microsoft Entra administrator** assigned so database sessions inherit centrally governed identities instead of unmanaged PostgreSQL accounts.
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_entra_i.risk: Without Entra ID authentication, stolen local passwords bypass **MFA** and conditional access, enabling persistent database logins. Missing administrators leaves the feature unusable, blocking security teams from rotating duties and allowing unauthorized access or **privilege escalation**.

remediation.cli:
az postgres flexible-server update --resource-group <resourceGroupName> --name <serverName> --active-directory-auth Enabled
az postgres flexible-server ad-admin create --resource-group <resourceGroupName> --server-name <serverName> --object-id <objectId> --display-name <displayName> --type User
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
data "azurerm_client_config" "current" {}

resource "azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server" "example" {
  name                = "pg-flex"
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.example.name
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.example.location
  sku_name            = "GP_Standard_D4s_v3"
  administrator_login = "pgadmin"
  administrator_password = "<complexPassword>"
  storage_mb          = 131072
  version             = "16"

  authentication {
    active_directory_auth_enabled = true
    tenant_id                     = data.azurerm_client_config.current.tenant_id
  }
}

resource "azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server_active_directory_administrator" "entra_admin" {
```
