```hcl
  server_id     = azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server.example.id
  object_id     = var.entra_object_id
  principal_name = var.entra_principal_name
  principal_type = "User"
  tenant_id     = data.azurerm_client_config.current.tenant_id
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure Portal, open Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server and select the target server.
2. Under Security > Authentication, set Microsoft Entra ID authentication (or combined mode) to Enabled and save the change.
3. Under Security > Microsoft Entra ID, add at least one administrator (user or group) linked to an Entra object ID and confirm the assignment.
remediation.recommendationText: Federate PostgreSQL Flexible Server access through **Microsoft Entra ID** so MFA, conditional access, and centralized RBAC govern logins. Maintain at least one delegated administrator group and rotate membership through identity governance processes.

azure.postgresql_flexible_server_entra_i.notes: This check fails when Microsoft Entra ID authentication is disabled or no administrators are returned by the flexible server microsoft-entra-admin API.

azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_che.title: PostgreSQL Flexible Server has checkpoint logging enabled
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_che.description: **Azure PostgreSQL Flexible Server** has **checkpoint logging** enabled when `log_checkpoints=on`, recording each checkpoint in the server logs
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_che.risk: Without **checkpoint logging**, visibility into write and recovery activity is reduced, hindering incident investigation and tamper detection. Unseen checkpoint storms or WAL pressure can degrade I/O and recovery, threatening **availability** and data **integrity**.

remediation.cli: az postgres flexible-server parameter set --resource-group <resourceGroupName> --server-name <serverName> --name log_checkpoints --value ON
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server_configuration" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name      = "log_checkpoints"
  server_id = "<example_resource_id>"
  
  value = "ON" # CRITICAL: enables checkpoint logging to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, open your Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server
2. Go to Settings > Server parameters
3. Search for "log_checkpoints"
4. Set the value to ON
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable `log_checkpoints=on` and send logs to centralized, tamper-resistant storage. Monitor checkpoint frequency and failures with alerts. Apply **least privilege** to log access and set retention to support forensics as part of a **defense-in-depth** logging strategy.

azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_con.title: PostgreSQL flexible server has log_connections enabled
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_con.description:
**Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server** evaluates the `log_connections` setting that controls logging of client connection attempts and authentication results.

The finding indicates whether this parameter is set to `ON`.
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_con.risk: Without **connection logging**, visibility of access attempts is lost, making **brute force** and **credential stuffing** harder to detect. This weakens **confidentiality** and **integrity**, hinders incident investigations, and can mask **lateral movement** or unauthorized data access.

remediation.other:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal
2. Go to: Azure Database for PostgreSQL > Flexible servers > select <example_resource_name>
3. Under Settings, open Server parameters and search for "log_connections"
4. Confirm the parameter shows Value: ON and is Read-only (no change required)
remediation.recommendationText: Set `log_connections` to `ON` and integrate logs with centralized monitoring. Define retention and alerts for abnormal patterns. Combine with **least privilege**, strong authentication, and network restrictions to deliver **defense in depth** and prevent unauthorized access.

azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_dis.title: PostgreSQL Flexible Server has disconnection logging enabled
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_dis.description: **Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server** uses the `log_disconnections` setting to record when client sessions end and how long they lasted.
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_dis.risk:
Without **disconnection logs**, session timelines and user activity are opaque, weakening **auditability** and **forensics**.

Abuse such as stolen credentials, short-lived access, or hijacked sessions can go unnoticed, enabling data exfiltration and privilege misuse, impacting **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

remediation.cli: az postgres flexible-server parameter set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --server-name <SERVER_NAME> --name log_disconnections --value on
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable log_disconnections on a PostgreSQL Flexible Server
resource "azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server_configuration" "log_disconnections" {
  server_id = "<example_resource_id>"
  name      = "log_disconnections"
  value     = "on" # Critical: turns log_disconnections ON to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible servers
2. Select your server
3. Under Settings, open Server parameters
4. Search for log_disconnections
5. Set it to ON
6. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable `log_disconnections` on all Flexible Servers. Complement with `log_connections` and appropriate duration/statement logging, centralize and retain logs, and alert on abnormal connect/disconnect patterns. Restrict log access. This enforces **accountability**, supports **defense in depth**, and speeds incident response.

azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_dis.notes: Enabling this setting will enable a log of all disconnections. If this is enabled for a high traffic server, the log may grow exponentially.

azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_ret.title: PostgreSQL flexible server log_retention_days is between 4 and 7 days
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_ret.description: Log retention on **Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server** is governed by `log_retention_days`. Configuration is assessed as set and within `4-7` days versus unset or outside this range.
azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_ret.risk: **Insufficient or disabled log retention** limits the audit trail needed to detect brute-force, SQL injection, or insider misuse, impeding investigation. **Excessive retention** enlarges exposure if logs are accessed, risking sensitive query data leakage and policy violations. This reduces visibility and weakens confidentiality and integrity.

remediation.cli: az postgres flexible-server parameter set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --server-name <SERVER_NAME> --name logfiles.retention_days --value 7
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server_configuration" "<example_resource_name>" {
  server_id = "<example_resource_id>"
  name      = "logfiles.retention_days"
  value     = "7" # Critical: sets retention within 4-7 to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Azure Database for PostgreSQL > Flexible servers and open your server
2. Select Server parameters
3. Search for logfiles.retention_days
4. Set the value to a number between 4 and 7 (e.g., 7)
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Set `log_retention_days` to `4-7` to balance visibility and exposure. Export logs to centralized SIEM or secure storage for longer retention and analysis. Enforce **least privilege**, encryption, and immutability on log data, and monitor for gaps. Apply **defense in depth** with alerts on anomalous queries and failed logins.

azure.postgresql_flexible_server_log_ret.notes: Configuring this setting will result in logs being retained for the specified number of days. If this is configured on a high traffic server, the log may grow quickly to occupy a large amount of disk space. In this case you may want to set this to a lower number.

azure.sqlserver_auditing_enabled.title: SQL Server has an auditing policy configured
azure.sqlserver_auditing_enabled.description: **Azure SQL Server** auditing is assessed at the server level to confirm audit logging is active. Configurations with any auditing policy state set to `Disabled` indicate auditing is not configured for the server and its databases.
azure.sqlserver_auditing_enabled.risk: Without **SQL auditing**, visibility into logins, privilege changes, and query activity is lost. Stealthy data exfiltration and tampering can go undetected, impacting **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Absent audit trails hinder **forensics**, slow incident response, and weaken compliance evidence.

remediation.cli: az sql server audit-policy update --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME> --name <SERVER_NAME> --state Enabled --storage-account <STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME>
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable server-level auditing to Azure Storage
resource "azurerm_mssql_server_extended_auditing_policy" "<example_resource_name>" {
  server_id                  = "<example_resource_id>"
  storage_endpoint           = "https://<STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME>.blob.core.windows.net/" # Critical: audit log destination
  storage_account_access_key = "<STORAGE_ACCOUNT_KEY>"                                  # Critical: allows writing audit logs
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to SQL servers and select your server
2. Under Security, click Auditing
3. Set Auditing to On
4. Select Storage as the destination and choose a Storage account
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable server-level **auditing** and send logs to a centralized, tamper-resistant store with defined retention. Enforce **least privilege** and **separation of duties** for log access, integrate with monitoring for alerts, and periodically validate coverage. Use database-level auditing only for specific exceptions.

azure.sqlserver_auditing_retention_90_da.title: SQL server has auditing enabled with retention greater than 90 days
azure.sqlserver_auditing_retention_90_da.description: **Azure SQL Server auditing** settings are evaluated to ensure **auditing is enabled** and log retention is greater than `90` days. It considers the auditing policy state and the configured `retention_days` value.
azure.sqlserver_auditing_retention_90_da.risk: Without adequate retention or with auditing disabled, **activity trails expire too soon**, limiting detection and investigation of **unauthorized access, data exfiltration, and privilege abuse**. This weakens **confidentiality** and **integrity** and slows incident response.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable server-level auditing with retention > 90 days
resource "azurerm_mssql_server_extended_auditing_policy" "audit" {
  server_id          = "<example_resource_id>"
  log_monitoring_enabled = true   # Critical: enable Log Analytics target
  retention_in_days      = 91     # Critical: > 90 days
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to SQL servers and select <example_resource_name>
2. Under Security, click Auditing
3. Set Auditing to On
4. Destination: select Log Analytics workspace and choose your workspace
5. Set Retention (days) to 91
6. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **server-level auditing** and set retention above `90` days, aligned with policy needs. Store logs in **tamper-resistant, centralized storage**, restrict access with **least privilege**, and integrate alerting and review. Apply **defense in depth** with continuous monitoring.

azure.sqlserver_azuread_administrator_en.title: SQL Server has an Azure Active Directory administrator configured
azure.sqlserver_azuread_administrator_en.description: **Azure SQL Server** is configured with a **Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) administrator** at the server scope, indicated by `administrator_type` set to `ActiveDirectory`.
azure.sqlserver_azuread_administrator_en.risk: Without a **Microsoft Entra admin**, the server can't use Entra identities, pushing reliance on **SQL authentication**. This weakens confidentiality and integrity: no MFA/conditional access, harder offboarding and auditing, and compromised passwords can enable unauthorized data access and privilege escalation.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Set Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) admin on an existing SQL Server
resource "azurerm_mssql_active_directory_administrator" "<example_resource_name>" {
  server_id = "<example_resource_id>"  # CRITICAL: target SQL server resource ID
  login     = "<AAD_ADMIN_NAME>"        # CRITICAL: AAD admin display name
  object_id = "<AAD_OBJECT_ID>"         # CRITICAL: AAD object (GUID)
  tenant_id = "<TENANT_ID>"             # CRITICAL: Tenant where the AAD object exists
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to SQL servers and select <SERVER_NAME>
2. Select Active Directory admin
3. Click Set admin
4. Select the desired Microsoft Entra user or group and click Select
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Assign a **Microsoft Entra administrator** (prefer a security group) at the server level and manage access via Entra groups. Enforce **least privilege**, require **MFA/conditional access**, and use **managed identities** for services. *If feasible*, adopt Entra-only authentication and phase out shared SQL logins.

azure.sqlserver_microsoft_defender_enabl.title: SQL Server has Microsoft Defender for SQL enabled
azure.sqlserver_microsoft_defender_enabl.description: **Azure SQL Server** instances are evaluated for the server-level **security alert policy** of **Microsoft Defender for SQL**, expecting the policy state to be `Enabled`.
azure.sqlserver_microsoft_defender_enabl.risk: Without **Defender for SQL**, anomalous logins, SQL injection patterns, and risky configurations may go undetected, enabling data exfiltration (**confidentiality**), unauthorized changes (**integrity**), and disruptive queries or ransomware (**availability**).

remediation.other:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal > SQL servers > select <SERVER_NAME>
2. Under Security, select Microsoft Defender for SQL (or Microsoft Defender for Cloud)
3. Toggle to On (Enable) and click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **Microsoft Defender for SQL** across all servers and managed instances, preferably at subscription scope. Apply **least privilege**, restrict public exposure, and integrate alerts with your SOC. Regularly review **vulnerability assessment** results and harden findings as part of **defense in depth**.

azure.sqlserver_microsoft_defender_enabl.notes: Microsoft Defender for SQL is a paid feature and will incur additional cost for each SQL server.

azure.sqlserver_recommended_minimal_tls_.title: SQL server enforces minimal TLS version 1.2 or 1.3
azure.sqlserver_recommended_minimal_tls_.description: **Azure SQL logical servers** are assessed for the configured **minimum TLS version** for client connections. The finding determines whether the minimal accepted version aligns with recommended modern values such as `1.2` or `1.3`.
azure.sqlserver_recommended_minimal_tls_.risk: Without a modern minimum, clients can negotiate **weak TLS** or be downgraded, enabling **MITM** and decryption. This jeopardizes **confidentiality** (credential/data exposure) and **integrity** (query tampering), and may disrupt **availability** via session resets during handshake interference.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enforce minimum TLS 1.2 on Azure SQL logical server
resource "azurerm_mssql_server" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                         = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name          = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                     = "<example_location>"
  version                      = "12.0"
  administrator_login          = "<example_admin>"
  administrator_login_password = "<example_password>"

  minimum_tls_version = "1.2" # Critical: Enforces TLS 1.2+ for client connections
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to SQL servers and select your server
2. Open Networking > Connectivity
3. Set Minimum TLS Version to 1.2 (or 1.3)
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Set the **minimum TLS** to `1.2` or higher (prefer `1.3` when supported). Upgrade client libraries and OS trust stores; remove legacy protocols and weak ciphers to prevent downgrades. Validate compatibility before enforcement and monitor connections for outdated TLS. Uphold **encryption in transit** and **defense in depth**.

azure.sqlserver_recommended_minimal_tls_.notes: Verify support for the TLS version from the application side before changing the minimal version.

azure.sqlserver_tde_encrypted_with_cmk.title: SQL server uses a customer-managed key for the TDE protector and all databases have TDE enabled
azure.sqlserver_tde_encrypted_with_cmk.description: **Azure SQL Server** uses **Transparent Data Encryption** with a **customer-managed key** in Azure Key Vault, and each database has TDE `Enabled`
azure.sqlserver_tde_encrypted_with_cmk.risk: Without **TDE with CMK**, data at rest may be unencrypted or controlled by service keys, weakening **confidentiality** and **key custody**. Attackers or insiders could read backups, snapshots, or stolen disks, and you cannot enforce **rotation**, **revocation**, or **separation of duties**, raising compliance and incident response risks.

remediation.cli: az rest --method PUT --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID>/resourceGroups/<RESOURCE_GROUP>/providers/Microsoft.Sql/servers/<SERVER_NAME>/encryptionProtector/current?api-version=2021-11-01" --body '{"properties":{"serverKeyType":"AzureKeyVault","serverKeyName":"<KEY_VAULT_NAME>_<KEY_NAME>_<KEY_VERSION>"}}' && az sql db tde set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --server <SERVER_NAME> --database <DATABASE_NAME> --status Enabled
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to SQL servers > select <server>
2. Under Security, open Transparent data encryption
3. Select Customer-managed key and choose the key from Azure Key Vault, then Save
4. For each database on this server: go to SQL databases > select <database> > Transparent data encryption
5. Set Status to On and Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Use a **customer-managed TDE protector** in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM and ensure TDE is `Enabled` for every database.
- Apply **least privilege** to key access
- Enable **rotation** and monitor key use
- Protect keys with soft-delete and purge protection
- Enforce via **policy** and maintain key backups for restores

azure.sqlserver_tde_encrypted_with_cmk.notes: Once TDE protector is encrypted with a Customer-managed key, it transfers entire responsibility of respective key management on to you, and hence you should be more careful about doing any operations on the particular key in order to keep data from corresponding SQL server and Databases hosted accessible. When deploying Customer Managed Keys, it is prudent to ensure that you also deploy an automated toolset for managing these keys (this should include discovery and key rotation), and Keys should be stored in an HSM or hardware backed keystore, such as Azure Key Vault. As far as toolsets go, check with your cryptographic key provider, as they may well provide one as an add-on to their service.

azure.sqlserver_tde_encryption_enabled.title: SQL database has Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) enabled
azure.sqlserver_tde_encryption_enabled.description:
**Azure SQL user databases** have **Transparent Data Encryption** (`TDE`) enabled, ensuring encryption of database files, backups, and transaction logs at rest.

*The `master` system database is excluded from evaluation.*
azure.sqlserver_tde_encryption_enabled.risk:
Without **TDE**, data at rest remains unencrypted:
- Stolen backups, snapshots, or compromised storage enable offline data disclosure
- Attackers with substrate access can bypass DB auth, harming **confidentiality** and enabling **exfiltration**

remediation.cli: az sql db tde set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --server <SERVER_NAME> --database <DATABASE_NAME> --status Enabled
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_mssql_database" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name      = "<example_resource_name>"
  server_id = "<example_resource_id>"

  transparent_data_encryption_enabled = true # critical: enables TDE
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to SQL databases and select the target database (not master)
2. Under Settings, open Transparent data encryption
3. Set Transparent data encryption to On (Enabled) and click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **TDE** on all Azure SQL user databases. Prefer **customer-managed keys** in Key Vault or Managed HSM for control, rotation, and revocation. Apply **least privilege** and **separation of duties** to key access, enforce via **policy**, and monitor key/audit logs. *Maintain key backups and lifecycle to prevent availability loss.*

azure.sqlserver_unrestricted_inbound_acc.title: Azure SQL Server does not have firewall rules allowing 0.0.0.0-255.255.255.255
azure.sqlserver_unrestricted_inbound_acc.description:
**Azure SQL Server** server-level firewall rules are evaluated for an entry that allows the entire IPv4 space (`0.0.0.0` to `255.255.255.255`).

The finding identifies presence of this Internet-wide rule on the server firewall.
azure.sqlserver_unrestricted_inbound_acc.risk:
An Internet-wide rule permits unsolicited access from any host, enabling mass scanning, brute force, and exploitation of weak configurations.
- Confidentiality: unauthorized data access/exfiltration
- Integrity: malicious data/DDL changes
- Availability: resource abuse or DoS via excessive connections

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Replace any allow-all firewall rule with a restricted range
resource "azurerm_mssql_firewall_rule" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name             = "<example_resource_name>"
  server_id        = "<example_resource_id>"
  start_ip_address = "<START_IP>" # Critical: not 0.0.0.0
  end_ip_address   = "<END_IP>"   # Critical: not 255.255.255.255
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to SQL servers and select your server
2. Open Security > Networking
3. Under Firewall rules, find any rule with Start IP 0.0.0.0 and End IP 255.255.255.255
4. Select the rule and click Delete
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Remove the all-open rule and enforce **least privilege**.
- Restrict access to specific IPs/ranges
- Prefer **private endpoints** or VNet rules to avoid Internet exposure
- Layer controls (NSGs, Azure Firewall)
- Avoid broad exceptions like `Allow Azure services` and never use `0.0.0.0/0`

azure.sqlserver_va_emails_notifications_.title: SQL Server has Vulnerability Assessment enabled and email notifications to subscription admins configured
azure.sqlserver_va_emails_notifications_.description: **Azure SQL Server** Vulnerability Assessment configuration, specifically whether recurring scans are set to email results to subscription admins/owners via `Also send email notifications to admins and subscription owners`.
azure.sqlserver_va_emails_notifications_.risk: Without these notifications, findings may go unnoticed, delaying fixes. Prolonged exposure of misconfigurations and weak permissions threatens data **confidentiality** and **integrity**, can affect **availability**, and slows **incident response** and audit readiness.

remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to SQL servers and open <SERVER_NAME>
2. Under Security, select Vulnerability assessment (classic)
3. Select a Storage account container and click Save (ensures a storage container path)
4. Enable Recurring scans
5. Enable Send scan reports to subscription admins
6. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable VA email alerts for admins/owners (`Also send...`) so findings reach accountable staff promptly.

- Route to a monitored security group and SIEM
- Review recipients regularly; remove stale accounts
- Apply **least privilege** and maintain recurring scans for **defense in depth**

azure.sqlserver_va_emails_notifications_.notes: Enabling the Microsoft Defender for SQL features will incur additional costs for each SQL server.

azure.sqlserver_va_periodic_recurring_sc.title: SQL Server has Vulnerability Assessment periodic recurring scans enabled
azure.sqlserver_va_periodic_recurring_sc.description:
**Azure SQL servers** are evaluated for **Vulnerability Assessment** configuration and whether **periodic recurring scans** are scheduled (e.g., weekly) for the server and its databases.

Servers with Vulnerability Assessment missing or scans not scheduled are identified.
azure.sqlserver_va_periodic_recurring_sc.risk: Without scheduled scans, new misconfigurations and vulnerable settings can persist unnoticed, weakening **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Attackers can exploit stale permissions, unsafe firewall rules, or unpatched features to read or alter data and pivot to other resources.

remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to SQL servers > select <your server>
2. Under Security, open Vulnerability assessment (classic configuration)
3. Set Storage container to an existing blob container and Save
4. Turn Recurring scans to On
5. Click Save to apply
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **recurring Vulnerability Assessment scans** at server scope and ensure results are retained securely (*express configuration or secured storage*). Apply **least privilege**, maintain baselines, and promptly remediate findings. Automate alerting and periodic reviews as part of **defense in depth** and change management.

azure.sqlserver_va_periodic_recurring_sc.notes: Enabling the Azure Defender for SQL feature will incur additional costs for each SQL server.

azure.sqlserver_va_scan_reports_configur.title: SQL server has Vulnerability Assessment enabled and scan report recipients configured
azure.sqlserver_va_scan_reports_configur.description: **Azure SQL Server** vulnerability assessment uses **recurring scans** and emails results to designated recipients. This evaluates that VA is enabled and that `Send scan reports to` (or subscription admin notifications) is configured so scan reports are delivered.
azure.sqlserver_va_scan_reports_configur.risk: If VA reports aren't sent to responsible owners, findings can be missed, delaying fixes. Attackers may exploit misconfigurations, excessive permissions, or outdated settings, leading to data exposure (C), unauthorized changes (I), and potential service disruption (A).

remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to SQL servers and select <your server>
2. Under Security, open Vulnerability assessment
3. Select a Storage account and Container, then Save
4. In Recurring scans, turn On and enable Send to subscription admins (or add at least one email)
5. Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **Vulnerability Assessment**, keep **recurring scans** active, and configure `Send scan reports to` with accountable security owners or subscription admins. Integrate notifications with central alerting, apply **least privilege** to recipients, and enforce SLAs to triage and remediate findings promptly.

azure.sqlserver_va_scan_reports_configur.notes: Enabling the Microsoft Defender for SQL features will incur additional costs for each SQL server.

azure.sqlserver_vulnerability_assessment.title: SQL server has vulnerability assessment enabled with storage container configured
azure.sqlserver_vulnerability_assessment.description: **Azure SQL Server** has **Vulnerability Assessment** configured with a defined location to persist assessment reports and scan results
azure.sqlserver_vulnerability_assessment.risk:
Without **Vulnerability Assessment**, misconfigurations and excessive permissions can go unnoticed.

Adversaries may exploit weak server or database settings to escalate privileges, exfiltrate data, or alter records, degrading confidentiality and integrity.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable server security alert policy (required by VA)
resource "azurerm_mssql_server_security_alert_policy" "<example_resource_name>" {
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  server_name         = "<example_resource_name>"
  state               = "Enabled"
}

# Configure VA (classic) with storage container
resource "azurerm_mssql_server_vulnerability_assessment" "<example_resource_name>" {
  server_security_alert_policy_id = azurerm_mssql_server_security_alert_policy.<example_resource_name>.id
  storage_container_path          = "https://<example_resource_name>.blob.core.windows.net/<example_resource_name>" # CRITICAL: sets storage container path so the check passes
  storage_account_access_key      = "<example_resource_name>"
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to SQL servers and open <SERVER_NAME>
2. Under Security, select Microsoft Defender for SQL (or Defender for Cloud > Microsoft Defender for SQL)
3. In Vulnerability assessment settings, click Configure
4. Select the Storage account and the target Container
5. Save

Verification: Open the server's Vulnerability assessment blade and confirm a storage container is shown.
remediation.recommendationText: Enable and standardize **Vulnerability Assessment** across SQL servers and databases, retaining scan results in a secure repository. Run scans routinely, review findings, set `baselines`, and remediate promptly. Apply **least privilege** to report access and integrate results into change management for **defense in depth**.

azure.sqlserver_vulnerability_assessment.notes: Enabling the Microsoft Defender for SQL features will incur additional costs for each SQL server.

azure.storage_account_key_access_disable.title: Storage account has shared key access disabled
azure.storage_account_key_access_disable.description: **Azure Storage accounts** are evaluated for whether **Shared Key (account key) authorization** is disabled, requiring identity-based access via **Microsoft Entra ID** and RBAC.
azure.storage_account_key_access_disable.risk:
Allowing **Shared Key** undermines **confidentiality, integrity, and availability**:
- A leaked key grants broad read/write/delete across the account
- Access bypasses **RBAC** and Conditional Access, reducing accountability
- Activity is hard to attribute, easing data exfiltration and tampering

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "main" {
  name                     = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name      = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                 = "<example_resource_name>"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"

  shared_access_key_enabled = false # Critical: disables Shared Key authorization to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, open the target Storage account
2. Go to Settings > Configuration
3. Set "Allow storage account key access" to "Disabled"
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Disallow **Shared Key** and require **Microsoft Entra ID** with least-privilege RBAC for all data access.
- Prefer user delegation SAS over account/service SAS
- Apply Conditional Access and separation of duties
- Monitor and phase out key-based clients; rotate and revoke unused keys

azure.storage_account_public_network_acc.title: Storage account has 'Public Network Access' disabled
azure.storage_account_public_network_acc.description: **Azure Storage accounts** with **public network access** disabled cannot be reached from public networks. Setting `publicNetworkAccess` to `Disabled` overrides the public access settings of individual containers and forces access through private endpoints or trusted services. This is independent from the 'Allow Blob Anonymous Access' setting.
azure.storage_account_public_network_acc.risk:
Leaving **public network access** enabled exposes the storage account endpoints to the **public Internet**, widening the attack surface and undermining **defense in depth**.

This increases the risk of **unauthorized access**, **data exfiltration**, and reconnaissance against the account, especially when combined with weak network rules or overly permissive access policies.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                          = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name           = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                      = "<example_location>"
  account_tier                  = "Standard"
  account_replication_type      = "LRS"
  public_network_access_enabled = false # Critical: disables public network access
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Storage accounts and select the target account
2. Under Security + networking, click Networking
3. Set Public network access to Disabled
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Disable **public network access** on the storage account and reach it through **private endpoints** or trusted Azure services only. Combine this with **least privilege** RBAC, short-lived `SAS` tokens, and network restrictions. Validate client connectivity before disabling public access in production.

azure.storage_account_public_network_acc.notes: This check evaluates the storage account publicNetworkAccess property. It is independent from the 'Allow Blob Anonymous Access' setting evaluated by storage_blob_public_access_level_is_disabled.

azure.storage_blob_public_access_level_i.title: Storage account has 'Allow Blob Anonymous Access' disabled
azure.storage_blob_public_access_level_i.description: **Azure Storage accounts** with **blob anonymous (public) access** disabled prevent containers or blobs from being set to a public access level. Setting `allowBlobPublicAccess` to `false` enforces no anonymous reads across the account. This is independent from the account's 'Public Network Access' setting, which is evaluated by storage_account_public_network_access_disabled.
azure.storage_blob_public_access_level_i.risk:
Allowing public access permits unauthenticated users to read blob data or enumerate container contents when any container is made public, compromising confidentiality.

Exposed objects can be scraped at scale, enabling data exfiltration and intelligence gathering without audit attribution.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                     = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name      = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                 = "<example_location>"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"
  allow_blob_public_access = false # Critical: disables anonymous/public blob access
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Storage accounts and select the target account
2. Under Settings, open Configuration
3. Set "Allow Blob public access" to Disabled
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Disable **blob public access** at the account and enforce authenticated access based on **least privilege**. Prefer **private endpoints** or restricted networks, use short-lived `SAS` or federated identities, and apply **RBAC** with container-level permissions. Monitor access and review exposure regularly.

azure.storage_blob_public_access_level_i.notes: This check evaluates the 'Allow Blob Anonymous Access' (allowBlobPublicAccess) setting. The account's 'Public Network Access' (publicNetworkAccess) setting is evaluated by storage_account_public_network_access_disabled.

azure.storage_blob_versioning_is_enabled.title: Storage account has blob versioning enabled
azure.storage_blob_versioning_is_enabled.description: **Azure Storage accounts** have **blob versioning** enabled (`IsVersioningEnabled`) to automatically retain previous versions of blobs created by updates or deletes
azure.storage_blob_versioning_is_enabled.risk:
Without **blob versioning**:
- **Integrity**: overwrites can't be reverted
- **Availability**: deletes or ransomware remove usable copies
- **Forensics**: no immutable history for investigation and scoped recovery

Mistakes or compromised identities can cause irreversible object loss and wider impact.

remediation.cli: az storage account blob-service-properties update --resource-group <resource_group> --account-name <storage-account> --enable-versioning true
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Storage accounts and open your storage account
2. Under Data management, select Data protection
3. In Tracking, set Enable versioning for blobs to Enabled
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **blob versioning** for accounts holding critical data. Pair with **blob soft delete** and lifecycle rules to retain and age off versions. Enforce **least privilege** on write and version-delete actions, and monitor access. *For high-churn data*, isolate into separate accounts with tailored retention to balance security and cost.

azure.storage_cross_tenant_replication_d.title: Storage account has cross-tenant replication disabled
azure.storage_cross_tenant_replication_d.description: **Azure Storage accounts** are assessed for whether **cross-tenant object replication** is disallowed via `AllowCrossTenantReplication=false`, limiting replication policies to the same tenant.
azure.storage_cross_tenant_replication_d.risk: Permitting cross-tenant replication can copy sensitive blobs into external tenants, undermining **confidentiality**. A compromised or mismanaged destination enables **data exfiltration**; mirrored updates/deletes can impact **integrity** and retention, complicating auditability and incident response.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "main" {
  name                     = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name      = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                 = "<example_resource_name>"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"

  cross_tenant_replication_enabled = false # Critical: disallow cross-tenant object replication
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Storage accounts and open your storage account
2. Under Data management, select Object replication
3. Click Advanced settings
4. Uncheck Allow cross-tenant replication
5. Click OK/Save
6. If the option is unavailable, delete any existing cross-tenant object replication policies first, then retry
remediation.recommendationText: Enforce `AllowCrossTenantReplication=false` and keep replication within the same tenant. Apply **least privilege** and **separation of duties** for replication management, backed by **policy-based governance** to prevent drift. *If cross-tenant transfer is required*, use formal data-sharing controls, monitoring, and time-bound approvals.

azure.storage_default_network_access_rul.title: Storage account default network access rule is set to Deny
azure.storage_default_network_access_rul.description: **Azure Storage accounts** configure the **default network access rule** to `Deny`, so the **public endpoint** only accepts traffic from explicitly allowed virtual networks, IP ranges, or private endpoints
azure.storage_default_network_access_rul.risk: With the default action set to `Allow`, the public endpoint is reachable from any network. This removes a network boundary, so **stolen access keys** or leaked **SAS tokens** can be abused from anywhere, enabling **data exfiltration**, tampering, and destructive writes-impacting confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Set default network access to Deny on an existing Storage Account
resource "azurerm_storage_account_network_rules" "<example_resource_name>" {
  storage_account_id = "<example_resource_id>"
  default_action     = "Deny" # Critical: sets default network access to Deny so the check passes
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, open your Storage account
2. Go to Security + networking > Networking
3. Under Public network access, select Enable > Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses
4. Click Save

This sets the default network access rule to Deny
remediation.recommendationText: Set the default network access to `Deny` and permit only required sources: selected VNets, specific IP ranges, or preferably **private endpoints**. Apply **least privilege**, minimize service bypass, and use short-lived, scoped SAS to limit blast radius if credentials leak.

azure.storage_default_network_access_rul.notes: All allowed networks will need to be whitelisted on each specific network, creating administrative overhead. This may result in loss of network connectivity, so do not turn on for critical resources during business hours.

azure.storage_default_to_entra_authoriza.title: Storage account uses Microsoft Entra authorization by default
azure.storage_default_to_entra_authoriza.description: **Azure Storage accounts** with `Default to Microsoft Entra authorization in the Azure portal` use **token-based Microsoft Entra ID (Azure RBAC)** by default to access blobs, files, queues, and tables, rather than account keys
azure.storage_default_to_entra_authoriza.risk: Defaulting to **access keys/Shared Key** enables broad, non-scoped access and weak **auditing**. A stolen key grants full data access, risking **confidentiality** (exfiltration), **integrity** (unauthorized writes/deletes), and **availability** (destructive actions). It can also bypass **least privilege** and enable lateral movement via key reuse.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable Microsoft Entra authorization by default for the storage account in the portal
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                     = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name      = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                 = "<example_location>"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"

  default_to_oauth_authentication = true # Critical: defaults portal data access to Microsoft Entra authorization
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Storage accounts and select your account
2. Under Settings, select Configuration
3. Set "Default to Microsoft Entra authorization in the Azure portal" to Enabled
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable this setting so the portal uses **Microsoft Entra ID** by default. Apply **least privilege** with Azure RBAC, prefer **managed identities** and user-delegation SAS, and *where feasible* disable Shared Key use. Rotate any existing keys, and monitor access with logs to enforce **defense in depth**.

azure.storage_ensure_azure_services_are_.title: Storage account has 'Allow trusted Microsoft services to access this storage account' enabled
azure.storage_ensure_azure_services_are_.description: **Azure Storage account** network rules include the `AzureServices` bypass so **trusted Microsoft services** can reach the account even when firewalls restrict public access
azure.storage_ensure_azure_services_are_.risk: Without this exception, platform services relying on the account (backup, monitoring, replication) can be blocked, causing failed backups, missing logs, and stalled workflows-affecting **availability** and **integrity**. Teams may over-broaden network access to compensate, increasing **confidentiality** risk.

remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Storage accounts and select your account
2. Navigate to Security + networking > Networking
3. Under Exceptions, check Allow trusted Microsoft services to access this storage account
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable the **trusted services** exception (`AzureServices`) for storage accounts used by platform services.
- Enforce **least privilege** with RBAC and managed identities
- Keep networks restricted; prefer **private endpoints**
- Monitor access and review exceptions regularly

azure.storage_ensure_encryption_with_cus.title: Azure Storage account uses customer-managed keys (CMKs) for encryption
azure.storage_ensure_encryption_with_cus.description: **Azure Storage accounts** use **customer-managed keys** (`CMK`) from **Key Vault/Managed HSM** for service-side encryption of data at rest, rather than platform-managed keys (`encryption_type`=`Microsoft.Keyvault`).
azure.storage_ensure_encryption_with_cus.risk:
Without **CMK**, keys are provider-controlled, reducing **confidentiality** and governance.
- Cannot promptly revoke access during incidents
- No custom rotation or separation of duties
- Limited key-use auditing
This weakens data sovereignty and hinders effective crypto-shredding.

remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, open your Storage account
2. Go to Settings > Encryption (or Security + networking > Encryption)
3. Select Customer-managed keys
4. Click Select a key vault and key, choose your Key Vault and key
5. If prompted, enable System-assigned managed identity and grant the key permissions get, wrapKey, unwrapKey
6. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Adopt **CMK** with keys in Key Vault or Managed HSM. Enforce **least privilege** for the storage identity, regular **key rotation**, and **separation of duties** between key custodians and operators. Audit key usage, enable tamper-resistant key protection (soft-delete/purge protection), and plan for **key revocation/crypto-shredding**.

azure.storage_ensure_file_shares_soft_de.title: Storage account has soft delete enabled for file shares
azure.storage_ensure_file_shares_soft_de.description: **Azure Storage file shares** have **soft delete** with a retention period (`days`). The evaluation determines if the storage account's file service has this setting enabled and records the retention duration applied to all shares.
azure.storage_ensure_file_shares_soft_de.risk: Without **soft delete**, deletions are irreversible, reducing **availability** and **integrity**. Mistakes or insiders can wipe shares, causing outages, data loss, and lengthy restores. Destructive deletes can magnify ransomware impact and block timely recovery.

remediation.cli: az storage account file-service-properties update --resource-group <resource-group> --account-name <storage-account-name> --enable-delete-retention true --delete-retention-days 7
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Storage accounts and open <storage-account-name>
2. Under Data storage, select File shares
3. Set Soft delete to Enabled
4. Set Retention period (days) to 7
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **soft delete** for all Azure file shares and choose a retention window aligned to `RPO/RTO` and data criticality (e.g., `7-90` days). Apply **least privilege** to delete actions, layer **snapshots/backup** for defense in depth, consider **resource locks**, and monitor delete events for misuse.

azure.storage_ensure_minimum_tls_version.title: Storage account minimum TLS version is 1.2
azure.storage_ensure_minimum_tls_version.description: **Azure Storage accounts** enforce a `minimum TLS version` of `1.2` for client connections to data services
azure.storage_ensure_minimum_tls_version.risk: Allowing TLS `1.0`/`1.1` enables protocol downgrades and exploitation of known flaws (e.g., BEAST), weakening **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Attackers can intercept or modify data in transit and harvest credentials via weakened cipher suites.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Storage account with minimum TLS 1.2
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                     = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name      = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                 = "<example_location>"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"

  min_tls_version = "TLS1_2" # CRITICAL: Enforces minimum TLS 1.2 to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure Portal, go to Storage accounts and open your account
2. Select Settings > Configuration
3. Set Minimum TLS version to Version 1.2
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Set the storage account `minimum TLS version` to at least `1.2` (prefer `1.3` where supported) and disable legacy protocols. Apply **defense in depth** by restricting network access, using **least privilege** credentials, and monitoring handshake failures to identify outdated clients.

azure.storage_ensure_private_endpoints_i.title: Storage account has private endpoint connections
azure.storage_ensure_private_endpoints_i.description: **Azure Storage accounts** are evaluated for the presence of **Private Endpoint** connections. When configured, traffic flows over a VNet private IP via Private Link; when absent, access occurs through the storage account's public endpoint.
azure.storage_ensure_private_endpoints_i.risk:
Relying on the **public endpoint** widens exposure:
- Confidentiality: higher risk of key/SAS compromise and unauthorized reads
- Integrity: abused creds enable writes/deletes
- Availability: subject to DDoS and internet scanning
It can also bypass egress controls, easing covert data exfiltration.

remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Storage accounts > select your account
2. Under Security + networking, choose Networking > Private endpoint connections
3. Click + Private endpoint > Create
4. Resource type: Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts; Resource: your account; Target subresource: blob
5. Select the Virtual network and Subnet, then Review + create > Create
remediation.recommendationText:
Prefer **Private Endpoints** for storage access and minimize public exposure:
- Limit or disable `Public network access`
- Use private DNS so names resolve to private IPs
- Enforce **least privilege** and **defense in depth** with segmentation and logging
- Monitor access and rotate keys/SAS *as part of routine hygiene*.

azure.storage_ensure_soft_delete_is_enab.title: Storage account has soft delete for containers enabled
azure.storage_ensure_soft_delete_is_enab.description: **Azure Storage accounts** have **container soft delete** enabled via a retention policy that keeps deleted containers for a set period.
azure.storage_ensure_soft_delete_is_enab.risk: Without this, container deletions are permanent, reducing **availability** and **integrity**. A compromised user or faulty automation could erase entire datasets, forcing slow restores from backups and extending RTO/RPO, with potential downstream app outages.

remediation.cli: az storage account blob-service-properties update --resource-group <example_resource_name> --account-name <example_resource_name> --enable-container-delete-retention true --container-delete-retention-days 7
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Storage accounts and open <storage account>
2. Under Data management, select Data protection
3. In the Containers section, turn on Soft delete for containers and set Retention (days) to a value (e.g., 7)
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **container soft delete** and choose a retention window (`7-365` days) that meets your RPO. Pair with **blob soft delete** and **versioning** for layered recovery. Enforce **least privilege** on delete actions and apply resource **locks** to prevent destructive changes.

azure.storage_ensure_soft_delete_is_enab.notes: Additional storage costs may be incurred as snapshots are retained.

azure.storage_geo_redundant_enabled.title: Azure Storage account uses geo-redundant replication (GRS, GZRS, RA-GRS, or RA-GZRS)
azure.storage_geo_redundant_enabled.description:
**Azure Storage accounts** configured for **geo-redundant replication** via `Standard_GRS`, `Standard_GZRS`, `Standard_RAGRS`, or `Standard_RAGZRS`.

The setting indicates data is copied to a paired secondary region, with `RA-*` allowing read access during primary-region unavailability.
azure.storage_geo_redundant_enabled.risk: Absent **geo-replication**, data resides in one region, undermining **availability** and **durability** during regional failures. Disasters can cause prolonged downtime or unrecoverable loss. With geo-replication but without `RA-*`, the secondary is unreadable, increasing RTO and interrupting business continuity.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "example" {
  name                     = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name      = "<example_resource_group_name>"
  location                 = "<example_location>"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "GRS" # Critical: enables geo-redundant replication to pass the check
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Storage accounts and open your storage account
2. Under Data management, select Redundancy
3. Change Redundancy to GRS, GZRS, RA-GRS, or RA-GZRS
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Adopt **GRS/GZRS** for critical workloads (prefer `Standard_GZRS` where supported) to achieve cross-region resilience. *If read continuity is required*, use `Standard_RAGRS` or `Standard_RAGZRS`. Define RPO/RTO, regularly test failover, and design for **defense in depth** across regions and zones.

azure.storage_infrastructure_encryption_.title: Storage account has infrastructure encryption enabled
azure.storage_infrastructure_encryption_.description: **Azure Storage accounts** have **infrastructure encryption** enabled, providing **double encryption at rest** alongside service-level encryption (`requireInfrastructureEncryption=true`).
azure.storage_infrastructure_encryption_.risk: Without this second layer, compromise of the service-level key or algorithm can expose stored data, degrading **confidentiality** and weakening **defense in depth**. Insider misuse or key theft is more likely to yield readable blobs, files, or tables.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Storage account with infrastructure encryption enabled
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                     = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name      = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                 = "<location>"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"

  infrastructure_encryption_enabled = true # Critical: enables infrastructure-level encryption (double encryption)
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Storage accounts and click Create
2. Choose a supported type (StorageV2 or a premium blob/page/file account)
3. Open the Encryption tab and set Enable infrastructure encryption to Enabled
4. Click Review + create, then Create
5. Migrate data from the old account to this new account and decommission the old one (infrastructure encryption cannot be enabled on existing accounts)
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **infrastructure encryption** for accounts or scopes handling sensitive data to strengthen **defense in depth**. Plan it at creation, as the setting is immutable. Maintain strong key hygiene for service-level encryption (use CMK where appropriate, rotate, restrict access) and enforce guardrails with policy.

azure.storage_key_rotation_90_days.title: Storage account has access key expiration period set to 90 days or less
azure.storage_key_rotation_90_days.description: **Azure Storage accounts** must define a `key expiration period` for access-key rotation, with a maximum of `90` days. The evaluation looks for accounts lacking this setting or exceeding that limit.
azure.storage_key_rotation_90_days.risk: Long-lived storage access keys undermine **confidentiality** and **integrity**: a leaked or reused key grants full data access and can sign SAS tokens. Extended validity enables persistent unauthorized access, data exfiltration, and tampering, and complicates revocation and incident response.

remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to your storage account
2. Navigate to Security + networking > Access keys
3. Click Set rotation reminder
4. Enable key rotation reminders and set the period to 90 days or less
5. Click Save
6. If Set rotation reminder is disabled, first regenerate both keys (Regenerate for key1, then key2), then repeat steps 3-5
remediation.recommendationText: Enforce a `key expiration period` of `<= 90` days and automate rotation. Prefer **Microsoft Entra ID** with managed identities over Shared Key; when SAS is needed, use user-delegation SAS. Apply **least privilege**, minimize key distribution, monitor usage, rotate on suspected exposure, and disable Shared Key when feasible.

azure.storage_secure_transfer_required_i.title: Storage account has secure transfer required enabled
azure.storage_secure_transfer_required_i.description: **Azure Storage accounts** are evaluated for **secure transfer enforcement**, requiring all client requests to use `HTTPS` only (`enableHttpsTrafficOnly`) and blocking `HTTP`.
azure.storage_secure_transfer_required_i.risk:
Allowing `HTTP` to storage endpoints enables **man-in-the-middle** and **TLS-stripping** attacks.
Intercepted traffic can expose credentials, SAS tokens, or data (**confidentiality**) and allow request tampering (**integrity**), leading to unauthorized access and **data exfiltration**.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable secure transfer (HTTPS only) on a Storage Account
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                     = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name      = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                 = "<location>"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"

  enable_https_traffic_only = true # Critical: require HTTPS-only (secure transfer)
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Storage accounts and select the account
2. Under Settings, open Configuration
3. Set Secure transfer required to Enabled
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Enforce **HTTPS-only** on all storage accounts (`enableHttpsTrafficOnly`) and use modern TLS.
Apply **least privilege** to SAS and keys, rotate if exposure is suspected, and use **defense in depth**: prefer private endpoints, restrict public access, block `HTTP` at network controls, and ensure all clients use `https://` endpoints.

azure.storage_smb_channel_encryption_wit.title: Storage account uses AES-256-GCM for SMB channel encryption on file shares
azure.storage_smb_channel_encryption_wit.description:
**Azure Storage file shares (SMB)** are evaluated for **SMB channel encryption** and whether the allowed ciphers include the recommended `AES-256-GCM`.

This identifies if encryption is configured and a secure algorithm is present in the SMB settings for file shares within the storage account.
azure.storage_smb_channel_encryption_wit.risk: Missing or weak SMB channel encryption undermines **confidentiality** and **integrity**. On-path attackers could read sensitive files, capture hashes, or modify data in transit. Allowing legacy ciphers increases downgrade risks and can facilitate **lateral movement**, eroding trust boundaries across networks.

remediation.cli: az storage account file-service-properties update --resource-group <resource-group> --account-name <storage-account> --channel-encryption AES-256-GCM
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, open your storage account
2. Go to Data storage > File shares
3. Under File share settings, click Security
4. Select Custom
5. Under SMB channel encryption, select AES-256-GCM
6. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Enforce **defense in depth** by restricting SMB channel encryption to `AES-256-GCM` on SMB `3.1.1`, removing weaker options.

- Prefer private access (private endpoints/VPN)
- Require secure transfer and modern TLS
- Apply **least privilege** on shares
- Validate client support and monitor connections during rollout

azure.storage_smb_channel_encryption_wit.notes: This check passes only if every SMB channel encryption algorithm allowed on the file shares is in the recommended list, which is configurable via azure.recommended_smb_channel_encryption_algorithms and defaults to AES-256-GCM only, as required by CIS.

azure.storage_smb_protocol_version_is_la.title: Storage account allows only the latest SMB protocol version for file shares
azure.storage_smb_protocol_version_is_la.description: **Azure Storage file shares (SMB)** are configured to allow **only the latest SMB protocol version**, blocking legacy SMB versions at the storage account level
azure.storage_smb_protocol_version_is_la.risk: Allowing legacy SMB versions enables **protocol downgrade** and weak cipher negotiation, reducing **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Adversaries can intercept or alter traffic, bypass strong signing/encryption, and exploit known flaws for lateral movement or credential replay

remediation.cli: az storage account file-service-properties update --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --account-name <STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME> --versions SMB3.1.1
remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Storage accounts and open your storage account
2. Navigate to Data storage > File shares
3. Under File share settings, select Security
4. Choose Profile: Custom, then under SMB protocol versions select only SMB 3.1.1
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Restrict SMB to the newest version (e.g., `SMB 3.1.1`) and disable older versions. Enforce **encryption in transit** and prefer **Kerberos** over NTLM. Validate client compatibility, apply **least privilege** on shares, and monitor access to maintain **defense in depth**

azure.vm_backup_enabled.title: Virtual Machine is protected by Azure Backup
azure.vm_backup_enabled.description:
**Azure VMs** are evaluated for protection by **Azure Backup** by confirming they exist as VM backup items in a **Recovery Services vault**.

VMs absent from any vault item indicate no configured backup coverage.
azure.vm_backup_enabled.risk: Unprotected VMs jeopardize **availability** and **integrity**. Deletion, corruption, or ransomware can wipe data, and without recovery points recovery is slow or impossible, causing extended outages, missed `RPO/RTO`, and cascading impact on dependent services.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Protect an existing VM with Azure Backup
resource "azurerm_backup_protected_vm" "<example_resource_name>" {
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"   # vault's resource group
  recovery_vault_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  source_vm_id        = "<example_resource_id>"     # critical: VM to protect
  backup_policy_id    = "<example_resource_id>"     # critical: policy that enables backup
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Virtual machines > <VM> > Backup
2. Select a Recovery Services vault in the same region (or create one if prompted)
3. Choose the DefaultPolicy (or an existing VM backup policy)
4. Click Enable backup
remediation.recommendationText: Protect all VMs with **Azure Backup** in a **Recovery Services vault** under a standardized policy. Align schedules and retention to `RPO/RTO`, use `GRS`/`ZRS` and `immutable` vault features, enforce least privilege on backup operations, automate enrollment at provisioning, and regularly test restores.

azure.vm_desired_sku_size.title: Virtual Machine uses an organization-approved SKU size
azure.vm_desired_sku_size.description:
**Azure virtual machines** are compared against an organization **allowlist of VM size SKUs** defined in `desired_vm_sku_sizes`.

Instances using sizes outside this list are flagged as non-standard.
azure.vm_desired_sku_size.risk:
Unrestricted VM sizes enable over-provisioned or exotic SKUs, leading to:
- Sudden cost spikes and quota exhaustion (availability)
- Use of hardware lacking required security features (confidentiality/integrity)
- Abuse by compromised accounts for cryptomining at scale

remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Virtual machines and select the VM
2. Under Availability + scale, select Size
3. Choose an approved size (e.g., <desired-sku-1>) and click Resize
4. If the size isn't listed, Stop (deallocate) the VM, then retry Resize
remediation.recommendationText:
Adopt a **least privilege, policy-enforced allowlist** of VM size SKUs per workload tier and region.
- Deny creation of non-approved sizes across scopes
- Require exception reviews with time-bound overrides
- Reassess the list regularly for cost, performance, and compliance
- Monitor provisioning and cost anomalies for drift

azure.vm_desired_sku_size.notes: This check requires configuration of the desired VM SKU sizes in the Prowler configuration file. Configure the azure.desired_vm_sku_sizes list in your Prowler configuration file (see https://docs.prowler.com/projects/prowler-open-source/en/latest/tutorials/configuration_file/) with the SKU sizes approved by your organization.

azure.vm_ensure_attached_disks_encrypted.title: Virtual Machine OS or data disk is encrypted with a customer-managed key (CMK)
azure.vm_ensure_attached_disks_encrypted.description: **Attached Azure managed disks** (OS and data) are assessed to confirm encryption uses **customer-managed keys** (`CMK`) via disk encryption sets rather than platform-managed keys. Scope includes disks currently attached to VMs, evaluating their encryption type to verify CMK is applied.
azure.vm_ensure_attached_disks_encrypted.risk: Without **CMK**, you lose control over key lifecycle and access. This weakens confidentiality and compliance: you can't enforce independent rotation, promptly revoke keys to crypto-lock stolen copies/snapshots, or separate duties. Misuse or compromise may keep data readable beyond your trust boundary.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Encrypt a managed disk with a customer-managed key via Disk Encryption Set (DES)
resource "azurerm_managed_disk" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<LOCATION>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  storage_account_type = "Standard_LRS"
  create_option        = "Empty"
  disk_size_gb         = 32

  # CRITICAL: Attach DES to enable SSE with CMK and pass the check
  disk_encryption_set_id = "<example_resource_id>" # critical: DES ID
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, open the target VM and click Stop to deallocate it.
2. For each data disk: Go to VM > Disks > select the data disk > Detach > Save.
3. In the portal search box, open Disks, select the detached disk > Encryption.
4. Set Encryption type to Customer-managed key (Disk encryption set), select your Disk Encryption Set, then Save.
5. Reattach the disk: VM > Disks > Add data disk (select the same disk) > Save.
6. For OS disk, use Swap OS disk: create a new managed disk from a snapshot/image with Encryption type = Customer-managed key (select the same DES), then VM > Disks > Swap OS disk and choose that disk.
7. Start the VM.
remediation.recommendationText:
Use **CMK** with disk encryption sets for all attached OS and data disks.
- Enforce **least privilege** on key usage and scope
- Enable periodic key rotation and auditing
- Store keys in HSM-backed vaults; separate key and data admins
- Combine with **encryption at host** to cover temp disks and caches

azure.vm_ensure_attached_disks_encrypted.notes: Using CMK/BYOK will entail additional management of keys.

azure.vm_ensure_unattached_disks_encrypt.title: Unattached disk is encrypted with a customer-managed key (CMK)
azure.vm_ensure_unattached_disks_encrypt.description: Unattached **Azure managed disks** use **Customer-Managed Keys** (`CMK`) for server-side encryption rather than platform-managed keys. Only disks not currently attached to a VM are in scope.
azure.vm_ensure_unattached_disks_encrypt.risk: Without **CMK**, you lack independent key control on unattached disks. A compromised admin could attach a disk to read or alter data before you can revoke access. Missing customer-controlled rotation and revocation weakens **confidentiality** and **integrity**, and can hinder data-sovereignty compliance.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Associate an unattached managed disk with a Disk Encryption Set (CMK)
resource "azurerm_managed_disk" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<location>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  create_option       = "Empty"
  disk_size_gb        = 1

  disk_encryption_set_id = "<example_resource_id>" # CRITICAL: enables CMK by linking the Disk Encryption Set
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure portal, go to Disks and open the unattached disk
2. Select Encryption
3. Set Encryption type to Customer-managed key
4. Select the Disk encryption set to use
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Encrypt unattached disks with **CMK** backed by a hardened key service. Enforce **least privilege** for disk attachment and key usage, enable key rotation and auditing, and restrict access to keys. Apply lifecycle governance-*remove stale disks*-to reduce exposure and support **defense in depth**.

azure.vm_ensure_unattached_disks_encrypt.notes: You must have your key vault set up to utilize this. Encryption is available only on Standard tier VMs. This might cost you more. Utilizing and maintaining Customer-managed keys will require additional work to create, protect, and rotate keys.

azure.vm_ensure_using_approved_images.title: Virtual Machine uses an approved custom machine image
azure.vm_ensure_using_approved_images.description: **Azure VMs** are evaluated for use of an **approved custom image** by inspecting the VM image reference. The expected format is a subscription-scoped ID like `/subscriptions/.../providers/Microsoft.Compute/images/<image>`, not marketplace, gallery, or community sources.
azure.vm_ensure_using_approved_images.risk: Using **unapproved images** undermines **integrity** and **confidentiality** by introducing unknown packages, misconfigurations, or malware. Attackers can implant backdoors, weaken hardening, and bypass baselines, enabling data exfiltration and lateral movement, and harming **availability** with unpatched software.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# VM created from an approved custom managed image
resource "azurerm_windows_virtual_machine" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_id>"
  location            = "<example_resource_location>"
  size                = "Standard_DS1_v2"
  admin_username      = "<example_resource_name>"
  admin_password      = "<example_resource_id>"
  network_interface_ids = ["<example_resource_id>"]

  source_image_id = "/subscriptions/<subscription_id>/resourceGroups/<example_resource_id>/providers/Microsoft.Compute/images/<example_resource_name>" # CRITICAL: managed image ID ensures PASS

  os_disk {
    caching              = "ReadWrite"
    storage_account_type = "Standard_LRS"
  }
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Virtual machines > Create > Azure virtual machine
2. Under Image, click See all images, then select the My Images tab
3. Choose the approved managed image (type: Microsoft.Compute/images)
4. Complete required basics and create the VM
5. If replacing a non-compliant VM, migrate workload and delete the old VM
remediation.recommendationText:
Standardize on **golden images** maintained in an Azure Compute Gallery or managed images.
- Harden and patch each release; scan for vulnerabilities
- Restrict who can create/publish images (**least privilege**)
- Enforce deployments only from approved images via policy
- Version, sign, and retire images regularly

azure.vm_ensure_using_approved_images.notes: This check only validates if the VM was launched from a custom image. It does not validate the image content or security baseline.

azure.vm_ensure_using_managed_disks.title: Virtual Machine uses managed disks for OS and data disks
azure.vm_ensure_using_managed_disks.description:
**Azure virtual machines** use **managed disks** for the OS disk and every data disk, rather than page blob VHDs in storage accounts.

The evaluation confirms that all attached VM disks are managed.
azure.vm_ensure_using_managed_disks.risk: Using **unmanaged disks** ties VM data to storage account keys and SAS, increasing exposure of disk contents if those secrets leak (**confidentiality/integrity**). Limited platform resiliency and quotas increase **availability** risk. With Azure retiring unmanaged disks on `2026-03-31`, such VMs may be stopped and unable to start.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# VM attached to a managed OS disk
resource "azurerm_virtual_machine" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                  = "<example_resource_name>"
  location              = "<LOCATION>"
  resource_group_name   = "<RESOURCE_GROUP>"
  network_interface_ids = ["<example_resource_id>"]
  vm_size               = "Standard_DS1_v2"

  storage_os_disk {
    name            = "osdisk"
    create_option   = "Attach"
    managed_disk_id = "<example_resource_id>" # CRITICAL: use a managed disk for the OS disk
  }
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Virtual machines > select your VM
2. Click Stop to deallocate the VM
3. In the VM menu, select Disks
4. Click Migrate to managed disks, then click Migrate to start
5. After migration completes, click Start to power on the VM
6. If the VM is in an availability set: first go to Availability sets > select the set > Convert to managed (SKU: Aligned), then repeat steps 1-5
remediation.recommendationText:
Adopt **managed disks** for all VM OS and data volumes.
- Enforce **least privilege** via RBAC at disk scope
- Use encryption at rest; prefer `CMEK` when mandated
- Apply backups/snapshots and zone-aware designs for **defense in depth**
- After migration, delete orphaned VHD blobs to avoid data exposure and cost.

azure.vm_ensure_using_managed_disks.notes: There are additional costs for managed disks based off of disk space allocated. When converting to managed disks, VMs will be powered off and back on.

azure.vm_jit_access_enabled.title: Virtual Machine has Just-in-Time (JIT) access enabled
azure.vm_jit_access_enabled.description: **Azure virtual machines** are associated with a **Just-in-Time (JIT) network access policy** that opens management ports only for approved, time-bound requests from specified source IPs.
azure.vm_jit_access_enabled.risk:
Without **JIT**, management ports like `22`/`3389` may stay reachable, enabling:
- brute-force and password-spray attempts
- exploitation of remote access flaws or stolen keys
This threatens **confidentiality** (data exfiltration), **integrity** (unauthorized changes), and **availability** (service disruption).

remediation.other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Microsoft Defender for Cloud
2. Select Workload protections > Just-in-time VM access
3. Open the Not configured tab, select the VM, and click Enable JIT on VMs
4. Keep the default port (22 for Linux or 3389 for Windows) and click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable **JIT network access** and apply **least privilege** and **zero trust**:
- keep admin ports closed by default
- approve only specific IPs, minimal ports (e.g., `22`, `3389`), and short windows
- favor **private access** (VPN, Bastion)
- layer controls (**defense in depth**) and audit access requests

azure.vm_jit_access_enabled.notes: JIT access can only be enabled via the Azure Portal. Ensure Security Center standard pricing tier for servers is enabled.

azure.vm_linux_enforce_ssh_authenticatio.title: Linux Virtual Machine has password authentication disabled (SSH key authentication enforced)
azure.vm_linux_enforce_ssh_authenticatio.description: **Azure Linux virtual machines** are assessed for SSH configuration where `disablePasswordAuthentication` is set to `true`, allowing only **public key authentication** and disallowing interactive passwords.
azure.vm_linux_enforce_ssh_authenticatio.risk: With **password-based SSH**, attackers can run brute-force or password-spray campaigns. A successful login grants remote shell, enabling command execution, data exfiltration, and lateral movement, degrading **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Minimal Terraform to enforce SSH key authentication on a Linux VM
resource "azurerm_linux_virtual_machine" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<example_location>"
  size                = "Standard_B1s"
  network_interface_ids = ["<example_resource_id>"]
  admin_username        = "azureuser"

  disable_password_authentication = true  # CRITICAL: Disables password-based SSH; enforces SSH key authentication

  admin_ssh_key {                         # Required when password auth is disabled
    username   = "azureuser"
    public_key = "<example_public_key>"
  }

  os_disk {
    caching              = "ReadWrite"
    storage_account_type = "Standard_LRS"
  }

  source_image_reference {
    publisher = "Canonical"
    offer     = "0001-com-ubuntu-server-focal"
    sku       = "20_04-lts"
    version   = "latest"
  }
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to your Linux VM > Settings > Export template
2. Click Edit template
3. Find properties.osProfile.linuxConfiguration and set disablePasswordAuthentication to true
4. Ensure an SSH public key is provided (adminPassword must be absent)
5. Click Save, then Review + create to deploy the update
remediation.recommendationText: Enforce **key-only SSH** by setting `disablePasswordAuthentication` to `true` and disallowing OS password logins. Use strong, passphrase-protected keys with rotation; restrict SSH via NSGs and private access or **Azure Bastion**; enable JIT; and apply **least privilege**.

azure.vm_scaleset_associated_with_load_b.title: Virtual Machine Scale Set is associated with a load balancer backend pool
azure.vm_scaleset_associated_with_load_b.description:
**Azure VM scale sets** are associated with at least one **load balancer backend pool**.

The evaluation looks for a backend pool link on each scale set's network configuration.
azure.vm_scaleset_associated_with_load_b.risk: Without a load balancer, traffic targets instances directly, bypassing health-based distribution. This degrades **availability** (overloads, no failover) and **reliability** (dropped sessions, uneven scaling) and can amplify **DoS** impact by concentrating flows on fewer nodes, increasing outage risk.

remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Load balancers > select <LB_NAME>
2. Under Settings, open Backend pools and select the target backend pool
3. Click Add > IP configurations
4. Choose Virtual machine scale set, select <VMSS_NAME> and its IP configuration
5. Click Add, then Save to attach the scale set to the backend pool
remediation.recommendationText:
Associate VM scale sets with a **Standard Load Balancer** backend pool to enforce health-probed, even distribution and seamless failover.

Design for **high availability**: run multiple instances across zones, enable autoscale, and apply **defense in depth** with limited exposure and NSG controls. *Prefer SKU `Standard` over legacy Basic.*

azure.vm_scaleset_not_empty.title: Virtual Machine Scale Set has at least one VM instance
azure.vm_scaleset_not_empty.description: **Azure VM scale sets** with `0` VM instances are identified as **empty**.
azure.vm_scaleset_not_empty.risk: Orphaned scale sets degrade governance and can hide **stale autoscale** or permissive identities. If reactivated, they may launch VMs from **outdated images**, exposing vulnerable services and enabling lateral movement, impacting **confidentiality** and **availability**. They also create inventory sprawl and unnecessary spend.

remediation.other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Virtual machine scale sets and select <scale-set-name>
2. Under Settings, click Scaling
3. Set Instance count to 1
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Decommission empty scale sets or consolidate capacity. Apply **resource lifecycle** and **governance policies** to prevent drift; require tagging and owners, review regularly.
