- **Data exfiltration** from compromised workloads (confidentiality)
- **Supply chain compromise** via unvetted base images

remediation.other:
1. In the Google Cloud console, go to APIs & Services > Library
2. Search for "Container Scanning API"
3. Click the result and then click "Enable"
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable `containerscanning.googleapis.com` and integrate results into CI/CD gates. Apply **defense in depth**:
- Use **Binary Authorization** to block noncompliant images
- Enforce **least privilege** over who can disable scanning
- Rebuild and patch frequently; prefer trusted, signed base images

gcp.gcr_container_scanning_enabled.notes: By default, GCR Container Scanning is disabled.

gcp.gemini_api_disabled.title: Gemini (Generative Language) API is disabled
gcp.gemini_api_disabled.description: The Gemini API (a.k.a. Generative Language API, `generativelanguage.googleapis.com`) should not be used. It does not adhere to GCP's general security & compliance standards.
gcp.gemini_api_disabled.risk: The API does not support GCP IAM for authentication, impacting confidentiality of uploaded files and cached content. It provides no SLA, reducing availability guarantees. It is not covered by compliance certifications such as ISO 27001, SOC 2, C5, and HIPAA, which can diminish your compliance posture.

remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to "APIs & Services" > "Enabled APIs & services"
2. Click "Generative Language API" to view service details.
3. Click "Disable API" in the top bar and confirm the action.
remediation.recommendationText: Do not use the Gemini API. Instead, consider using Gemini through the Vertex AI API, which does not have the described issues.

gcp.gke_cluster_no_default_service_accou.title: GKE cluster does not use the Compute Engine default service account
gcp.gke_cluster_no_default_service_accou.description: **GKE clusters** are evaluated for use of the **Compute Engine default service account** (`default`) as the node identity. The expectation is that clusters and node pools run with dedicated, minimally privileged IAM service accounts instead of the project-wide default.
gcp.gke_cluster_no_default_service_accou.risk: **Default node service accounts** often have broad project access. If a node is compromised, its credentials can read secrets, modify resources, or delete infrastructure, enabling lateral movement and data exfiltration. This harms **confidentiality**, **integrity**, and **availability** across the environment.

remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to Kubernetes Engine > Clusters and open your cluster
2. Click Add node pool
3. In Security > Service account, select your non-default service account and click Create
4. In Nodes > Node Pools, delete the node pool(s) that show Service account = default
remediation.recommendationText:
Assign a **custom, least-privileged IAM service account** to each node pool instead of `default`.
- Grant only permissions required for node logging/monitoring and operations
- Enforce **separation of duties** and restrict impersonation
- Periodically review roles and audit usage for **defense in depth**

gcp.gke_cluster_no_default_service_accou.notes: By default, nodes use the Compute Engine default service account when you create a new cluster.

gcp.iam_account_access_approval_enabled.title: Project has Access Approval enabled
gcp.iam_account_access_approval_enabled.description: **GCP project** has **Access Approval** configured at the project level, requiring explicit customer authorization before Google personnel can access project data. The evaluation looks for Access Approval settings associated with the project.
gcp.iam_account_access_approval_enabled.risk: Without Access Approval, Google support or engineering may access Customer Data without prior consent, weakening **confidentiality** and **accountability**. Reduced visibility hinders incident response and raises exposure for sensitive or regulated workloads.

remediation.other:
1. In the Google Cloud Console, go to Security > Access Approval (or search "Access Approval")
2. Select the project <example_resource_id>
3. Click Enable (or Edit settings if already open)
4. Set Enrolled services to All Google Cloud services
5. Click Save (enable the API if prompted)
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **Access Approval** for projects and *where feasible* at higher hierarchy for consistency. Assign **least-privilege approvers** with **separation of duties**, integrate timely notifications, and monitor **Access Transparency** records to maintain **defense in depth**.

gcp.iam_audit_logs_enabled.title: GCP project has Cloud Audit Logs enabled
gcp.iam_audit_logs_enabled.description: **GCP project** has **Cloud Audit Logs** configured to capture administrative operations and data access events for services and principals (*per IAM Audit Logs*, including `ADMIN_READ`, `DATA_READ`, `DATA_WRITE`).
gcp.iam_audit_logs_enabled.risk:
Absent or partial audit logging reduces visibility into who accessed data or changed configurations, hindering detection and forensics.

Misused identities can alter IAM to persist access, exfiltrate data, or delete resources, impacting **confidentiality**, **integrity**, and **availability**.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Enable Cloud Audit Logs (Data Access) for all services
resource "google_project_iam_audit_config" "all" {
  project = "<example_resource_id>"
  service = "allServices" # Critical: apply to all services

  # Critical: enable Data Access audit log types to pass the check
  audit_log_config { log_type = "ADMIN_READ" }  # metadata/config reads
  audit_log_config { log_type = "DATA_READ" }   # data reads
  audit_log_config { log_type = "DATA_WRITE" }  # data writes
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Google Cloud console, go to IAM & Admin > Audit Logs
2. Click Set default configuration
3. Under Permission types, check Admin Read, Data Read, and Data Write
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable comprehensive **Cloud Audit Logs** for all services and principals, including `ADMIN_READ`, `DATA_READ`, `DATA_WRITE`. *Avoid exemptions.* Set org/folder defaults, centralize and retain logs, enforce least privilege on log access, protect logs from alteration, and alert on anomalous access.

gcp.iam_cloud_asset_inventory_enabled.title: Project has Cloud Asset Inventory API enabled
gcp.iam_cloud_asset_inventory_enabled.description: **Project service usage** includes the **Cloud Asset Inventory** API (`cloudasset.googleapis.com`), enabling resource and IAM policy inventory with time-series metadata and change history.
gcp.iam_cloud_asset_inventory_enabled.risk: Without **Cloud Asset Inventory**, gaps in asset and IAM visibility hinder detection of drift and unauthorized changes, weakening access control integrity and risking data confidentiality. Shadow assets and silent privilege escalation can persist, delaying incident response.

remediation.other:
1. In the Google Cloud Console, select the project <PROJECT_ID> from the project picker.
2. Go to APIs & Services > Library.
3. Search for "Cloud Asset Inventory API" and select it.
4. Click Enable.
5. Verify it appears under APIs & Services > Enabled APIs & services.
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **Cloud Asset Inventory** across all projects *and, if applicable, at the organization level* to maintain authoritative asset and IAM histories. Centralize analysis, retain records per policy, and use the data to enforce **least privilege** and **defense in depth**.

gcp.iam_no_service_roles_at_project_leve.title: Project has no IAM users assigned the Service Account User or Service Account Token Creator roles at project level
gcp.iam_no_service_roles_at_project_leve.description: **Google Cloud IAM policies** are inspected for **project-level grants** of `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` and `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` to principals. The focus is on bindings that enable attaching or impersonating service accounts at the project scope rather than on individual service accounts.
gcp.iam_no_service_roles_at_project_leve.risk: **Project-wide impersonation rights** enable **privilege escalation** and **lateral movement**. Holders can act as any service account, access data across services, modify resources, and persist access. New service accounts inherit exposure, undermining confidentiality and integrity.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Grant required access at the service account level instead of the project level
resource "google_service_account_iam_member" "<example_resource_name>" {
  service_account_id = "projects/<example_resource_id>/serviceAccounts/<example_resource_name>@<example_resource_id>.iam.gserviceaccount.com"  # CRITICAL: scope grant to a specific service account, not the project
  role               = "roles/iam.serviceAccountUser"  # CRITICAL: this role is granted only at the service account level
  member             = "user:<example_resource_name>@example.com"
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to IAM & Admin > IAM
2. Use the filter to find Role: Service Account User
3. Remove all project-level bindings for this role and click Save
4. Repeat steps 2-3 for Role: Service Account Token Creator
5. Do not add these roles at the project level; if needed, grant them on specific service accounts only (IAM & Admin > Service Accounts > select account > Permissions > Grant access)
remediation.recommendationText: Assign `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` and `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` only on the specific service account, not at project scope. Enforce **least privilege** and **separation of duties** with per-SA grants, conditional bindings, and time-bound access. Prefer **short-lived impersonation**; review grants regularly.

gcp.iam_organization_essential_contacts_.title: Organization has Essential Contacts configured
gcp.iam_organization_essential_contacts_.description:
Google Cloud organization has **Essential Contacts** defined at the organization level for categories such as `SECURITY`, `BILLING`, `LEGAL`, `SUSPENSION`, `TECHNICAL`, or `PRODUCT_UPDATES`.

Evaluates whether at least one contact is configured.
gcp.iam_organization_essential_contacts_.risk:
Missing **Essential Contacts** means security, abuse, and billing notices can go unnoticed or to inappropriate recipients, slowing response.

Consequences: data exposure via unaddressed alerts (C), unauthorized changes persisting (I), and suspensions/outages from unresolved issues (A).

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "google_essential_contacts_contact" "<example_resource_name>" {
  parent = "organizations/<example_resource_id>"            # Critical: set at org level to satisfy the check
  email  = "<EMAIL>"                                        # Critical: creates the essential contact
  notification_category_subscriptions = ["ALL"]             # Critical: required; ensures the contact is created
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In the Google Cloud console, go to Essential Contacts
2. In the resource selector, choose your Organization
3. Click Add contact
4. Enter the contact email and select category All
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Configure **Essential Contacts** at the organization (and inherit to folders/projects) with group aliases for `SECURITY`, `BILLING`, `LEGAL`, `SUSPENSION`, `TECHNICAL`, and `PRODUCT_UPDATES`.

Apply **least privilege** and **separation of duties**. Review quarterly, verify delivery, and restrict contacts to approved domains.

gcp.iam_role_kms_enforce_separation_of_d.title: Project members are not assigned both Cloud KMS Admin and CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter roles
gcp.iam_role_kms_enforce_separation_of_d.description: Project IAM assignments are analyzed for **Cloud KMS** separation of duties: principals simultaneously granted `roles/cloudkms.admin` and any of `roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter`, `roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypter`, or `roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyDecrypter`.
gcp.iam_role_kms_enforce_separation_of_d.risk:
Combining key management and key usage undermines **confidentiality**, **integrity**, and **availability**:
- Unauthorized decryption of sensitive data
- Tampering with policies or rotation to conceal access
- Disabling or destroying keys, causing outages

This concentration of power reduces oversight and auditability.

remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to IAM & Admin > IAM
2. Locate the principal listed in the finding and click Edit principal
3. Remove either "Cloud KMS Admin" or any of the "Cloud KMS CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter" roles from the project
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Apply **least privilege** and **separation of duties**:
- Never combine `roles/cloudkms.admin` with any `roles/cloudkms.cryptoKey*`
- Isolate key management and usage in dedicated projects
- Require approvals, log all key access, and monitor
- Avoid broad `roles/owner` on key scopes

gcp.iam_role_sa_enforce_separation_of_du.title: Project enforces separation of duties for Service Account Admin and Service Account User roles
gcp.iam_role_sa_enforce_separation_of_du.description: Google Cloud IAM policies are evaluated to find principals granted both `roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin` and `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` within a project. **Service-account related roles** are expected to be segregated so that service account lifecycle management is distinct from their use or impersonation.
gcp.iam_role_sa_enforce_separation_of_du.risk: With both roles, a principal can create or modify service accounts and then use or attach them to workloads, enabling unchecked impersonation. This endangers confidentiality (expanded data access), integrity (policy/workload changes), and availability (persistence or sabotage via privileged automation).

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Remove all project-level principals from Service Account User
resource "google_project_iam_binding" "sa_user_none" {
  project = "<example_resource_id>"
  role    = "roles/iam.serviceAccountUser"  # critical: target role to clear at project level
  members = []                                # critical: empty list removes the binding (no members)
}

# Remove all project-level principals from Service Account Admin
resource "google_project_iam_binding" "sa_admin_none" {
  project = "<example_resource_id>"
  role    = "roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin"  # critical: target role to clear at project level
  members = []                                 # critical: empty list removes the binding (no members)
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to IAM & Admin > IAM
2. Click the View by Role tab
3. Select the role Service Account Admin (roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin)
4. Remove all listed principals from this role and click Save
5. Select the role Service Account User (roles/iam.serviceAccountUser)
6. Remove all listed principals from this role and click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Enforce separation of duties: assign `roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin` for lifecycle tasks and `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` for attach/impersonate, never both to one principal.
- Apply **least privilege** with narrow scope and conditions
- Use temporary elevation/approvals
- Regularly audit IAM bindings and logs

gcp.iam_sa_no_administrative_privileges.title: Service account has no administrative privileges
gcp.iam_sa_no_administrative_privileges.description: Google Cloud service accounts with **high-privilege IAM roles** are identified, including `roles/owner`, `roles/editor`, or any role containing `admin`. The evaluation looks for service accounts bound to these roles in IAM policies across the project hierarchy.
gcp.iam_sa_no_administrative_privileges.risk:
Over-privileged service accounts jeopardize the CIA triad:
- Confidentiality: data can be read and exfiltrated
- Integrity: configs, IAM, and code can be altered
- Availability: resources can be deleted or halted

Compromise via key theft or impersonation enables lateral movement and persistence.

remediation.other:
1. In the Google Cloud console, go to IAM & Admin > IAM
2. Select the project (or switch to the folder/organization) where the role is granted
3. Find the service account by email and click Edit principal
4. Remove roles: Owner, Editor, and any role with "Admin" in the name
5. Click Save
6. Repeat at folder/organization level if the role was inherited
remediation.recommendationText: Apply **least privilege**: replace `roles/owner`, `roles/editor`, and roles containing `admin` with narrowly scoped predefined or custom roles. Use **separation of duties**, **temporary elevation**, and **IAM Conditions** to limit scope and time. Prefer **impersonation** over long-lived keys and monitor SA usage.

gcp.iam_sa_no_user_managed_keys.title: Service account has no user-managed keys
gcp.iam_sa_no_user_managed_keys.description: **IAM service accounts** do not have keys of type `USER_MANAGED`; only Google-managed keys (or no keys) are present.
gcp.iam_sa_no_user_managed_keys.risk: **User-managed keys** are downloadable and long-lived, increasing theft and reuse risk. An attacker with a key can impersonate the service account, perform unauthorized API calls, exfiltrate data, and alter resources, impacting **confidentiality** and **integrity**, and potentially **availability**. Copies in repos or logs can evade centralized rotation and revocation.

remediation.other:
1. In the Google Cloud console, go to IAM & Admin > Service Accounts
2. Select your project and click the affected service account
3. Open the Keys tab
4. For each key with Type "User-managed", click Delete and confirm
5. Verify no User-managed keys remain for that service account
6. Repeat for any other affected service accounts
remediation.recommendationText: Avoid **user-managed keys**. Use **service account impersonation** or **Workload Identity Federation** for short-lived credentials and **least privilege**. Enforce `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`, restrict who can create keys, and monitor usage. *If exceptions are unavoidable*, tightly scope, rotate aggressively, and store keys securely.

gcp.iam_sa_user_managed_key_rotate_90_da.title: Service account user-managed key has been rotated within the last 90 days
gcp.iam_sa_user_managed_key_rotate_90_da.description: **GCP IAM service account user-managed keys** are evaluated by last rotation. Keys of type `USER_MANAGED` older than `90` days are identified; those rotated within `90` days align with the expected rotation cadence.
gcp.iam_sa_user_managed_key_rotate_90_da.risk: **Stale service account keys** extend exposure of **long-lived credentials**. A leaked or retained key can grant persistent API access, enabling **data exfiltration**, tampering, and lateral movement. Weak rotation reduces revocation effectiveness and erodes **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to IAM & Admin > Service Accounts
2. Open the service account, then go to the Keys tab
3. If the workload still needs a key: click Add key > Create new key (JSON), download it, and update the workload to use it
4. Delete the user-managed key(s) older than 90 days by clicking Delete next to each
5. Re-run the check to confirm only recent keys remain
remediation.recommendationText:
Rotate **user-managed keys** at least every `90` days and prefer **Workload Identity Federation** or other short-lived credentials over static keys.
- Minimize key count; remove unused keys
- Enforce **least privilege** on service accounts
- Automate rotation and alert on aged keys
- Set key expiry as **defense in depth**

gcp.iam_sa_user_managed_key_unused.title: User-managed service account key was used within the allowed inactivity period
gcp.iam_sa_user_managed_key_unused.description: **User-managed service account keys** with no recorded activity during the last `max_unused_account_days` are identified using key-usage metrics per service account.
gcp.iam_sa_user_managed_key_unused.risk: **Stale user-managed keys** expand exposure of long-lived credentials. If leaked, an attacker can authenticate as the service account off-platform, bypass network controls, access data, alter resources, and persist-compromising confidentiality and integrity, and risking availability via destructive changes.

remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to IAM & Admin > Service Accounts
2. Select your project and click the service account with the unused user-managed key
3. Open the Keys tab
4. Find the unused key (Type: User-managed), click Delete, and confirm
remediation.recommendationText: Prefer **managed workload identities** and **service account impersonation** over user-managed keys. Enforce `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`, remove unused keys, and use short key lifetimes with rotation when unavoidable. Apply **least privilege**, monitor key usage, and enforce **separation of duties** to limit blast radius.

gcp.iam_service_account_unused.title: Service account was used within the configured maximum unused period
gcp.iam_service_account_unused.description:
Google Cloud service accounts are evaluated for **recent usage** within a configurable window (default `180` days) using usage telemetry.

It highlights which accounts show activity versus those with **no observed use** in that period.
gcp.iam_service_account_unused.risk:
Dormant but permissioned service accounts threaten **confidentiality** and **integrity** via:
- **Impersonation/privilege escalation** through stale roles or leaked keys
- **Lateral movement** and persistent access
They also weaken **accountability**, obscuring audit trails when reactivated unnoticed.

remediation.other:
1. In the Google Cloud console, open the IAM Service Account Credentials API reference for "GenerateAccessToken" and click "Try this method" (APIs Explorer)
2. Set name to: projects/-/serviceAccounts/<SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL>
3. Add scope: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform
4. Click Execute (use an identity with roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator on the service account)
5. The generated token records recent usage for the service account, changing the finding to PASS
remediation.recommendationText:
Apply **least privilege** and **reduce attack surface**:
- Verify inactivity, then *disable* and later delete unused accounts
- Revoke role bindings and keys; favor short-lived impersonation over keys
- Avoid powerful defaults; enforce separation of duties
- Continuously monitor usage and alert on dormancy

gcp.kms_key_not_publicly_accessible.title: Cloud KMS key has no public IAM access
gcp.kms_key_not_publicly_accessible.description:
**Cloud KMS crypto keys** are evaluated for **public principals** in their IAM bindings, specifically `allUsers` and `allAuthenticatedUsers`.

The finding reflects whether these memberships are present on a key.
gcp.kms_key_not_publicly_accessible.risk:
Granting **public principals** access lets anyone on the Internet or any Google account use permissions on the key.
- **Confidentiality** loss via unauthorized `decrypt`
- **Integrity** compromise via illicit `sign`
- **Availability** impact from disable, rotation, or destruction

remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to Security > Key Management > Key rings
2. Open the key ring, then select the affected key
3. Click the Permissions tab
4. Remove principals "allUsers" and "allAuthenticatedUsers" from all roles
5. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Remove `allUsers` and `allAuthenticatedUsers` from key IAM. Grant access only to specific groups or service accounts with **least privilege** at the key scope. Enforce **separation of duties** between admins and users, and regularly review inherited bindings and audit logs.

gcp.kms_key_rotation_enabled.title: KMS key is rotated at least annually
gcp.kms_key_rotation_enabled.description:
Google Cloud KMS customer-managed keys have **automatic rotation** enabled or a rotation interval  `365` days.

The evaluation reviews each key's rotation settings to confirm periodic creation of new key versions.
gcp.kms_key_rotation_enabled.risk: Without timely rotation, a stolen key can decrypt an expanding volume of data, eroding **confidentiality**. Prolonged key lifetimes widen windows for misuse, impact **integrity** of protected workloads, and make emergency rollover harder, risking **availability** disruptions.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "google_kms_crypto_key" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name     = "<example_resource_name>"
  key_ring = "<example_resource_id>"
  purpose  = "ENCRYPT_DECRYPT"

  rotation_period = "31536000s" # Critical: sets automatic rotation to 365 days (<= 365 ensures PASS)
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to Security > Key Management > Key rings
2. Open the key ring and select the key
3. Click Edit rotation schedule (or Set rotation schedule)
4. Set Rotation period to 365 days or less
5. Set Next rotation date/time
6. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable **auto-rotation** for customer-managed keys with an interval  `365` days.

Adopt a **key lifecycle** policy: enforce **least privilege** on key usage, apply **separation of duties** between key admins and users, monitor key access, and rehearse emergency rotation to minimize blast radius.

gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.title: Log metric filter for audit configuration changes has an associated alert policy
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.description: **Cloud Logging** log-based metrics capture **audit configuration changes** (e.g., `SetIamPolicy` with `auditConfigDeltas`), and an associated **Cloud Monitoring alert policy** notifies when such log entries occur.
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.risk: Unmonitored **Audit Config** changes can reduce or disable **Admin Activity/Data Access** logging, creating blind spots. Adversaries could suppress evidence, evade detection, and alter permissions unnoticed, degrading **confidentiality**, **integrity**, and the **availability** of forensic telemetry.

remediation.other:
1. In Cloud Console, go to Logging > Logs-based metrics and click Create metric
2. Set Metric type to Counter, Name to <example_resource_name>, and Filter to:
   protoPayload.methodName="SetIamPolicy" AND protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.auditConfigDeltas:*
3. Save the metric
4. Go to Monitoring > Alerting > Create policy > Add condition
5. Select Metric as the condition type, then choose metric: logging.googleapis.com/user/<example_resource_name>
6. Set condition to is above 0 for 1 minute and click Done
7. Name the policy and click Create (notification channels are optional for this check)
remediation.recommendationText:
Create a log-based metric for **audit configuration changes** and pair it with a **log-based alert policy** that notifies responders.
- Enforce **least privilege** on logging/IAM changes
- Apply **change control** and **separation of duties**
- Route alerts to durable channels and include response runbooks for **defense in depth**

gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.title: Log metric filter for Cloud Storage IAM permission changes has an associated alert policy
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.description: **Cloud Logging** defines a log-based metric for **Cloud Storage IAM changes** using filter `resource.type="gcs_bucket" AND protoPayload.methodName="storage.setIamPermissions"`, and a **Cloud Monitoring alert policy** that references that metric.
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.risk:
Lack of alerting on bucket IAM changes degrades **confidentiality and integrity**. Adversaries or misconfigurations can:
- grant broad/public access
- persist access by adding roles
- read, alter, or delete data
Delays in detection enable **data exfiltration**, tampering, and disruptive actions.

remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud console, go to Logging > Logs-based metrics
2. Click Create metric
3. Name: <example_resource_name>
4. In Filter, paste: resource.type="gcs_bucket" AND protoPayload.methodName="storage.setIamPermissions"
5. Click Create
6. In the metrics list, click the three dots for the new metric and select Create alert from metric
7. Keep condition as Count > 0 for Most recent value and click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Establish a **log-based metric** for bucket IAM permission changes with filter `resource.type="gcs_bucket" AND protoPayload.methodName="storage.setIamPermissions"` and link a **log-based alert policy** with clear notifications. Enforce **least privilege** and **separation of duties**, and routinely review alerts and audit logs to prevent and contain unauthorized access.

gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.title: Compute Engine configuration changes are monitored with log metric filters and alerts
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.description: Log metric filters and alerts for **Compute Engine configuration changes** provide visibility into modifications to instances, disks, networks, firewalls, and routes. These monitoring controls enable security teams to detect unauthorized changes and investigate suspicious infrastructure modifications.
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.risk: Without monitoring for Compute Engine configuration changes, **unauthorized modifications** may go undetected. Attackers can establish **persistence**, escalate privileges, disable security controls, or pivot to other resources, compromising **confidentiality**, **integrity**, and **availability** of workloads.

remediation.cli: gcloud logging metrics create compute_config_changes --description="Compute Engine configuration changes" --log-filter='protoPayload.serviceName="compute.googleapis.com"' && gcloud alpha monitoring policies create --notification-channels=CHANNEL_ID --display-name="Compute Engine Configuration Changes Alert" --condition-threshold-value=1 --condition-threshold-duration=0s --condition-filter='metric.type="logging.googleapis.com/user/compute_config_changes"'
remediation.other:
1. Open the Google Cloud Console
2. Navigate to Logging > Logs-based Metrics
3. Click 'Create Metric'
4. Set Metric Type to 'Counter'
5. Enter filter: protoPayload.serviceName="compute.googleapis.com"
6. Click 'Create Metric'
7. Navigate to Monitoring > Alerting
8. Click 'Create Policy'
9. Click 'Add Condition'
10. Select your log metric in the metric dropdown
11. Set threshold and conditions
12. Add notification channels
13. Click 'Save'
remediation.recommendationText: Configure log-based metric filters to detect Compute Engine configuration changes and create alert policies that trigger notifications when these metrics increment. Apply the **principle of least privilege** to limit who can modify compute resources, and establish **change management processes** to review and approve infrastructure modifications.

gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.title: Log metric filter for IAM custom role changes has an associated alert policy
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.description: Cloud projects are assessed for log-based metrics that filter `resource.type="iam_role"` and the methods `CreateRole`, `DeleteRole`, `UpdateRole`, and for an associated Cloud Monitoring **alert policy** that references those metrics.
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.risk: Without alerts on custom role changes, privilege modifications can go unnoticed, enabling **privilege escalation**, unauthorized data access (confidentiality), permission tampering (integrity), and accidental revocations that disrupt services (availability). Insider misuse or compromised admins can silently reshape access across projects.

remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to Logging > Logs-based metrics
2. Click Create metric (Counter), set Name to <example_resource_name>
3. In Filter, paste exactly: resource.type="iam_role" AND (protoPayload.methodName="google.iam.admin.v1.CreateRole" OR protoPayload.methodName="google.iam.admin.v1.DeleteRole" OR protoPayload.methodName="google.iam.admin.v1.UpdateRole") and Save
4. Go to Monitoring > Alerting > Create policy
5. Add Condition > Metric
6. For Metric, search and select logging.googleapis.com/user/<example_resource_name>
7. Set threshold > 0 and duration 0 min (or 0s), then Save the policy
remediation.recommendationText:
Define log-based metrics capturing `resource.type="iam_role"` events for `CreateRole`, `DeleteRole`, and `UpdateRole`, and attach **alert policies** to notify responders.

Enforce **least privilege**, **separation of duties**, and **change control** for role management, and retain **audit logs** for investigation.

gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.title: Log metric filter for project ownership assignments/changes has an associated alert policy
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.description: Cloud Logging contains a **log-based metric** targeting project ownership changes in Cloud Resource Manager events, and Cloud Monitoring has an **alerting policy** tied to that metric. It detects metrics matching `roles/owner` additions/removals or ownership invites, and whether an alert references that metric.
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.risk: Lack of alerts on ownership changes enables **privilege escalation** and **project takeover**. Attackers can add/remove `roles/owner`, causing unauthorized data access (confidentiality), unauthorized config/billing changes (integrity), and resource deletion or lockout (availability) without timely detection.

remediation.other:
1. In the Google Cloud console, go to Logging > Logs-based metrics and click Create metric
2. Set Name to <example_resource_name>
3. In Filter, paste:
   (protoPayload.serviceName="cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com") AND (ProjectOwnership OR projectOwnerInvitee) OR (protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas.action="REMOVE" AND protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas.role="roles/owner") OR (protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas.action="ADD" AND protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas.role="roles/owner")
4. Click Create
5. Go to Monitoring > Alerting > Create policy > Add condition
6. Choose Metric, then select metric type logging.googleapis.com/user/<example_resource_name>
7. Set condition to Greater than 0 with a duration of 0 minutes, then click Add
8. Click Create policy (notification channels optional)
9. Verify the alert condition filter contains <example_resource_name>
remediation.recommendationText: Create a log-based metric for ownership assignment/removal events and link it to an alerting policy that notifies a monitored channel. Minimize use of `roles/owner` per **least privilege**, require approvals and separation of duties, and apply **defense in depth** with centralized monitoring of IAM changes across projects.

gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.title: Log metric filter for Cloud SQL instance configuration changes has an associated alert policy
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.description: **Cloud Logging** has a log-based metric matching Cloud SQL instance updates (`protoPayload.methodName="cloudsql.instances.update"`) and a **Cloud Monitoring** alert policy references that metric to notify on configuration changes.
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.risk: Without this visibility, **unauthorized or accidental Cloud SQL configuration changes** can persist undetected. Attackers or insiders might open public access, relax TLS, alter authorized networks, or disable backups, degrading **confidentiality**, **integrity**, and **availability** and delaying containment.

remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud console, go to Logging > Logs-based metrics and click Create metric
2. Set Name to <example_resource_name> and Filter to: protoPayload.methodName="cloudsql.instances.update" then click Create
3. Go to Monitoring > Alerting > Create policy
4. Click Add condition > Metric
5. For Metric, select logging.googleapis.com/user/<example_resource_name>
6. Set threshold to Greater than 0 over 0 minutes and click Add
7. Click Save policy
remediation.recommendationText: Implement a **log-based metric** for Cloud SQL update events and attach a **Monitoring alert policy** that routes timely notifications. Apply **least privilege** for admin actions, enforce **change management** and **separation of duties**, and integrate alerts with on-call workflows to speed triage and prevent misconfigurations.

gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.title: Log metric filter for VPC network firewall rule changes has an associated alert policy
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.description: Cloud Logging has a log-based metric for **VPC firewall rule** changes, matching `resource.type="gce_firewall_rule"` and `protoPayload.methodName` of `compute.firewalls.insert`, `compute.firewalls.patch`, or `compute.firewalls.delete`, and Cloud Monitoring includes an alerting policy that references this metric.
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.risk:
Without alerts on firewall rule changes, unauthorized or accidental modifications can go unnoticed, exposing services or blocking critical traffic.

Confidentiality suffers (opened ports), integrity is reduced (tampered controls), and availability can be impacted (outages), enabling lateral movement and data exfiltration.

remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to Logging > Logs-based metrics
2. Click Create metric, set Name to <example_resource_name>
3. In Filter, paste: resource.type="gce_firewall_rule" AND (protoPayload.methodName:"compute.firewalls.patch" OR protoPayload.methodName:"compute.firewalls.insert" OR protoPayload.methodName:"compute.firewalls.delete")
4. Save the metric
5. Go to Monitoring > Alerting > Create policy
6. Add Condition > Metric threshold
7. For Metric, select User-defined and choose logging.googleapis.com/user/<example_resource_name>
8. Set condition to > 0 with duration 0 minutes (or the minimum allowed)
9. Create the policy (notification channels are optional)
remediation.recommendationText:
Establish a log-based metric for `gce_firewall_rule` insert/patch/delete events and tie it to an alerting policy that notifies responders.

Enforce **least privilege** and change control on firewall updates, apply **separation of duties**, and monitor all projects for rapid, auditable detection of network control changes.

gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.title: Log metric filter for VPC network changes has an associated alert policy
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.description:
Cloud projects are evaluated for a **log-based metric** with a linked **Cloud Monitoring alert** that targets **VPC network changes** on `gce_network` audit events: `compute.networks.insert`, `patch`, `delete`, `addPeering`, `removePeering`.

It checks that these changes are captured and generate notifications.
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.risk:
Missing alerts on VPC changes lets **unauthorized or accidental modifications** go unnoticed, risking:
- Data exposure via unintended peering or new networks
- Segmentation bypass through routing/subnet edits
- Outages from deletions or misconfigurations

This affects confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

remediation.other:
1. In the Google Cloud Console, go to Logging > Logs-based metrics > + Create metric
2. Name: <example_resource_name>
3. In Filter, paste exactly:
   resource.type="gce_network" AND (protoPayload.methodName:"compute.networks.insert" OR protoPayload.methodName:"compute.networks.patch" OR protoPayload.methodName:"compute.networks.delete" OR protoPayload.methodName:"compute.networks.removePeering" OR protoPayload.methodName:"compute.networks.addPeering")
4. Click Create metric
5. Go to Monitoring > Alerting > + Create policy > Add condition
6. Select the metric logging.googleapis.com/user/<example_resource_name>
7. Condition: Greater than, Threshold: 0, For: 0 minutes; click Add
8. Name the policy and click Create policy
remediation.recommendationText:
Implement a **log-based metric** for VPC change audit events and attach an **alerting policy** that notifies accountable teams.

Apply **least privilege** for network admins, enforce **change approval**, and adopt **defense in depth** to prevent and quickly detect unintended network changes.

gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.title: Log metric filter for VPC network route changes has an associated alert policy
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.description:
**Cloud Logging** includes a **log-based metric** for **VPC route modifications** and a linked **Cloud Monitoring alert**.

It targets `gce_route` entries for `compute.routes.insert` and `compute.routes.delete` so route creations or deletions generate alertable signals.
gcp.logging_log_metric_filter_and_alert_.risk:
Without visibility into **route changes**, attackers or mistakes can:
- Reroute traffic to bypass inspection  **data exfiltration** (confidentiality)
- Alter paths enabling **lateral movement** (integrity)
- Blackhole networks causing **outages** (availability)

remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to Logging > Logs-based metrics and click Create metric
2. Set Name to <example_resource_name>
3. In Filter, paste: resource.type="gce_route" AND (protoPayload.methodName:"compute.routes.delete" OR protoPayload.methodName:"compute.routes.insert")
4. Click Create metric
5. Go to Monitoring > Alerting > Create policy
6. Add Condition: Metric threshold; Select metric logging.googleapis.com/user/<example_resource_name>; Set condition to > 0 for 0 minutes
7. Click Create policy (skip notification channels if not needed)
remediation.recommendationText:
Create a **log-based metric** for `compute.routes.insert` and `compute.routes.delete`, and attach a **log-based alert** with reliable notifications.

Apply **least privilege** to route management, require **change approval**, and use **defense in depth** (egress filtering, private routing, durable audit logs).

gcp.logging_sink_created.title: Project has at least one logging sink exporting copies of all log entries
gcp.logging_sink_created.description: **Cloud Logging** project contains at least one **sink** that exports a copy of **all log entries** to a destination for centralized retention or processing
gcp.logging_sink_created.risk: Without exporting all logs, audit evidence can expire or be altered in-project, reducing the **availability** and **integrity** of telemetry. This hinders threat detection and forensics, prevents cross-project correlation, and can let attacker actions evade scrutiny after log rotation or deletion.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
# Create a project-level logging sink exporting all logs
resource "google_logging_project_sink" "sink" {
  name        = "<example_resource_name>" # critical: creates the sink required by the check
  destination = "logging.googleapis.com/projects/<example_resource_id>" # critical: required destination
  # No filter set -> exports all log entries (fixes the finding)
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to Logging > Log Router
2. Click Create sink
3. Set Sink name to <example_resource_name>
4. For Sink destination, select Google Cloud project and choose <example_resource_id>
5. Leave the inclusion filter empty (exports all logs)
6. Click Create
remediation.recommendationText: Create a **centralized export sink** that routes all logs to a secured, durable, preferably **immutable** destination with extended retention. Apply **least privilege** to sink identities, separate duties by isolating destinations, use **defense in depth** (encryption, access controls), and monitor sink health for continuity.

github.githubactions_workflow_security_s.title: GitHub Actions workflows have no security issues detected by zizmor
github.githubactions_workflow_security_s.description: Scan GitHub Actions workflow files for security issues such as template injection, excessive permissions, unpinned actions, and other misconfigurations using the zizmor static analysis tool.
github.githubactions_workflow_security_s.risk: Insecure GitHub Actions workflows can lead to supply chain attacks, credential theft, code injection, and unauthorized access to repository secrets.

remediation.other: Review and fix the security issues identified by zizmor in your GitHub Actions workflow files.
remediation.recommendationText: Review your GitHub Actions workflows for security best practices including pinning actions to commit SHAs, using minimal permissions, avoiding template injection, and securing workflow triggers.

github.githubactions_workflow_security_s.notes: This check requires zizmor to be installed. If zizmor is not available, the check will be skipped gracefully.

github.organization_default_repository_p.title: Organization base repository permission is read or none
github.organization_default_repository_p.description: **GitHub organization** base repository permission for members uses a **strict setting** such as `read` or `none` rather than permissive options like `write` or `admin`. *Applies to members, not outside collaborators.*
github.organization_default_repository_p.risk:
**Excessive default permissions** (`write`/`admin`) erode code **integrity** and **availability**.

Any member-or a compromised account-can alter many repos, inject malicious commits, change tags/releases, or delete branches, enabling supply-chain compromise and large-scale disruptions.

remediation.other:
1. Sign in to GitHub as an organization owner
2. Go to the organization > Settings
3. Under "Access" in the sidebar, click "Member privileges"
4. Under "Base permissions", select "Read" (or "None")
5. Click "Change default permission" to confirm
remediation.recommendationText:
Apply **least privilege**: set base permission to `none` or `read`.

Grant higher access explicitly via teams per repo and enforce **separation of duties** with required reviews and **branch protection**. Regularly audit memberships and access to limit blast radius and maintain **defense in depth**.

github.organization_members_mfa_required.title: Organization requires members to have two-factor authentication enabled
github.organization_members_mfa_required.description:
GitHub organization settings require all members to use **two-factor authentication** (2FA).

The evaluation determines whether access to organization resources is conditioned on members having 2FA enabled.
github.organization_members_mfa_required.risk:
Without enforced **2FA**, stolen or reused passwords enable account takeover, leading to:
- Loss of code integrity via unauthorized commits
- Confidential data exposure from repos and secrets
- Availability impact from settings changes, token revocation, or deletions

remediation.other:
1. Sign in to GitHub as an organization owner with 2FA enabled
2. Go to your organization > Settings
3. In the left sidebar, click Security > Authentication security
4. Under Two-factor authentication, select Require two-factor authentication for everyone in your organization
5. Click Save, then Confirm
remediation.recommendationText:
Enforce org-wide **2FA** for all members and collaborators, preferring **secure methods** (passkeys, security keys, authenticator apps, GitHub Mobile) over SMS.

Apply **least privilege**, integrate with **SSO**, restrict token scopes, and use **branch protection** for defense-in-depth. Include bots/service accounts and define recovery options.

github.organization_repository_creation_.title: Organization repository creation is limited to trusted members
github.organization_repository_creation_.description: **GitHub organization** repository creation is restricted so that only trusted owners or specific teams can create new repositories within the organization.
github.organization_repository_creation_.risk: **Excessive default permissions** (`write`/`admin`) erode code **integrity** and **availability**.Any member-or a compromised account-can alter many repos, inject malicious commits, change tags/releases, or delete branches, enabling supply-chain compromise and large-scale disruptions.

remediation.other:
1. Sign in to GitHub as an organization owner
2. Go to your organization > Settings
3. In the left sidebar, click "Access" > "Member privileges"
4. Under "Repository creation", select "Restrict repository creation"
5. Click "Save"
remediation.recommendationText: Disable repository creation for members or limit it to specific trusted teams by adjusting **Member privileges** in the organization's settings.

github.organization_repository_deletion_.title: Organization repository deletion and transfer is restricted to owners
github.organization_repository_deletion_.description: Ensure repository deletion/transfer is restricted so only trusted organization users (owners) can delete or transfer repositories.
github.organization_repository_deletion_.risk: If members can delete or transfer repositories, accidental or malicious deletions can cause irreversible data loss, service disruption, and increased blast radius from compromised accounts.

remediation.other:
1. Sign in to GitHub as an organization owner
2. Go to Organization > Settings
3. Under "Access", click "Member privileges"
4. Disable "Allow members to delete or transfer repositories"
5. Save changes
remediation.recommendationText: Disable member repository deletion/transfer privileges so only organization owners can delete or transfer repositories.

github.organization_verified_badge.title: Organization has a verified badge
github.organization_verified_badge.risk: **Unverified organizations** may be easier to impersonate, increasing the risk of phishing or trust abuse.

remediation.other:
1. Sign in to GitHub as an organization owner
2. Go to your organization > Settings
3. In the left sidebar, click "Verification"
4. Click "Verify"
remediation.recommendationText: Verify the organization identity by completing **GitHub organization verification**.

github.organization_verified_badge.notes: This check uses the GitHub API field is_verified from organization metadata.

github.repository_branch_delete_on_merge.title: Repository deletes branches after pull request merge
github.repository_branch_delete_on_merge.description: **GitHub repository** setting that enables **automatic deletion of head branches** when pull requests merge into the default branch (`delete_branch_on_merge`).
github.repository_branch_delete_on_merge.risk: Without automatic deletion, merged branches persist, weakening **integrity** and **confidentiality**: outdated code may be reused, secret remnants can linger, and reviews become ambiguous. Stale refs can still trigger CI with obsolete workflows, raising risks of supply-chain tampering and faulty deployments.

remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, open the repository and click Settings
2. Under General, scroll to Pull Requests
3. Check Automatically delete head branches
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable **automatic head-branch deletion** after merges to minimize stale refs and confusion.
- Enforce **least privilege** for branch creation
- Apply **branch protection** and rulesets
- Prefer short-lived feature branches with periodic pruning
- Guard CI to avoid runs from obsolete branches

github.repository_default_branch_deletio.title: Repository denies default branch deletion
github.repository_default_branch_deletio.description: **GitHub repository default branch** have **branch protections** or **rulesets** with `Allow deletions` disabled.
github.repository_default_branch_deletio.risk:
Permitting default branch deletion undermines **availability** by breaking CI/CD, releases, and PR targets.

It also impacts **integrity**: the canonical ref can be removed, enabling history tampering, branch hijacking, and harder audits/rollbacks.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "github_branch_protection_v3" "<example_resource_name>" {
  repository_id    = "<example_resource_name>"
  pattern          = "<default_branch>"
  allows_deletions = false  # Critical: disables deletion of the default branch
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, open the repository and go to Settings > Branches
2. Edit the branch protection rule for the default branch (or Add rule if none exists)
3. Ensure "Allow deletions" is unchecked
4. Click Save changes
remediation.recommendationText: Disable deletions on the **default branch** using **branch protection** or **rulesets** (`Allow deletions=false`). Apply controls to admins, minimize bypass lists, and enforce **least privilege**. Combine with required pull requests and status checks for **defense in depth**.

github.repository_default_branch_disallo.title: Repository default branch denies force pushes
github.repository_default_branch_disallo.description:
**GitHub repository default branch** blocks **force pushes** through branch protection.

Evaluates whether the default branch permits force pushes.
github.repository_default_branch_disallo.risk: Allowing **force pushes on the default branch** erodes **integrity** and **auditability** by enabling history rewrites and deletion of commits. Attackers or insiders can inject unreviewed code, bypass reviews and status checks, and corrupt PRs, risking supply-chain compromise and reduced **availability**.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "github_branch_protection_v3" "<example_resource_name>" {
  repository_id       = "<example_resource_id>"
  pattern             = "<default_branch_name>"

  allows_force_pushes = false # Critical: disallows force pushes on the default branch
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, open the repository and go to Settings
2. In the sidebar, click Branches
3. Edit the protection rule for the default branch (or Add rule with the default branch name)
4. Ensure Allow force pushes is unchecked/disabled
5. Click Save changes
remediation.recommendationText: Disable `Allow force pushes` on the default branch. Enforce PR-based changes with required reviews and status checks, require signed commits and linear history, and restrict bypass to minimal actors. Apply protections to admins too to uphold **least privilege** and **defense in depth**.

github.repository_default_branch_dismiss.title: Repository default branch dismisses stale pull request approvals
github.repository_default_branch_dismiss.description: GitHub repository default branch ensures that when new commits are pushed to an open pull request, any previously granted approvals are automatically dismissed, requiring fresh reviews before the pull request can be merged.
github.repository_default_branch_dismiss.risk: Without this setting, a contributor can receive approvals on a clean version of their code, then push malicious or unauthorized changes afterward. The pull request retains its approvals and can be merged without anyone reviewing the new changes, bypassing the entire code review process.

remediation.other: Using Rulesets (recommended): 1. Go to repository Settings > Rules > Rulesets. 2. Click 'New ruleset' > 'New branch ruleset' (or edit an existing one targeting the default branch). 3. Under 'Require a pull request before merging', enable 'Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed'. 4. Click 'Create' or 'Save changes'. Using classic branch protection: 1. Go to repository Settings > Branches. 2. Edit or add a branch protection rule for the default branch. 3. Under 'Require a pull request before merging', enable 'Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed'. 4. Click 'Save changes'.
remediation.recommendationText: Enable "Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed" in your branch protection rules. This ensures every code change undergoes a fresh review before merging.

github.repository_default_branch_protect.title: Repository default branch protection applies to administrators
github.repository_default_branch_protect.description: **GitHub repository default branch** applies **branch protection rules** to **administrators** via `enforce_admins`, holding admin pushes to the same requirements as other contributors (reviews, status checks, and push restrictions).
github.repository_default_branch_protect.risk: Without admin enforcement, privileged users can bypass reviews and checks, enabling **unauthorized code changes**. A compromised admin token can inject backdoors, alter dependencies, or disable safeguards, undermining **integrity**, exposing secrets (**confidentiality**), and causing outages (**availability**).

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "github_branch_protection_v3" "<example_resource_name>" {
  repository     = "<example_resource_name>"
  branch         = "<DEFAULT_BRANCH>"
  enforce_admins = true  # Critical: applies branch protection to administrators
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, go to the repository > Settings > Branches
2. Edit the branch protection rule that targets the default branch (or Add rule for <DEFAULT_BRANCH>)
3. Enable: "Do not allow bypassing the above settings" (or "Include administrators")
4. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **branch protection for administrators** and disallow bypasses. Apply **least privilege** and **separation of duties** by requiring PR reviews, required status checks, and signed commits on critical branches. Limit force pushes and deletions, and regularly review admin roles and audit logs.

github.repository_default_branch_protect.title: Repository enforces branch protection on the default branch
github.repository_default_branch_protect.description: **GitHub repository default branch** has **branch protection rules** enabled to restrict direct changes and require reviewed, validated merges. The evaluation determines whether the default branch enforces such rules.
github.repository_default_branch_protect.risk:
Without default-branch protection, changes can bypass reviews and checks, enabling:
- Unauthorized direct pushes/force pushes
- Malicious code injection and workflow tampering
- Accidental deletions or unstable releases
This undermines code **integrity** and service **availability**.

remediation.cli: gh api -X PUT repos/<OWNER>/<REPO>/branches/<DEFAULT_BRANCH>/protection -f required_status_checks='null' -f required_pull_request_reviews='null' -f enforce_admins=false -f restrictions='null'
remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, open the repository and go to Settings
2. Under "Code and automation", click Branches
3. Click Add rule under "Branch protection rules"
4. Set Branch name pattern to the default branch (e.g., main)
5. Click Create to save the rule
remediation.recommendationText:
Enforce **branch protection** on the default branch:
- Require pull requests with approvals (least privilege)
- Enforce required status checks and conversation resolution
- Require signed commits and linear history; block force pushes/deletions
- Restrict push to trusted actors and apply rules to admins
Use **CODEOWNERS** to strengthen review accountability.

github.repository_default_branch_require.title: Repository default branch requires code owner approval for changes to owned code
github.repository_default_branch_require.description: **GitHub repository default branch** requires **Code Owners** approval for pull requests that modify paths declared in `CODEOWNERS`
github.repository_default_branch_require.risk:
Without required **Code Owners** review, non-owners can merge changes to sensitive code, undermining **integrity**.
This increases the chance of **malicious code injection**, hidden backdoors, or fragile changes that enable **data exfiltration** or cause outages, impacting confidentiality and availability.

remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, open the repository and go to Settings > Branches
2. Edit the branch protection rule for <DEFAULT_BRANCH> (or click Add rule)
3. Set Branch name pattern to <DEFAULT_BRANCH>
4. Check Require a pull request before merging
5. Under Pull request reviews, check Require review from Code Owners
6. Click Create/Save to apply
remediation.recommendationText:
Enforce **Code Owners** review on the default branch and keep `CODEOWNERS` accurate and team-based.
Apply **least privilege**, require **status checks** and **signed commits**, extend protections to admins, and audit ownership regularly. Co-own critical paths to ensure coverage and reduce single-point approval gaps.

github.repository_default_branch_require.title: Repository default branch requires conversation resolution before merging
github.repository_default_branch_require.description: **GitHub repository default branch** uses **branch protection** to require **conversation resolution** on pull requests (`Require conversation resolution before merging`).
github.repository_default_branch_require.risk: Unresolved threads let code with known concerns reach default, weakening **integrity** and **confidentiality**. Insecure changes or secrets may ship, enabling injection, auth bypass, or data exposure. **Availability** can suffer from regressions; review accountability is reduced.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "github_branch_protection" "<example_resource_name>" {
  repository_id = "<example_resource_name>"
  pattern       = "<default_branch_name>"

  require_conversation_resolution = true # Critical: require all PR conversations to be resolved before merge
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, go to the repository > Settings
2. Click Branches
3. Edit the branch protection rule for the default branch (e.g., main)
4. Check "Require conversation resolution before merging"
5. Click Save changes
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable `Require conversation resolution before merging` on the default branch.

Also enforce:
- Required approvals and CI checks
- **CODEOWNERS** on critical paths
- **Least privilege** for merge rights
- Apply rules to admins to prevent bypass

github.repository_default_branch_require.title: Repository default branch requires linear history
github.repository_default_branch_require.description: **GitHub repository default branch** enforces `Require linear history`, blocking merge commits and allowing only `squash` or `rebase` merges
github.repository_default_branch_require.risk:
Without a **linear history**, commit provenance is harder to verify, weakening **integrity** and **accountability**.

Merge commits can obscure diffs entering the default branch, hindering audits and rollbacks, enabling unnoticed **malicious or unreviewed code**, and delaying incident response.

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "github_branch_protection" "<example_resource_name>" {
  repository_id          = "<example_repository_id>"
  pattern                = "<DEFAULT_BRANCH>"
  require_linear_history = true # Critical: enforces linear history on the default branch
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, go to the repository > Settings > Branches
2. If a rule exists for the default branch, click Edit; otherwise click Add rule and set Branch name pattern to the default branch (e.g., main)
3. Check Require linear history
4. Click Create (or Save changes)
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable `Require linear history` on the default branch and allow only `squash` or `rebase` merges.

Reinforce with **branch protection**: require pull requests and reviews, **status checks**, and **signed commits**. Limit bypass to trusted roles (least privilege) to preserve **traceability** and **defense in depth**.

github.repository_default_branch_require.title: Repository default branch requires at least 2 approvals for code changes
github.repository_default_branch_require.description:
**GitHub repository default branch** enforces **required reviews** with a minimum of `2` approving reviews before a pull request can be merged.

Assesses whether an approval threshold of at least `2` is configured for code changes targeting the default branch.
github.repository_default_branch_require.risk:
Without multi-review approval on the default branch, a single actor can merge changes, degrading **integrity** and **accountability**. This enables:
- supply-chain tampering or backdoors
- introduction of exploitable bugs
- bypass of change control via compromised accounts

remediation.cli: gh api -X PUT repos/<OWNER>/<REPO>/branches/<DEFAULT_BRANCH>/protection -F required_status_checks=null -F enforce_admins=false -F restrictions=null -F required_pull_request_reviews.required_approving_review_count=2
remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, open the repository and go to Settings > Branches
2. Under Branch protection rules, click Add rule (or Edit for the default branch rule)
3. Set Branch name pattern to the default branch (e.g., main)
4. Check Require a pull request before merging
5. Set Require approvals to 2
6. Click Create/Save to apply
remediation.recommendationText:
Enforce the **four-eyes principle** by requiring at least `2` approvals for merges to the default branch.

Strengthen with **separation of duties** using code owner reviews, dismiss stale approvals, apply protections to admins, and pair with required status checks for **defense in depth**.

github.repository_default_branch_require.title: Repository default branch requires signed commits
github.repository_default_branch_require.description: **GitHub repository default branch** enforces **signed and verified commits** (`Require signed commits`), allowing only commits with valid cryptographic signatures to be pushed or merged.
github.repository_default_branch_require.risk:
Without required signing, commit authorship can be spoofed and unverified changes added, impacting integrity.
- Backdoor injection
- History tampering and forged identities
- Release pipeline abuse and supply-chain compromise

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "github_branch_protection_v3" "<example_resource_name>" {
  repository = "<example_repository_name>"
  pattern    = "<default_branch_name>"

  required_signatures = true # Critical: Enforces signed commits on the default branch
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, go to the repository > Settings
2. Click Branches
3. Edit the rule for the default branch (or Add rule targeting the default branch name)
4. Check Require signed commits
5. Click Save changes
remediation.recommendationText:
Enforce `Require signed commits` on default and release branches.
- Standardize GPG/SSH/S/MIME for humans and bots
- Protect and rotate signing keys; least privilege on bypass
- Pair with required reviews and status checks for defense-in-depth

github.repository_default_branch_status_.title: Repository default branch requires status checks
github.repository_default_branch_status_.description: **GitHub repository default branch** uses **required status checks**, indicating whether merges are gated by successful check results on pull requests
github.repository_default_branch_status_.risk: Without required checks, unvetted commits can be merged, degrading code **integrity** and **availability**. Skipped or failing validations may introduce vulnerable dependencies, break builds, or allow malicious code, enabling supply-chain compromise and rapid propagation to production.

remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, go to the repository > Settings > Branches
2. Next to Branch protection rules, click Add rule (or Edit for the default branch rule)
3. Set Branch name pattern to your default branch (e.g., main)
4. Check Require status checks to pass before merging
5. In the list, select at least one check (e.g., your CI workflow)
6. Click Create (or Save changes)
remediation.recommendationText:
Enforce branch protection to require **status checks** on the default branch.
- Gate merges on build, tests, and security scans
- Use `require up-to-date` behavior to reduce integration risk
- Apply to admins and limit bypasses
- Combine with **least privilege** and required reviews for defense in depth

github.repository_dependency_scanning_en.title: Repository has package vulnerability scanning (Dependabot alerts) enabled
github.repository_dependency_scanning_en.description: **GitHub repositories** are assessed for **dependency vulnerability scanning** enabled via `Dependabot alerts`, which monitors the dependency graph for known vulnerable packages and versions.
github.repository_dependency_scanning_en.risk: Without automated scanning, known vulnerable dependencies may persist unnoticed, enabling supply-chain compromise. Exploits in third-party libraries can drive RCE, data theft, or build tampering, undermining confidentiality, integrity, and availability across code and CI/CD.

remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, open the target repository
2. Click Settings > Code security and analysis
3. Under Dependabot alerts, click Enable
4. Verify the toggle shows Enabled
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **dependency vulnerability scanning** with `Dependabot alerts` or an equivalent SCA tool across repositories. Apply **defense in depth**: keep manifests and lockfiles current, triage alerts quickly, use automated security updates with required reviews, and surface results in PR checks and notifications.

github.repository_has_codeowners_file.title: Repository has a CODEOWNERS file
github.repository_has_codeowners_file.description: GitHub repositories declare **code ownership** via a `CODEOWNERS` file mapping file patterns to users or teams. This evaluation checks whether such a file exists in standard locations (`/`, `.github/`, or `docs/`) to enable automatic reviewer assignment.
github.repository_has_codeowners_file.risk:
Missing `CODEOWNERS` undermines **integrity** and **separation of duties**:
- PRs can merge without accountable, domain reviews
- Critical paths risk unauthorized or low-quality changes
This raises **software supply chain** exposure, enabling code tampering, hidden backdoors, and unsafe config modifications.

remediation.cli: gh api -X PUT repos/<example_org_or_user>/<example_repo>/contents/.github/CODEOWNERS -f message='add CODEOWNERS' -f content="$(printf '* @<example_owner>\n' | base64 | tr -d '\n')"
remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "github_repository_file" "<example_resource_name>" {
  repository = "<example_repo>"
  file       = ".github/CODEOWNERS"  # Critical: creates the CODEOWNERS file so the check passes
  content    = "* @<example_owner>"   # Critical: minimal valid content so the file is recognized
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, open the target repository
2. Click Add file > Create new file
3. Set the filename to .github/CODEOWNERS
4. Add a single line: `* @<example_owner>`
5. Click Commit new file (commit to the default branch)
remediation.recommendationText: Define and maintain a `CODEOWNERS` file mapping sensitive paths to responsible teams or users, preferring teams for resilience. Combine with branch protections requiring code-owner reviews to enforce **separation of duties** and **least privilege**. Keep entries current and cover critical directories to avoid pattern gaps.

github.repository_immutable_releases_ena.title: Repository has immutable releases enabled
github.repository_immutable_releases_ena.description: **GitHub repository** has **immutable releases** enabled to prevent modification or replacement of published artifacts after publication. When enabled, release assets and binaries become tamper-proof, ensuring artifact integrity throughout the software supply chain.
github.repository_immutable_releases_ena.risk: If immutable releases are disabled, release assets can be tampered with after publication, allowing attackers to substitute malicious binaries and undermining supply chain integrity.

remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, open the repository and go to Settings > Code and automation > Releases
2. Under "Immutable releases", toggle the switch to On
3. Click Save
remediation.recommendationText: Enable **immutable releases** in the repository settings so release artifacts cannot be altered once published.

github.repository_inactive_not_archived.title: Repository is archived or active within the configured inactivity threshold
github.repository_inactive_not_archived.description: **GitHub repository** that remains **unarchived** and show no activity beyond a configured inactivity window (e.g., `180` days) are identified. The evaluation considers the most recent repository activity to surface long-idle codebases that are still unarchived.
github.repository_inactive_not_archived.risk: Unarchived, long-inactive repos expand attack surface. Stale code and dependencies can hide unpatched flaws; writable state enables **integrity** compromise via malicious commits or workflow abuse; exposed secrets threaten **confidentiality**. Attackers can leverage them for lateral movement and supply-chain tampering.

remediation.other:
1. Open the repository on GitHub
2. Click Settings
3. Scroll to Danger Zone
4. Click Archive this repository
5. Type the repository name and confirm by clicking I understand the consequences, archive this repository
remediation.recommendationText:
Adopt **lifecycle management**:
- Archive or delete repos no longer needed
- If retained, update dependencies, rotate secrets, disable unused workflows, and restrict writes under **least privilege**
- Define an inactivity policy (e.g., `180` days) with periodic reviews to prevent dormant, writable codebases

github.repository_public_has_securitymd_.title: Public repository has a SECURITY.md file
github.repository_public_has_securitymd_.description: **GitHub public repository** include a `SECURITY.md` policy file that tells researchers how to report vulnerabilities. The evaluation focuses on the presence of this file in public repositories.
github.repository_public_has_securitymd_.risk: Without **SECURITY.md**, reporters may use public issues or ad-hoc channels, causing premature disclosure or missed reports. This widens the exploit window and impacts **confidentiality** (leaked details), **integrity** (unauthorized changes), and **availability** (DoS from unpatched flaws).

remediation.terraform:
```hcl
resource "github_repository_file" "security_md" {
  repository = "<example_resource_name>"
  file       = ".github/SECURITY.md"  # Critical: ensures SECURITY.md exists in a recognized location
  content    = "Report vulnerabilities to security@example.com"  # Critical: creates the file so the check passes
}
```
remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, open the target repository
2. Click Security > Policy (under Reporting)
3. Click Start setup
4. Add minimal instructions (e.g., how to report vulnerabilities)
5. Click Commit changes to create SECURITY.md
remediation.recommendationText: Publish a clear `SECURITY.md` for each public repo or an org default. Include private reporting channels, optional encryption keys, scope/supported versions, disclosure timelines, and safe-harbor terms. Link to any bounty program and review regularly. Align with **accountability** and **defense in depth** principles.

github.repository_secret_scanning_enable.title: Repository has secret scanning enabled to detect sensitive data
github.repository_secret_scanning_enable.description: **GitHub repository** configuration for **secret scanning**-which detects secrets (API keys, tokens, passwords) in commits and Git history-is evaluated to determine if detection is active.
github.repository_secret_scanning_enable.risk:
Without **secret scanning**, exposed credentials can persist unnoticed, enabling:
- Unauthorized access to cloud and third-party services
- **Supply-chain compromise** via tampered pipelines
- Data exfiltration and repo takeover

This degrades **confidentiality** and **integrity**, and increases blast radius of a single leaked key.

remediation.cli: gh api -X PATCH repos/<OWNER>/<REPO> -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"security_and_analysis":{"secret_scanning":{"status":"enabled"}}}'
remediation.other:
1. In GitHub, open the target repository and go to Settings
2. In the left sidebar, click Code security and analysis
3. Under Secret scanning, click Enable (or set to Enabled)
4. Confirm if prompted
remediation.recommendationText:
Enable **secret scanning** (and **push protection** where available) across repositories.
- Store secrets in a dedicated **secrets manager**, never in code
- Define custom patterns and enable generic detection for org-specific secrets
- Rotate and revoke exposed credentials quickly
- Enforce **least privilege** and add **defense-in-depth** monitoring

googleworkspace.additionalservices_exter.title: Access to external Google Groups is off for everyone
googleworkspace.additionalservices_exter.description: The Additional Google services configuration **disables access to external Google Groups** for all users. This setting controls whether users can access groups created outside the organization from their Google Workspace account.
googleworkspace.additionalservices_exter.risk: When external Google Groups access is enabled, users can access and participate in groups created **outside the organization**, potentially exposing them to **phishing, social engineering, or data leakage** through unmanaged external group communications.

remediation.other:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace** > **Additional Google services**
3. Scroll down to **Google Groups**
4. Set it to **OFF for everyone**
5. Click **Save**
remediation.recommendationText: Disable access to **external Google Groups** for all users. If specific users require access to external groups, enable it by exception for those users or groups only.

googleworkspace.additionalservices_exter.notes: This check covers the 'Additional Google services > Google Groups' toggle, which is distinct from the 'Groups for Business' sharing settings covered by the groups service checks.

googleworkspace.calendar_external_invita.title: External invitation warnings are enabled for Google Calendar
googleworkspace.calendar_external_invita.description: The domain-wide Google Calendar configuration **warns users** when they invite guests from outside the organization to an event. This prompt gives users a chance to reconsider before sharing meeting details with external parties, reducing the likelihood of **accidental information disclosure** through calendar invitations.
googleworkspace.calendar_external_invita.risk: Without external invitation warnings, users may unintentionally include **external guests** in internal meetings, exposing **confidential meeting details**, agendas, and internal attendee lists to unauthorized parties. This is a common vector for inadvertent data leakage through everyday calendar actions.

remediation.other:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace** > **Calendar**
3. Click **Sharing settings**
4. Under **External invitations**, check **Warn users when inviting guests outside of the domain**
5. Click **Save**
remediation.recommendationText: Enable external invitation warnings so users are notified whenever a meeting invitation includes guests outside the organization. This simple prompt helps prevent accidental disclosure of meeting details to unintended recipients.

googleworkspace.calendar_external_sharin.title: External sharing for primary calendars is restricted to free/busy only
googleworkspace.calendar_external_sharin.description: The domain-wide default for primary calendars shares **only free/busy information** with external users. When external sharing is set to share full event details, sensitive information such as meeting titles, attendees, locations, and descriptions is exposed to users outside the organization.
googleworkspace.calendar_external_sharin.risk: Overly permissive external sharing of primary calendars exposes **sensitive meeting metadata** — titles, attendees, locations, and descriptions — to users outside the organization. This increases the risk of **information disclosure**, **social engineering**, and **targeted phishing** based on insights into organizational activities.

remediation.other:
